prompt: A team is reviewing a new Amazon Bedrock workload and wants AWS-curated best practices that are specific to generative AI (prompt engineering, RAG accuracy, responsible AI, model selection) rather than generic guidance. Which resource should they use?

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Config conformance packs
The AWS Well-Architected Framework six pillars only
The AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens

explanation: The Generative AI Lens extends the Well-Architected Framework with design principles and best practices tailored to GenAI workloads. Not "AWS Trusted Advisor": Trusted Advisor gives cost/security/limits checks, not GenAI architectural best practices. Not "AWS Config conformance packs": Config evaluates resource compliance against rules; it is not a source of GenAI design guidance. Not "The AWS Well-Architected Framework six pillars only": The core pillars are general-purpose; the GenAI-specific guidance lives in the Generative AI Lens. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A company wants to formally review a generative AI workload against AWS best practices, identify high-risk issues (HRIs), and produce an improvement plan. Which tool should they use?

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Artifact
AWS Well-Architected Tool with the Generative AI Lens applied
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards

explanation: The WA Tool runs a structured review against the framework and any selected lens, surfaces HRIs, and generates an improvement plan. Not "AWS Cost Explorer": Cost Explorer analyzes spend, not architectural risk. Not "AWS Artifact": Artifact provides compliance reports/agreements, not workload reviews. Not "Amazon CloudWatch dashboards": CloudWatch monitors runtime metrics; it does not perform architectural reviews or produce improvement plans. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A generative AI application sometimes receives more requests than the foundation model endpoint can serve, and the team wants the system to degrade gracefully rather than fail outright. Which Well-Architected pillar most directly addresses this design goal?

options.text: Sustainability
Cost Optimization
Reliability
Operational Excellence

explanation: Graceful degradation, failover, and handling throttling are Reliability-pillar concerns. Not "Sustainability": Sustainability targets environmental impact, not failure handling. Not "Cost Optimization": Cost Optimization is about spending efficiently, not resilience to load. Not "Operational Excellence": Operational Excellence covers run/observe/improve processes; resilient behavior under failure maps to Reliability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: To control generative AI inference spend, an architect routes simple prompts to a smaller model and reserves a larger model for complex prompts, and uses distillation to create cheaper task-specific models. Which Well-Architected pillar do these decisions primarily serve?

options.text: Reliability
Performance Efficiency
Cost Optimization
Security

explanation: Right-sizing model choice, prompt routing, and distillation to cut inference cost are Cost Optimization practices. Not "Reliability": Reliability is about resilience and recovery, not cost. Not "Performance Efficiency": Performance Efficiency is related (model selection) but the explicit goal here is reducing cost. Not "Security": Security covers protecting data and workloads, not spend. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A team is applying the Reliability pillar to a Bedrock-based application that calls foundation models. Which TWO patterns improve resilience to FM call failures and regional issues? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disable retries to reduce latency
Increase the model temperature to add response variety
Implement circuit breakers in an AWS Step Functions workflow that stop calling the FM when error rates spike
Configure cross-Region failover so requests shift to a healthy Region
Store all prompts in a single Amazon S3 bucket in one Region

explanation: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by halting calls to a failing dependency. Cross-Region failover keeps the workload available during a regional impairment. Not "Disable retries to reduce latency": Removing retries reduces, not improves, resilience to transient failures. Not "Increase the model temperature to add response variety": Temperature affects output randomness, not reliability. Not "Store all prompts in a single Amazon S3 bucket in one Region": A single-Region store is a single point of failure, the opposite of resilient design. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: When an FM call fails, a system returns a cheaper cached or templated response instead of erroring out, preserving a usable experience. What is this pattern called?

options.text: Provisioned throughput
Continued pre-training
Graceful degradation
Blue/green deployment

explanation: Falling back to a reduced-quality but functional response when a dependency fails is graceful degradation. Not "Provisioned throughput": Provisioned throughput reserves model capacity; it is not a fallback pattern. Not "Continued pre-training": That is a model-training technique, not a resilience pattern. Not "Blue/green deployment": Blue/green is a deployment-cutover strategy, unrelated to runtime fallback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A reviewer wants to ensure a GenAI workload encrypts data, enforces least-privilege access to models, and filters harmful content. Which Well-Architected pillar groups these concerns?

options.text: Reliability
Performance Efficiency
Security
Operational Excellence

explanation: Data protection, least-privilege IAM, and content safeguards (guardrails) are Security-pillar best practices. Not "Reliability": Reliability concerns availability and recovery, not access control and encryption. Not "Performance Efficiency": Performance Efficiency targets effective resource use, not protection. Not "Operational Excellence": Operational Excellence is about running and improving workloads, not data protection controls. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An ML platform team wants to standardize model versioning and tie model promotion into a CI/CD pipeline so deployments are repeatable and auditable. Which Well-Architected pillar does this best support, and with which service?

options.text: Reliability — using Amazon Route 53
Operational Excellence — using the SageMaker Model Registry in a CI/CD pipeline
Security — using AWS WAF
Cost Optimization — using AWS Budgets

explanation: Versioned model catalogs feeding CI/CD are an Operational Excellence practice; the Model Registry provides this. Not "Reliability — using Amazon Route 53": Route 53 is DNS/failover; it does not manage model versions or CI/CD. Not "Security — using AWS WAF": WAF protects web apps from exploits; it is unrelated to model versioning. Not "Cost Optimization — using AWS Budgets": Budgets track spend; they do not provide model versioning or deployment automation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A team wants to change which foundation model a production application uses without redeploying application code. Which AWS service enables this configuration-driven change, supporting the Operational Excellence pillar?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
AWS AppConfig
AWS CodeDeploy

explanation: AppConfig externalizes runtime configuration (such as the model ID) so it can change without a code deployment. Not "AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager": Patch Manager handles OS patching, unrelated to model selection. Not "Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput": Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity; it does not switch models via config. Not "AWS CodeDeploy": CodeDeploy automates deployments of new code/artifacts, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid here. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A sustainability-focused review of a GenAI workload asks the team to minimize the environmental impact of inference. Which action best aligns with the Sustainability pillar?

options.text: Duplicate the workload into every Region
Run idle GPU endpoints continuously to avoid cold starts
Always select the largest available model for every task
Choose the smallest model that meets accuracy needs and use managed, efficiently-utilized services

explanation: Right-sizing models and maximizing utilization of managed infrastructure reduces energy/resource consumption. Not "Duplicate the workload into every Region": Unnecessary global duplication increases resource consumption. Not "Run idle GPU endpoints continuously to avoid cold starts": Keeping idle accelerators running wastes resources. Not "Always select the largest available model for every task": Oversized models waste compute and energy, contradicting sustainability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: During a Well-Architected review, the WA Tool flags several "High Risk Issues" (HRIs) for a GenAI workload. What is the correct interpretation of an HRI?

options.text: An issue likely to have a significant negative impact that should be prioritized for remediation
A mandatory AWS service quota increase
A billing anomaly detected in Cost Explorer
A model hallucination logged at runtime

explanation: HRIs are the highest-priority findings the WA Tool surfaces for an improvement plan. Not "A mandatory AWS service quota increase": HRIs are risk findings, not quota requests. Not "A billing anomaly detected in Cost Explorer": HRIs come from the architectural review, not billing analysis. Not "A model hallucination logged at runtime": HRIs are review findings about design, not runtime model outputs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An architect wants to reduce p95 latency for a chat application by selecting an appropriately sized model and adding response caching for repeated prompts. Which pillar best describes this work?

options.text: Performance Efficiency
Reliability
Security
Sustainability

explanation: Selecting the right model and using caching to meet latency targets is core Performance Efficiency. Not "Reliability": Reliability addresses availability/recovery, not latency tuning. Not "Security": Security is unrelated to latency optimization. Not "Sustainability": While related, the explicit goal here is meeting performance targets, not environmental impact. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A company is building responsible-AI controls into a Bedrock workload during a Well-Architected review. Which TWO are appropriate Security/responsible-AI best practices? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disable encryption to speed up inference
Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block denied topics and filter harmful content
Grant the application a wildcard IAM policy for all Bedrock actions
Redact PII from source data before indexing it for retrieval
Log nothing to reduce storage costs

explanation: Guardrails enforce content policies, a key responsible-AI safeguard. Removing PII before use limits exposure of sensitive data, a Security best practice. Not "Disable encryption to speed up inference": Turning off encryption directly violates the Security pillar. Not "Grant the application a wildcard IAM policy for all Bedro…": Wildcard permissions violate least privilege. Not "Log nothing to reduce storage costs": Disabling audit logging undermines security and compliance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between the Well-Architected Framework and a Lens such as the Generative AI Lens?

options.text: A Lens extends the framework with domain-specific design principles and best practices for a particular workload type
A Lens is a billing construct that discounts the workload
A Lens is a runtime guardrail enforced by Bedrock
A Lens replaces the six pillars entirely for that workload

explanation: Lenses layer specialized guidance (e.g., GenAI, Serverless, ML) on top of the six general pillars. Not "A Lens is a billing construct that discounts the workload": Lenses are guidance, not pricing mechanisms. Not "A Lens is a runtime guardrail enforced by Bedrock": Lenses are review guidance, not enforced runtime controls. Not "A Lens replaces the six pillars entirely for that workload": Lenses augment, not replace, the core pillars. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A developer can invoke Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Cohere, AI21, Stability AI, and Amazon Nova/Titan models through one consistent interface. What does Amazon Bedrock provide to make this possible?

options.text: A single unified API to access multiple foundation models from different providers
Direct SSH access to each provider's servers
A separate SDK that must be installed per model provider
A requirement to self-host each model on Amazon EC2

explanation: Bedrock exposes one API surface (e.g., InvokeModel/Converse) across many providers' models. Not "Direct SSH access to each provider's servers": Bedrock is a fully managed service; you never access provider servers. Not "A separate SDK that must be installed per model provider": Bedrock's value is one API, not per-provider SDKs. Not "A requirement to self-host each model on Amazon EC2": Bedrock is serverless and managed; self-hosting is not required. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team enabled a foundation model in us-east-1 but gets an access error when calling the same model in eu-west-1. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Foundation models can only ever run in us-east-1
Model access in Amazon Bedrock is granted per Region and must be enabled in each Region
Provisioned Throughput is required before any Region works
The account must switch to a different AWS partition

explanation: Bedrock model access is a per-Region setting; enabling it in one Region does not enable it elsewhere. Not "Foundation models can only ever run in us-east-1": Models are available in many Regions; access is just granted per Region. Not "Provisioned Throughput is required before any Region works": On-demand access works once granted; the issue is the per-Region grant, not throughput. Not "The account must switch to a different AWS partition": Partitions are unrelated; this is a per-Region access grant. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: During peak load a single-Region Bedrock application is throttled ("Too many requests"). The team must raise throughput using the same model and same API with minimal operational overhead. What should they use?

options.text: Intelligent Prompt Routing across two different models
A cross-Region inference profile to distribute traffic across Regions in the geography
Provisioned Throughput sized for the peak
A custom Lambda that retries in another Region

explanation: Cross-Region inference profiles automatically route invocations across Regions to absorb spikes, with no code or model change. Not "Intelligent Prompt Routing across two different models": Prompt routing uses different models in a family; the requirement is the same model. Not "Provisioned Throughput sized for the peak": Provisioned Throughput suits steady high volume and adds cost for occasional peaks. Not "A custom Lambda that retries in another Region": A custom failover Lambda adds operational overhead vs the built-in profile. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A platform team wants to track and attribute Bedrock inference costs per internal team while using cross-Region inference. Which capability lets them tag usage for cost tracking?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput model units
System-defined inference profiles, which you create and tag yourself
Application inference profiles, which are user-created and support tagging for cost allocation
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection profiles

explanation: Application inference profiles are custom profiles you create and tag, enabling cost tracking; system-defined profiles are AWS-managed. Not "Provisioned Throughput model units": Model Units reserve capacity; they are not the per-team tagging mechanism for cross-Region inference. Not "System-defined inference profiles, which you create and t…": System-defined profiles are predefined by AWS and are not user-tagged; application profiles are the taggable, custom ones. Not "AWS Cost Anomaly Detection profiles": That detects spend anomalies; it does not create taggable inference routing profiles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An IAM policy must restrict a role so it can only invoke a specific application inference profile. Which condition key is appropriate?

options.text: bedrock:PromptRouterArn
bedrock:InferenceProfileArn
bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier
aws:SourceVpce

explanation: This condition key scopes access to a particular inference profile ARN. Not "bedrock:PromptRouterArn": That scopes access to a prompt router, not an inference profile. Not "bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier": That enforces guardrail usage, not inference-profile scoping. Not "aws:SourceVpce": That restricts by VPC endpoint, unrelated to inference profiles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company needs guaranteed, consistent model capacity for a high-volume production workload and predictable performance. Which Amazon Bedrock option fits best?

options.text: A cross-Region inference profile
Provisioned Throughput, which reserves capacity measured in Model Units
Intelligent Prompt Routing
On-demand inference only

explanation: Provisioned Throughput guarantees dedicated capacity (per Model Unit) for steady, predictable workloads. Not "A cross-Region inference profile": Profiles spread load but do not reserve guaranteed capacity per model unit. Not "Intelligent Prompt Routing": Prompt routing optimizes cost/quality across a family; it does not reserve capacity. Not "On-demand inference only": On-demand is convenient but does not guarantee reserved capacity at peak. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team wants to deploy and serve a custom model they fine-tuned in Amazon Bedrock. Which prerequisite must they satisfy to run inference on the customized model?

options.text: Nothing — fine-tuned models are always available on-demand for free
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the customized model
Convert the model to ONNX and host on EC2
Enable a cross-Region inference profile

explanation: Customized (fine-tuned) Bedrock models are served via Provisioned Throughput, which is required to host them. Not "Nothing — fine-tuned models are always available on-deman…": Custom models require Provisioned Throughput to serve, unlike base models on-demand. Not "Convert the model to ONNX and host on EC2": Bedrock manages serving; manual EC2 hosting is not the mechanism. Not "Enable a cross-Region inference profile": Profiles route base-model traffic; they are not the requirement for serving a custom model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An application receives a mix of trivial and complex prompts. The team wants to send easy prompts to a cheaper model and hard prompts to a stronger model in the same family, through one endpoint, to cut cost ~30% without losing quality. What should they use?

options.text: A cross-Region inference profile
Provisioned Throughput on the larger model
Two unrelated models with manual if/else in code
Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing (a prompt router)

explanation: A prompt router analyzes each prompt and routes to the best model within the same family via a single serverless endpoint, reducing cost. Not "A cross-Region inference profile": Profiles spread load across Regions; they do not route by prompt complexity. Not "Provisioned Throughput on the larger model": That reserves capacity but does not route by complexity or save cost on easy prompts. Not "Two unrelated models with manual if/else in code": Hand-rolled routing adds maintenance; the managed prompt router is the intended solution. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A configuration restricts which prompt router a role can invoke. Which IAM condition key applies?

options.text: bedrock:GuardrailVersion
bedrock:PromptRouterArn
bedrock:ModelId
bedrock:InferenceProfileArn

explanation: This condition key scopes invocation to a specific prompt router ARN. Not "bedrock:GuardrailVersion": That pins a guardrail version, unrelated to routers. Not "bedrock:ModelId": There is no router-scoping behavior in a plain model-id key for this purpose. Not "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": That scopes inference profiles, not prompt routers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A requirement for Intelligent Prompt Routing must be respected when configuring a router. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The router only works for embeddings models
The router requires Provisioned Throughput on both models
The router routes between two or more models from the same model family
The router can route between any models from any providers

explanation: Prompt routers operate within a single family (e.g., Anthropic, Llama, or Nova variants). Not "The router only works for embeddings models": Prompt routing targets text-generation models, not embeddings. Not "The router requires Provisioned Throughput on both models": Routing is serverless and does not mandate provisioned capacity. Not "The router can route between any models from any providers": Routing is constrained to one model family, not arbitrary cross-provider mixing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company has thousands of labeled prompt-and-response examples and wants the model to adapt to their specific task using that supervised data. Which Bedrock customization technique fits?

options.text: Model distillation
Retrieval-augmented generation
Continued pre-training (unsupervised on raw text)
Fine-tuning (supervised, using labeled examples)

explanation: Fine-tuning trains on labeled input/output pairs to specialize a model for a task. Not "Model distillation": Distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher to a smaller student; it is not the labeled-data adaptation described. Not "Retrieval-augmented generation": RAG augments prompts at inference time; it does not train the model. Not "Continued pre-training (unsupervised on raw text)": Continued pre-training uses unlabeled domain text, not labeled task examples. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company has a large corpus of unlabeled internal documents in a specialized domain and wants the base model to absorb domain knowledge and vocabulary. Which technique is most appropriate?

options.text: Distillation from a teacher model
Fine-tuning with labeled examples
Continued pre-training on the raw domain text (unsupervised)
Prompt engineering only

explanation: Continued pre-training ingests unlabeled domain data to build domain familiarity. Not "Distillation from a teacher model": Distillation compresses a model; it does not inject a new unlabeled domain corpus. Not "Fine-tuning with labeled examples": Fine-tuning needs labeled task pairs; here the data is unlabeled. Not "Prompt engineering only": Prompt engineering does not add domain knowledge to the model weights. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team wants a smaller, cheaper, faster model that mimics the behavior of a larger high-quality model on their task. Which approach does Amazon Bedrock offer for this?

options.text: Model distillation — train a smaller "student" model using outputs from a larger "teacher" model
Continued pre-training on raw data
Hybrid search
Provisioned Throughput

explanation: Distillation transfers a teacher model's behavior into a smaller student for lower cost/latency. Not "Continued pre-training on raw data": That broadens domain knowledge but does not compress a teacher into a student. Not "Hybrid search": Hybrid search is a retrieval technique, not a model-compression method. Not "Provisioned Throughput": That reserves capacity; it does not produce a smaller model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team wants to customize a foundation model while training only a small number of parameters to reduce cost, and to maintain several lightweight task variants on one base model. Which TWO parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques apply? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Full-parameter retraining of the entire base model
Switching to on-demand inference
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), which adds small trainable matrices into model layers
Adapters, which insert small trainable layers between frozen model layers
Increasing the temperature parameter

explanation: LoRA injects low-rank matrices so only a small set of parameters is trained, cutting cost. Adapter modules add a few trainable layers while the base model stays frozen, enabling multiple variants. Not "Full-parameter retraining of the entire base model": Full retraining is the opposite of parameter-efficient; it updates all weights at high cost. Not "Switching to on-demand inference": Inference mode is unrelated to PEFT training. Not "Increasing the temperature parameter": Temperature is an inference setting, not a training technique. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: What is a key practical benefit of using adapters/LoRA (PEFT) rather than full fine-tuning when serving many task-specific behaviors?

options.text: It guarantees the model will never hallucinate
Several small adapters can be maintained for one base model to provide different "flavors" at lower training cost
It removes the need for any training data
It eliminates the need for Provisioned Throughput for custom models

explanation: PEFT lets you keep one base model and swap small adapters, reducing training cost and storage per variant. Not "It guarantees the model will never hallucinate": No training method guarantees zero hallucination. Not "It removes the need for any training data": PEFT still requires task data; it just trains fewer parameters. Not "It eliminates the need for Provisioned Throughput for cus…": Serving customized models still uses Provisioned Throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An MLOps team needs a versioned catalog of trained models with approval status that integrates into their CI/CD release process. Which service provides this?

options.text: AWS CodeArtifact
Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Amazon ECR

explanation: The Model Registry stores versioned models with approval states and integrates with CI/CD pipelines. Not "AWS CodeArtifact": CodeArtifact is a software package repository, not a model registry. Not "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management": Prompt Management versions prompts, not trained models. Not "Amazon ECR": ECR stores container images; the model-versioning/approval catalog is the Model Registry. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must choose a foundation model and wants to compare candidates on accuracy, robustness, and toxicity using both automatic metrics and human review before committing. Which Bedrock capability supports this?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation (automatic and human-based evaluation jobs)
AWS Glue Data Quality
Cross-Region inference profiles

explanation: Bedrock model evaluation runs automatic and human evaluations to compare models on quality and responsible-AI metrics. Not "Provisioned Throughput": That reserves capacity; it does not evaluate model quality. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": Glue Data Quality checks datasets, not model output quality. Not "Cross-Region inference profiles": Profiles route traffic; they do not evaluate models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A startup has spiky, unpredictable, low-to-moderate Bedrock usage and wants to pay only for what it uses without reserving capacity. Which inference option is most appropriate?

options.text: A dedicated EC2 GPU fleet
On-demand inference
Provisioned Throughput
Batch transform on SageMaker

explanation: On-demand bills per request and needs no capacity reservation, ideal for variable low/moderate usage. Not "A dedicated EC2 GPU fleet": Self-managed GPUs add cost and operational overhead versus on-demand Bedrock. Not "Provisioned Throughput": Provisioned Throughput reserves (and bills for) capacity, wasteful for spiky low usage. Not "Batch transform on SageMaker": Batch transform is for offline bulk jobs, not interactive on-demand calls. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team needs to process millions of documents through a foundation model overnight at the lowest cost, with no latency requirement. Which Amazon Bedrock approach fits best?

options.text: Intelligent Prompt Routing
Synchronous on-demand InvokeModel per document in a tight loop
Provisioned Throughput sized for daytime peaks
Amazon Bedrock batch inference

explanation: Batch inference processes large datasets asynchronously at lower cost than real-time, ideal when latency does not matter. Not "Intelligent Prompt Routing": Routing optimizes per-prompt model choice; it is not a bulk offline mechanism. Not "Synchronous on-demand InvokeModel per document in a tight…": Real-time per-call invocation is costlier and slower for huge offline volumes. Not "Provisioned Throughput sized for daytime peaks": Reserving real-time capacity is unnecessary and costlier for an offline batch. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company already trained a custom large language model with open weights outside AWS and wants to serve it through the Amazon Bedrock API alongside managed models. Which feature enables this?

options.text: Knowledge Bases
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import
Continued pre-training
Prompt Flows

explanation: Custom Model Import lets you bring supported open-weight custom models and serve them via Bedrock. Not "Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases provide RAG, not model import. Not "Continued pre-training": That trains a Bedrock base model further; it does not import external weights. Not "Prompt Flows": Prompt Flows orchestrate prompts; they do not import models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A model selection review weighs latency, cost, context window, modality, and quality for a summarization feature. Which statement reflects sound model-selection practice?

options.text: Always pick the model with the largest parameter count
Choose the smallest/cheapest model that meets the task's quality and latency requirements
Pick whichever model was released most recently
Choose based only on provider brand

explanation: Right-sizing to requirements balances cost, latency, and quality rather than defaulting to the biggest model. Not "Always pick the model with the largest parameter count": Bigger is not always better; it raises cost/latency without guaranteed task benefit. Not "Pick whichever model was released most recently": Recency alone is not a selection criterion; fit to requirements matters. Not "Choose based only on provider brand": Brand is not a substitute for evaluating fit, cost, and performance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Which description best fits the Amazon Titan and Amazon Nova model families available in Bedrock?

options.text: Tools for managing IAM roles
On-premises-only models
Amazon's own first-party foundation models (text, embeddings, and multimodal options) offered through Bedrock
Third-party models that require a separate Anthropic account

explanation: Titan and Nova are Amazon-built FMs accessible via the Bedrock unified API, including multimodal Nova variants. Not "Tools for managing IAM roles": They are foundation models, not IAM tooling. Not "On-premises-only models": They are cloud models served through Bedrock. Not "Third-party models that require a separate Anthropic account": Titan/Nova are Amazon's own models, not Anthropic's. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Before fine-tuning a base model in Amazon Bedrock, which statement about capacity is correct?

options.text: Fine-tuning is impossible in Bedrock
Fine-tuning requires migrating to Amazon EC2
Serving the resulting fine-tuned model requires Provisioned Throughput
Fine-tuned models are always served on-demand at no extra cost

explanation: Custom/fine-tuned Bedrock models are hosted via Provisioned Throughput. Not "Fine-tuning is impossible in Bedrock": Bedrock supports fine-tuning for supported models. Not "Fine-tuning requires migrating to Amazon EC2": Bedrock manages the training; EC2 migration is not required. Not "Fine-tuned models are always served on-demand at no extra…": Custom models need Provisioned Throughput, unlike base models on-demand. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An architect is designing for resilience of FM calls in a critical workflow. Which TWO are valid resilience patterns? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Use a Step Functions circuit breaker to stop calling the FM when failures exceed a threshold
Increase top-p to improve uptime
Remove all timeouts so calls wait indefinitely
Hard-code a single Region with no failover
Fall back to a cheaper or cached response (graceful degradation) when the FM is unavailable

explanation: Circuit breakers protect the system from a failing dependency. Graceful degradation preserves a usable experience during failures. Not "Increase top-p to improve uptime": top-p is an inference parameter and has nothing to do with availability. Not "Remove all timeouts so calls wait indefinitely": Unbounded waits worsen reliability and can exhaust resources. Not "Hard-code a single Region with no failover": A single Region with no failover is a single point of failure. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A developer wants the difference between a system-defined inference profile and an application inference profile. Which is correct?

options.text: System-defined profiles are predefined by AWS; application profiles are user-created and support tagging for cost tracking
Both are identical and interchangeable
System-defined profiles are user-created; application profiles are AWS-managed
Only application profiles can route across Regions

explanation: System-defined = automatic/AWS-managed; application = custom and taggable for cost allocation. Not "Both are identical and interchangeable": They differ in who creates them and whether they support custom tagging. Not "System-defined profiles are user-created; application pro…": This reverses the definitions. Not "Only application profiles can route across Regions": Both can support cross-Region routing; the distinction is creation/tagging. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A FinOps team wants per-application cost attribution for Bedrock inference without changing application code that already calls a model directly. Which is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Route calls through application inference profiles and tag them per application
Switch every model to Provisioned Throughput
Disable model invocation logging
Move to a single shared IAM user

explanation: Application inference profiles add taggable, attributable usage for cost tracking across applications. Not "Switch every model to Provisioned Throughput": That reserves capacity and changes cost model but does not provide per-app tagging by itself. Not "Disable model invocation logging": Removing logging reduces visibility, the opposite of what is needed. Not "Move to a single shared IAM user": Sharing identities harms attribution and security. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Which scenario is the best fit for Provisioned Throughput rather than on-demand inference?

options.text: An internal proof-of-concept with a few requests per day
A consistently high-volume production workload needing predictable, guaranteed capacity
Occasional traffic spikes a few hours per week
A one-time overnight bulk job

explanation: Provisioned Throughput shines for steady, high, predictable demand. Not "An internal proof-of-concept with a few requests per day": On-demand is cheaper for sporadic low usage. Not "Occasional traffic spikes a few hours per week": Cross-Region inference profiles better absorb occasional spikes without reserving capacity. Not "A one-time overnight bulk job": Batch inference is better for one-off offline volume. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team wants to swap the Bedrock model ID used by a running application based on an operational decision, with an auditable rollout and quick rollback, and no redeploy. Which combination is best?

options.text: Embed the model ID in a Lambda layer
Store the model ID in AWS AppConfig and read it at runtime
Use Provisioned Throughput to change the model
Hard-code the model ID and redeploy each time

explanation: AppConfig externalizes the model choice for safe, no-redeploy, rollback-friendly changes. Not "Embed the model ID in a Lambda layer": Layers still require redeployment to change values. Not "Use Provisioned Throughput to change the model": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity; it is not a config switch. Not "Hard-code the model ID and redeploy each time": Redeploying for each change is exactly what AppConfig avoids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Distillation in Amazon Bedrock is described as training a "student" using a "teacher." What is the primary motivation?

options.text: Add unlabeled domain data to the base model
Guarantee zero hallucinations
Increase the model's parameter count for higher accuracy
Produce a smaller, lower-cost, lower-latency model that approximates the teacher's quality on the task

explanation: Distillation trades a little quality for big cost/latency savings by compressing the teacher into a student. Not "Add unlabeled domain data to the base model": That describes continued pre-training, not distillation. Not "Guarantee zero hallucinations": No technique guarantees zero hallucination. Not "Increase the model's parameter count for higher accuracy": Distillation reduces size, not increases it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must enforce that a particular role can only call models through one approved cross-Region inference profile. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Rely on the application code to call the right profile
Attach an IAM policy using the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key scoped to that profile
Use bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier
Disable on-demand inference account-wide

explanation: The condition key restricts invocation to the approved inference profile ARN. Not "Rely on the application code to call the right profile": Code-only controls are not enforceable security; use IAM conditions. Not "Use bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier": That enforces guardrails, not inference-profile scoping. Not "Disable on-demand inference account-wide": That is a blunt change unrelated to scoping a specific profile. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A data engineering team wants to automatically detect anomalies and measure the quality of data in their data lake/ETL pipelines before it is used for training. Which service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Textract
Amazon Transcribe

explanation: Glue Data Quality computes rules and automatically detects anomalies in datasets within Glue pipelines. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend performs NLP analysis, not pipeline data-quality scoring. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts text from documents; it does not measure dataset quality. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe converts speech to text; unrelated to data-quality checks. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A data scientist wants a visual, GUI-based tool to import, explore, transform, and prepare tabular data for ML with minimal code. Which tool fits best?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon SageMaker Processing
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler

explanation: Data Wrangler is the low-code GUI for importing, visualizing, and transforming data for ML. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": Glue Data Quality scores data quality; it is not a visual data-prep canvas. Not "Amazon SageMaker Processing": Processing runs code-based processing jobs; it is not the GUI prep tool. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend analyzes text; it is not a tabular data-prep GUI. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team needs to run scalable, code-based data processing jobs (cleaning, feature transforms, batch scoring) on managed infrastructure as part of an ML workflow. Which service is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon SageMaker Processing
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Kendra

explanation: SageMaker Processing runs containerized data-processing/feature-engineering jobs on managed compute. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler": Data Wrangler is interactive GUI prep; Processing is for programmatic jobs at scale. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe is speech-to-text, not a processing-job service. Not "Amazon Kendra": Kendra is enterprise search, not a data-processing job runner. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A pipeline must convert recorded customer support phone calls into text so the transcripts can be fed to a foundation model. Which service performs the speech-to-text step?

options.text: Amazon Polly
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Textract

explanation: Transcribe converts audio speech to text, ideal for preparing call transcripts. Not "Amazon Polly": Polly is text-to-speech, the reverse operation. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend analyzes text; it does not transcribe audio. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts text from documents/images, not audio. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A company must extract text, forms, and tables from scanned PDF invoices to feed downstream processing. Which service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend

explanation: Textract extracts printed/handwritten text, forms, and tables from scanned documents. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe handles audio, not documents. Not "Amazon Rekognition": Rekognition analyzes images/video for objects and faces, not structured document text extraction. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend analyzes already-extracted text; it does not OCR documents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Before indexing customer emails for a GenAI search app, a team must detect and redact personally identifiable information (PII) from the text. Which managed NLP service does this?

options.text: Amazon Macie
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend

explanation: Comprehend detects and can redact PII entities from text, suited to pre-processing for FMs. Not "Amazon Macie": Macie discovers/classifies sensitive data in S3 for security posture; it is not a text PII-redaction step for GenAI pipelines. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe converts audio to text; it is not a PII redactor for documents. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts text; it does not redact PII. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Where can Amazon Comprehend add value in a foundation-model pipeline? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Post-processing FM output (e.g., scanning generated text for PII or sentiment)
Transcribing audio to text
Reserving guaranteed FM inference capacity
Pre-processing input text (e.g., detecting entities/sentiment, redacting PII) before it reaches the FM
Storing vectors for RAG

explanation: Comprehend can analyze model outputs after generation. Comprehend can clean and enrich inputs before inference. Not "Transcribing audio to text": That is Transcribe's job, not Comprehend's. Not "Reserving guaranteed FM inference capacity": That is Provisioned Throughput, not Comprehend. Not "Storing vectors for RAG": Vector storage is handled by vector stores, not Comprehend. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A multimodal ingestion pipeline must take audio recordings, transcribe them, then detect and redact PII before the transcripts are embedded for RAG. Which ordered combination of services is correct?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe → Amazon Comprehend (PII redaction) → embed for the knowledge base
Amazon Rekognition → Amazon Comprehend → embed
Amazon Comprehend → Amazon Transcribe → embed
Amazon Textract → Amazon Polly → embed

explanation: Transcribe converts audio to text, Comprehend redacts PII, then the cleaned text is embedded. Not "Amazon Rekognition → Amazon Comprehend → embed": Rekognition analyzes images/video, not audio transcription. Not "Amazon Comprehend → Amazon Transcribe → embed": You must transcribe audio to text before Comprehend can analyze it; the order is reversed. Not "Amazon Textract → Amazon Polly → embed": Textract is for documents and Polly is text-to-speech; neither fits audio transcription + redaction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants to scan an Amazon S3 data lake to discover and classify where sensitive data (like PII) resides for security and compliance posture. Which service is the right fit?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Macie
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Textract

explanation: Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3 for security/compliance visibility. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": Glue Data Quality scores dataset quality, not sensitive-data discovery. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend detects/redacts PII in text you send it, but discovery/classification across an S3 lake is Macie's role. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts text from documents; it is not a data-discovery tool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes Amazon Textract from Amazon Comprehend?

options.text: Textract analyzes sentiment; Comprehend does OCR
Both perform speech-to-text
Textract extracts text/forms/tables from documents; Comprehend analyzes text (entities, sentiment, PII)
Both are vector databases

explanation: Textract is OCR/extraction; Comprehend is NLP analysis of text. Not "Textract analyzes sentiment; Comprehend does OCR": This reverses their roles. Not "Both perform speech-to-text": Neither does speech-to-text; that is Transcribe. Not "Both are vector databases": Neither is a vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team building a chatbot wants automated, low-code intelligent document processing to extract content from mixed documents and media (text, tables, images, audio, video) to feed Bedrock. Which AWS capability is designed for this multimodal extraction?

options.text: Amazon Polly
Amazon Kendra
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation

explanation: Bedrock Data Automation extracts and normalizes content from unstructured multimodal documents/media for GenAI use. Not "Amazon Polly": Polly is text-to-speech only. Not "Amazon Kendra": Kendra provides search over data; it is not a multimodal extraction pipeline. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": Glue Data Quality scores datasets; it does not extract multimodal content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team needs repeatable, scheduled, large-scale feature engineering on terabytes of tabular data with custom Python/Spark code as part of an ML pipeline. Which is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe batch jobs
Amazon Comprehend custom classification
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler interactive sessions
Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs

explanation: Processing jobs run custom containerized code at scale on managed infrastructure, ideal for repeatable pipelines. Not "Amazon Transcribe batch jobs": Transcribe handles audio, not tabular feature engineering. Not "Amazon Comprehend custom classification": That is for text classification, not general tabular feature engineering. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler interactive sessions": Data Wrangler is for interactive exploration; large-scale repeatable jobs fit Processing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants to add automated data-quality rules (completeness, uniqueness, freshness) that fail a pipeline run when thresholds are breached, before data is used to fine-tune a model. Which service provides built-in rule evaluation and anomaly detection?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics
Amazon Athena
AWS Glue Data Quality

explanation: Glue Data Quality defines and evaluates rules and detects anomalies inside Glue pipelines. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend analyzes text content, not data-quality rule thresholds. Not "Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics": Synthetics tests endpoints/canaries, not dataset quality. Not "Amazon Athena": Athena queries data; it does not provide built-in data-quality rules/anomaly detection like Glue Data Quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team must redact PII from free-text fields, but keep the text otherwise intact and usable for retrieval. Which is the best approach?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend PII detection/redaction on the text before indexing
Encrypt the entire field so it cannot be read
Drop all free-text fields
Add a system prompt asking the FM not to reveal PII

explanation: Comprehend reliably detects and redacts PII entities while preserving the remaining content. Not "Encrypt the entire field so it cannot be read": Encryption protects at rest but does not selectively redact PII for usable retrieval. Not "Drop all free-text fields": Discarding the data destroys its usefulness for retrieval. Not "Add a system prompt asking the FM not to reveal PII": Prompt instructions are not reliable and can be bypassed; redact before indexing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Which service should transform raw, messy tabular data into ML-ready features using a point-and-click flow that can then be exported to a SageMaker pipeline?

options.text: Amazon Textract
Amazon Macie
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

explanation: Data Wrangler offers visual transforms and can export the flow into a pipeline/processing job. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts document text, not tabular feature transforms. Not "Amazon Macie": Macie discovers sensitive data; it is not a data-prep canvas. Not "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases handle RAG ingestion, not tabular feature prep. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: An ingestion flow processes scanned contracts. The team needs both the raw text AND the key-value pairs from form fields. Which service extracts both?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Textract (text plus forms/tables via its analysis APIs)
Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe

explanation: Textract returns raw text and structured form key-value pairs and tables. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend analyzes text but does not OCR documents or pull form fields. Not "Amazon Polly": Polly is text-to-speech. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe handles audio, not document forms. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants sentiment, key phrases, and entity recognition on millions of product reviews to enrich metadata before RAG indexing. Which service is the best fit?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend

explanation: Comprehend provides sentiment, key-phrase, and entity extraction at scale for text enrichment. Not "Amazon Transcribe": Transcribe converts speech to text; not NLP enrichment. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": Glue Data Quality scores dataset quality, not text NLP. Not "Amazon Textract": Textract extracts text from documents; it does not perform sentiment/entity NLP. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Which pairing correctly maps a service to its primary role in data preparation?

options.text: All three reserve model capacity
Transcribe = OCR; Textract = sentiment; Comprehend = audio
All three are vector databases
Transcribe = speech-to-text; Textract = document text extraction; Comprehend = NLP analysis/PII

explanation: This correctly summarizes each service's core role. Not "All three reserve model capacity": Capacity reservation is Provisioned Throughput, not these services. Not "Transcribe = OCR; Textract = sentiment; Comprehend = audio": These roles are scrambled. Not "All three are vector databases": None of them is a vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team is choosing between Amazon Comprehend and Amazon Macie for handling PII. Which guidance is correct?

options.text: Use Comprehend to scan an entire S3 lake for sensitive data classification
Use Comprehend to detect/redact PII in text you process; use Macie to discover/classify sensitive data across S3
Use Macie to redact PII inside chatbot prompts in real time
They are interchangeable for all PII tasks

explanation: Comprehend redacts text content; Macie is for S3-wide sensitive-data discovery and posture. Not "Use Comprehend to scan an entire S3 lake for sensitive da…": Lake-wide discovery/classification is Macie's role. Not "Use Macie to redact PII inside chatbot prompts in real time": Macie is a discovery/classification service for S3, not a real-time text redactor. Not "They are interchangeable for all PII tasks": They serve different purposes and are not interchangeable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A GenAI ingestion pipeline must handle PDFs, images, audio, and video and output normalized text/insights for a knowledge base with the least custom code. Which is the most fitting first choice?

Not "Write custom Lambda parsers for every file type": Hand-built parsers per format add significant operational overhead. Not "Amazon Textract alone": Textract only covers documents/images, not audio/video. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants managed Retrieval-Augmented Generation that automatically chunks documents, generates embeddings, and stores them in a vector store, exposing retrieval to a foundation model. Which Amazon Bedrock feature provides this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

Not "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows": Prompt Flows orchestrate prompt steps; they are not a managed RAG ingestion pipeline. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails filter content; they do not build a RAG pipeline. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: When you create an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and accept the defaults for the vector store, which vector database is provisioned by default?

prompt: Which TWO are supported vector stores you can use with an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base? (Select all that apply.)

Amazon CloudFront

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A developer needs only the relevant retrieved document chunks back from a Knowledge Base so they can build a fully custom prompt themselves. Which API should they call?

prompt: A team wants the Knowledge Base to both retrieve relevant chunks AND have a foundation model generate a grounded answer in one managed call. Which API fits?

options.text: Converse
Retrieve

Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Which TWO data sources can an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base ingest from for RAG? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A web crawler data source
Amazon S3
An Amazon SQS queue
An Amazon EC2 instance store
AWS IAM

Not "An Amazon EC2 instance store": Instance store is ephemeral local disk, not a KB data source. Not "AWS IAM": IAM manages access; it is not a data source. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: For a Bedrock Knowledge Base to read from and write to its OpenSearch Serverless vector store, what must be configured?

options.text: A public internet gateway on the collection

An IAM role granting Bedrock permission to access the vector store
Provisioned Throughput on OpenSearch

explanation: Bedrock assumes an IAM role with permissions to the vector collection to ingest and query. Not "A NAT gateway in every subnet": Network plumbing alone does not grant Bedrock access; the IAM role does. Not "Provisioned Throughput on OpenSearch": OpenSearch capacity is OCU-based; the access requirement is an IAM role. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A company runs frequent, high-throughput, low-latency vector searches and wants a managed vector store that autoscales without capacity planning, also used as the default for Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Which is the best fit?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon DocumentDB
Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless autoscales for frequent low-latency vector search and is the KB default. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB has no native vector search. Not "Amazon DocumentDB": DocumentDB supports vectors but is not the autoscaling default for KB high-throughput search. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors": S3 Vectors targets cost-effective, infrequent queries, not high-throughput low-latency workloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: In Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, capacity is measured in OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs). Which statement is correct?

OCUs measure storage only
A single OCU type covers both search and indexing and cannot be separated
OCUs apply only to time-series logs, not vector search

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless scales indexing and search capacity separately, matching workloads that read a lot but index rarely. Not "OCUs measure storage only": OCUs measure compute capacity, not just storage. Not "A single OCU type covers both search and indexing and can…": OCUs are split into search and indexing, which scale independently. Not "OCUs apply only to time-series logs, not vector search": OpenSearch Serverless supports time-series, search, and vector workloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team uses a self-managed Amazon OpenSearch Service domain for vector search. Which plugin enables k-nearest-neighbor vector similarity search?

options.text: The k-NN plugin
The Alerting plugin
The SQL plugin
The Index State Management plugin

explanation: The k-NN plugin provides approximate/exact nearest-neighbor vector search in OpenSearch. Not "The Alerting plugin": Alerting triggers notifications; it is not for vector search. Not "The SQL plugin": The SQL plugin enables SQL queries, not vector kNN search. Not "The Index State Management plugin": ISM manages index lifecycle, not vector similarity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Within OpenSearch, which plugin enables neural/semantic search and retrieval that can integrate with Bedrock for RAG-style queries?

options.text: The Anomaly Detection plugin
The Neural Search plugin
The Security plugin
The Cross-cluster Replication plugin

explanation: Neural Search enables semantic vector retrieval and can integrate with Bedrock models. Not "The Cross-cluster Replication plugin": That replicates indices across clusters; it is not semantic search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An engineer increases the number of shards in an OpenSearch vector index. What is a likely trade-off to be aware of?

options.text: More shards allow storing more data but can increase query latency
Shards have no effect on capacity
Shards only matter for text search, never vectors
More shards always reduce latency with no downside

explanation: Sharding scales capacity but adds coordination overhead that can raise latency.
