Not "Shards only matter for text search, never vectors": Sharding affects vector indices too. Not "More shards always reduce latency with no downside": Over-sharding can hurt latency; it is a trade-off, not a free win. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team tunes an HNSW vector index in OpenSearch. What does the "m" parameter control?

options.text: The maximum number of connections per node — higher m improves recall/accuracy but uses more RAM and can slow search
The embedding dimension
The temperature of generation
The number of documents per shard

explanation: m sets graph connectivity; raising it boosts accuracy at the cost of memory and speed. Not "The embedding dimension": Dimension is a property of the vectors, not the HNSW m parameter. Not "The temperature of generation": Temperature is an inference parameter, unrelated to HNSW. Not "The number of documents per shard": That is shard sizing, not the HNSW m parameter. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: In an HNSW index, what does increasing "ef_construction" do?

options.text: Increases index build quality/accuracy at the cost of slower indexing
Reduces the embedding dimension automatically
Disables sharding
Controls the FM's max tokens

explanation: ef_construction sets the candidate list size during graph construction — higher is more accurate but slower to build. Not "Reduces the embedding dimension automatically": It does not change vector dimensionality. Not "Disables sharding": It is unrelated to sharding. Not "Controls the FM's max tokens": It is an index parameter, not an inference setting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Beyond vector search, what else is Amazon OpenSearch Service commonly used for?

options.text: Only storing relational transactions
Only training foundation models
Only message queuing
Full-text search and log/analytics (e.g., time-series and observability)

explanation: OpenSearch is a search and analytics suite covering full-text search, logs, and time-series in addition to vectors. Not "Only storing relational transactions": Relational OLTP is for databases like Aurora, not OpenSearch. Not "Only training foundation models": OpenSearch does not train FMs. Not "Only message queuing": Queuing is SQS; OpenSearch is search/analytics. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A company stores JSON documents in Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible) and wants to add vector similarity search to the same datastore. Which is true?

options.text: DocumentDB supports vector search (e.g., HNSW and IVFFlat) over its JSON documents
DocumentDB cannot do vector search at all
DocumentDB stores arbitrary binary objects, not JSON
DocumentDB requires DynamoDB to perform vector search

explanation: DocumentDB adds vector search indexes such as HNSW and IVFFlat for its JSON data. Not "DocumentDB cannot do vector search at all": It does support vector search. Not "DocumentDB stores arbitrary binary objects, not JSON": DocumentDB is for JSON documents, not arbitrary blob objects. Not "DocumentDB requires DynamoDB to perform vector search": DocumentDB performs vector search itself; DynamoDB is unrelated. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team needs a relational database that can store transactional data AND vector embeddings together for a RAG feature. Which option fits best?

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Neptune (graph) without Analytics
Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector combines relational data with vector search in one store. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB is NoSQL and lacks native vector search. Not "Amazon Neptune (graph) without Analytics": Standard Neptune is a graph DB; relational + vectors is Aurora pgvector. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors": S3 Vectors stores vectors but is not a relational transactional database. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A company wants enterprise search across internal content with built-in connectors to sources like Salesforce, SharePoint, and ServiceNow, and no custom ETL to keep data fresh. Which service fits best?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight
Amazon Athena
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Kendra

explanation: Kendra provides intelligent enterprise search with managed connectors to third-party sources, refreshing on a schedule without custom ETL. Not "Amazon QuickSight": QuickSight is BI dashboards, not enterprise search. Not "Amazon Athena": Athena queries data in S3 via SQL; it has no enterprise-search connectors. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend is NLP analysis, not enterprise search with connectors. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: What are TWO advantages of using Amazon Kendra's managed connectors for sources like SharePoint or ServiceNow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It guarantees the FM will never hallucinate
No need to build custom ETL pipelines for each source
Automatic scheduled syncs keep the index up to date
It eliminates the need for any IAM permissions
It trains a custom foundation model for you

explanation: Kendra ships managed connectors, removing custom ingestion code. Connectors can sync on a schedule so content stays current. Not "It guarantees the FM will never hallucinate": Search quality helps grounding but does not guarantee zero hallucination. Not "It eliminates the need for any IAM permissions": Access still requires properly scoped permissions. Not "It trains a custom foundation model for you": Kendra is search; it does not train FMs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A diagnostic app stores 50 million image embeddings and runs similarity searches only occasionally, wanting the most cost-effective, serverless option with no infrastructure to manage. Which vector store is best?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon DynamoDB with custom Lambda search
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector
Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: S3 Vectors is serverless, scales to billions of vectors, and is cost-optimized for infrequent queries — ideal here. Not "Amazon OpenSearch Serverless": OpenSearch Serverless is built for frequent low-latency search; provisioned capacity sits idle for rare queries. Not "Amazon DynamoDB with custom Lambda search": DynamoDB has no native vector search; custom logic adds latency and cost. Not "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector": Aurora requires managing a database instance and is not cost-optimal for infrequent workloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: In Amazon S3 Vectors, how is vector data organized?

options.text: Within a vector bucket you create one or more vector indexes, each defining dimension and distance metric, and you query within an index
Vectors are stored as standard S3 objects in a normal general-purpose bucket
Vectors live in DynamoDB tables behind S3
Each vector requires its own bucket

explanation: S3 Vectors uses vector buckets containing vector indexes; an index fixes dimension/metric and is the unit you query. Not "Vectors are stored as standard S3 objects in a normal gen…": S3 Vectors uses a dedicated vector bucket type with vector indexes, not ordinary objects. Not "Vectors live in DynamoDB tables behind S3": S3 Vectors stores vectors natively; DynamoDB is not involved. Not "Each vector requires its own bucket": Many vectors and many indexes live within one vector bucket. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team wants S3 Vectors as the vector store for a Bedrock Knowledge Base. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: S3 Vectors cannot be used with Bedrock Knowledge Bases
S3 Vectors only stores text, not embeddings
Bedrock can use S3 Vectors as a Knowledge Base vector store, handling chunking, embedding, and storing vectors in the S3 Vectors index
Using S3 Vectors requires running your own OpenSearch cluster

explanation: S3 Vectors is a supported KB vector store; Bedrock ingests and writes embeddings into the S3 Vectors index. Not "S3 Vectors cannot be used with Bedrock Knowledge Bases": It is supported as a KB vector store. Not "S3 Vectors only stores text, not embeddings": S3 Vectors is purpose-built to store and query embeddings. Not "Using S3 Vectors requires running your own OpenSearch clu…": S3 Vectors is independent of OpenSearch. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Which guidance best contrasts DynamoDB, OpenSearch, and Aurora pgvector for vector workloads?

options.text: Aurora pgvector cannot store relational data
OpenSearch cannot do vector search
DynamoDB scales well but has no MongoDB compatibility/native vector search; OpenSearch is strongest for vectors; Aurora pgvector combines relational data with vectors
DynamoDB is the best dedicated vector engine

explanation: This matches each option's strengths for vector use cases. Not "Aurora pgvector cannot store relational data": Aurora is relational and adds vectors via pgvector. Not "OpenSearch cannot do vector search": OpenSearch is a leading vector-search option. Not "DynamoDB is the best dedicated vector engine": DynamoDB lacks native vector search; OpenSearch is the strong vector choice. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A near-real-time, resilient ingestion pipeline must add newly uploaded S3 documents to a Knowledge Base ASAP and remove deleted ones ASAP, tolerating spikes. Which architecture is best?

options.text: Manual re-ingestion through the console
EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to scan S3 and re-sync
S3 Event Notifications → Amazon SQS → Lambda that calls IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments
S3 → Lambda directly with no queue

explanation: SQS buffers spikes and provides retries between S3 events and the Lambda, making ingestion resilient and event-driven. Not "Manual re-ingestion through the console": Manual steps do not meet the automated, near-real-time requirement. Not "EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to scan S3 and re-sync": Polling on a schedule is time-based, not near-real-time, and is inefficient. Not "S3 → Lambda directly with no queue": Direct invocation lacks buffering/retries and can fail under load. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team needs to monitor Knowledge Base data ingestion to troubleshoot why some documents fail to process (e.g., ignored, embedding failed, indexing failed). Which solution is correct?

options.text: Use AWS CloudTrail to see document-level processing details
Use Bedrock model invocation logging
Enable Knowledge Base logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and query statuses with Logs Insights
Enable CloudWatch Application Signals

explanation: KB logging records per-file ingestion status (e.g., RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, INDEXING_FAILED) to CloudWatch. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail to see document-level processing details": CloudTrail logs API calls, not per-document ingestion status. Not "Use Bedrock model invocation logging": That logs inference calls, not KB ingestion. Not "Enable CloudWatch Application Signals": Application Signals monitors app performance, not KB ingestion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: For exam purposes, which vector store is generally the "default/expected" answer for building RAG with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases when no special cost or relational requirement is stated?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached)
Amazon Redshift
Amazon Timestream

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless is the default and most commonly expected KB vector store for RAG. Not "Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached)": Memcached is a cache without vector search. Not "Amazon Redshift": Redshift is a warehouse, not the KB vector store. Not "Amazon Timestream": Timestream is a time-series DB, not a KB vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A Knowledge Base must pull content from a managed SaaS source. Which TWO are valid Bedrock Knowledge Base data-source connectors? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
Amazon Inspector
Confluence
Salesforce
AWS Step Functions

explanation: Confluence is a supported KB data source connector. Salesforce is a supported KB data source connector. Not "Amazon Lightsail": Lightsail is simplified compute hosting, not a data source connector. Not "Amazon Inspector": Inspector is vulnerability scanning, not a data source. Not "AWS Step Functions": Step Functions orchestrates workflows; it is not a KB data source. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Which statement about the Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate APIs is correct?

options.text: Both always call a foundation model
Retrieve returns chunks only; RetrieveAndGenerate returns chunks plus an FM-generated answer
Neither can be used for RAG
RetrieveAndGenerate returns only raw chunks

explanation: Retrieve = retrieval only; RetrieveAndGenerate = retrieval + generation. Not "Both always call a foundation model": Retrieve does not call an FM. Not "Neither can be used for RAG": Both are core RAG APIs for Knowledge Bases. Not "RetrieveAndGenerate returns only raw chunks": It also generates an answer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team must store binary (quantized) vectors to save memory in their vector store for a Knowledge Base. Which store supports binary vectors?

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors
Amazon OpenSearch (Serverless or managed cluster)
Amazon Timestream
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless and managed clusters are the KB vector stores that support binary vectors. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors": S3 Vectors is cost-optimized but is not the binary-vector option among these stores. Not "Amazon Timestream": Timestream is time-series, not a vector store. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB has no native vector support. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An OpenSearch Serverless workload ingests new data rarely but serves a very high volume of vector queries. How should capacity be approached?

options.text: Scale search OCUs up for query volume while keeping indexing OCUs low, since they scale independently
Add a NAT gateway to improve query speed
Increase indexing OCUs to speed up queries
Switch to Provisioned Throughput model units

explanation: Because search and indexing scale separately, you can right-size each to the workload. Not "Add a NAT gateway to improve query speed": Networking does not change OCU-based search capacity. Not "Increase indexing OCUs to speed up queries": Indexing OCUs do not serve query throughput; search OCUs do. Not "Switch to Provisioned Throughput model units": Model Units are a Bedrock model-capacity concept, not OpenSearch query capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team chose Amazon Kendra and wants to combine it with a Bedrock FM for grounded answers. What is the typical role split?

options.text: Kendra generates the final answer and the FM indexes data
Kendra retrieves relevant passages from indexed enterprise content; the Bedrock FM generates the answer from those passages
Kendra reserves model capacity for the FM
Both train a new model on each query

explanation: Kendra supplies retrieval/grounding; the FM composes the final response. Not "Kendra generates the final answer and the FM indexes data": This reverses their roles. Not "Kendra reserves model capacity for the FM": Capacity reservation is Provisioned Throughput, unrelated to Kendra. Not "Both train a new model on each query": Neither trains a model per query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Which statement about IVFFlat vs HNSW indexes (as used in stores like DocumentDB) is most accurate?

options.text: They only apply to relational joins
Both are approximate-nearest-neighbor index types for vector search, trading off build time, memory, and recall differently
They are encryption algorithms for vectors
They are foundation models

explanation: HNSW (graph-based) and IVFFlat (inverted-file) are both ANN index types with different performance/recall trade-offs. Not "They only apply to relational joins": They are for vector similarity search, not relational joins. Not "They are encryption algorithms for vectors": They are index structures, not encryption. Not "They are foundation models": They are vector index types, not models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A retrieval system over highly connected/graph-structured knowledge wants vector search integrated with graph relationships in a managed store usable by a Knowledge Base. Which option fits?

options.text: Amazon S3 (general-purpose bucket)
Amazon Neptune Analytics
Amazon CloudSearch
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation: Neptune Analytics combines graph analytics with vector search and is a supported KB vector store. Not "Amazon S3 (general-purpose bucket)": A standard bucket is object storage, not a graph+vector store. Not "Amazon CloudSearch": CloudSearch is legacy text search, not a graph+vector KB store. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB is key-value/document without graph+vector capability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: In a Bedrock Knowledge Base, why is the source content split into "chunks" before embedding?

options.text: To reserve model capacity
To encrypt the documents
To convert audio to text
So each piece fits embedding/context limits and retrieval returns focused, relevant passages

explanation: Chunking keeps units small enough to embed and retrieve precisely, improving relevance and fitting context windows. Not "To reserve model capacity": That is Provisioned Throughput, not chunking. Not "To encrypt the documents": Chunking is about segmentation for retrieval, not encryption. Not "To convert audio to text": That is transcription, unrelated to chunking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which TWO chunking strategies are offered by Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: OCU chunking
Fixed-size chunking
Semantic chunking
Temperature chunking
Shard chunking

explanation: Fixed-size splits text into uniform token/character windows. Semantic chunking splits on meaning boundaries to keep coherent ideas together. Not "OCU chunking": OCUs are OpenSearch capacity units, not a chunking strategy. Not "Temperature chunking": There is no "temperature chunking"; temperature is an inference parameter. Not "Shard chunking": Sharding is a vector-index concept, not a KB chunking strategy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A document set has nested structure (sections, subsections) and the team wants retrieval to use both fine-grained child chunks and broader parent context. Which chunking strategy fits best?

options.text: No chunking (one big document)
Fixed-size only
Hierarchical chunking
Custom chunking with random splits

explanation: Hierarchical chunking creates parent/child chunks so retrieval can use granular matches with broader context. Not "No chunking (one big document)": A single large chunk loses granularity and hurts retrieval precision. Not "Fixed-size only": Fixed-size ignores the document's nested structure. Not "Custom chunking with random splits": Random splits do not capture hierarchy and degrade relevance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team has small, self-contained records where each document is already a single coherent unit. Which Knowledge Base chunking option may be appropriate?

options.text: Semantic chunking with tiny windows
Fixed-size chunking at 10 tokens
Hierarchical chunking with many levels
No chunking — treat each document as one chunk

explanation: When documents are short and self-contained, the "no chunking" option indexes each as a single chunk. Not "Semantic chunking with tiny windows": Over-splitting atomic records can fragment meaning. Not "Fixed-size chunking at 10 tokens": Extremely small fixed chunks destroy context for whole-record content. Not "Hierarchical chunking with many levels": Hierarchy adds needless complexity for already-atomic records. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team needs full control over how content is split (e.g., by their own delimiters or a Lambda transformation) in a Bedrock Knowledge Base. Which option supports this?

options.text: Sharding
Fixed-size chunking only
Custom chunking (e.g., via a Lambda transformation)
No chunking

explanation: Custom chunking lets you define your own splitting logic, including a Lambda-based transformation. Not "Sharding": Sharding is a storage-layer concept, not content splitting. Not "Fixed-size chunking only": Fixed-size cannot express custom delimiter logic. Not "No chunking": No chunking is the opposite of fine-grained custom control. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Amazon Titan Text Embeddings supports configurable output dimensions. Which set of dimensions is supported?

options.text: 256, 512, or 1024 dimensions
16, 32, or 64 dimensions
Exactly 1 dimension
Unlimited arbitrary dimensions

explanation: Titan embeddings can output 256, 512, or 1024 dimensions, trading storage/speed against fidelity. Not "16, 32, or 64 dimensions": These are not the supported Titan embedding sizes. Not "Exactly 1 dimension": Embeddings are high-dimensional vectors, not scalars. Not "Unlimited arbitrary dimensions": Titan supports specific sizes (256/512/1024), not arbitrary values. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: What is a practical trade-off of choosing a smaller embedding dimension (e.g., 256 vs 1024) with Titan?

options.text: Smaller dimensions always improve accuracy
Smaller dimensions require Provisioned Throughput
Smaller dimensions reduce storage and can speed search, potentially at some loss of representational fidelity
Dimension size has no effect on storage

explanation: Lower-dimensional vectors cost less to store/search but may capture slightly less nuance. Not "Smaller dimensions always improve accuracy": Fewer dimensions can reduce fidelity; it is a trade-off, not a pure win. Not "Smaller dimensions require Provisioned Throughput": Dimension choice is unrelated to capacity reservation. Not "Dimension size has no effect on storage": Dimension directly affects vector storage size. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A search experience must match both exact keywords (like product codes) and semantic meaning. Which retrieval approach combines both?

options.text: Pure keyword search only
Pure vector search only
Random retrieval
Hybrid search — combining keyword (BM25) and semantic vector search

explanation: Hybrid search blends lexical BM25 matching with vector semantic matching for better coverage. Not "Pure keyword search only": Keyword-only misses semantic matches and paraphrases. Not "Pure vector search only": Vector-only can miss exact tokens like codes/IDs. Not "Random retrieval": Randomness is not a retrieval strategy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: In hybrid search, what does the "BM25" component contribute?

options.text: Neural embedding generation
Vector dimensionality reduction
Lexical/keyword relevance scoring based on term frequency
Document chunking

explanation: BM25 is a classic keyword ranking function; it provides the lexical half of hybrid search. Not "Neural embedding generation": Embeddings power the vector half, not BM25. Not "Vector dimensionality reduction": BM25 is a ranking function, not a dimensionality technique. Not "Document chunking": BM25 ranks, it does not chunk. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: After initial retrieval, the most relevant passages sometimes rank below less relevant ones. The team wants a managed way to reorder results by query relevance with minimal custom code. Which Bedrock capability fits?

options.text: The Amazon Bedrock Rerank API with a reranker model
Switching to no chunking
Increasing model temperature
Sharding the vector index

explanation: The Rerank API uses a cross-encoder reranker to reorder retrieved passages by relevance to the query. Not "Switching to no chunking": Chunking strategy does not reorder results by relevance. Not "Increasing model temperature": Temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval ordering. Not "Sharding the vector index": Sharding affects capacity/latency, not relevance ranking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which TWO reranker models are available through the Amazon Bedrock Rerank API? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Cohere Rerank 3.5
Claude Rerank 2
Titan Image Generator
Stable Diffusion
Amazon Rerank 1.0

explanation: Cohere Rerank 3.5 is available via the Bedrock Rerank API. Amazon Rerank 1.0 is offered through the Rerank API. Not "Claude Rerank 2": No such Bedrock reranker model; rerankers are Amazon Rerank and Cohere Rerank. Not "Titan Image Generator": That is an image model, not a reranker. Not "Stable Diffusion": Stable Diffusion is an image model, not a reranker. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: How can reranking be applied to a Bedrock Knowledge Base query?

options.text: Reranking requires Provisioned Throughput on the embeddings model
Reranking is only available outside AWS
Enable the reranker as a setting in the Retrieve / RetrieveAndGenerate request
It can only be used by training a custom model

explanation: KB users turn on reranking through the Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate APIs. Not "Reranking requires Provisioned Throughput on the embeddin…": Reranking is invoked via the API; it does not mandate provisioned embeddings capacity. Not "Reranking is only available outside AWS": It is available in Amazon Bedrock. Not "It can only be used by training a custom model": Reranking is a managed feature, no custom training needed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Why does a reranker (cross-encoder) often improve RAG relevance compared to vector similarity alone?

options.text: It guarantees deterministic generation
It jointly examines the query and each candidate passage to score true relevance, refining the first-stage results
It increases the embedding dimension automatically
It removes the need for any retrieval step

explanation: Cross-encoders consider query+passage together, capturing relevance signals a single-vector similarity may miss. Not "It guarantees deterministic generation": Reranking orders passages; it does not control generation determinism. Not "It increases the embedding dimension automatically": Reranking does not change embedding dimensions. Not "It removes the need for any retrieval step": Reranking refines retrieved candidates; retrieval still happens first. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A RAG app starts returning "no relevant information found" after a deploy. The FM invokes fine, OpenSearch is healthy, latency is normal, and there are no errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The temperature parameter was increased
The query embeddings are now generated by a different embedding model/version than the one used to index the documents
The IAM role lost bedrock:InvokeModel
The vector index was sharded

explanation: Embedding drift creates a vector-space mismatch between queries and stored vectors, silently breaking retrieval. Not "The temperature parameter was increased": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval matching. Not "The IAM role lost bedrock:InvokeModel": The FM invokes successfully, so the permission is present. Not "The vector index was sharded": Sharding affects capacity/latency, not vector-space alignment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which rule must hold for vector retrieval to work correctly?

options.text: Embeddings must be regenerated for every query at index time
Any embedding model can be mixed freely
Queries must always use a larger embedding model than indexing
Query embeddings must be produced by the same embedding model used to index the documents

explanation: Matching the embedding model/version keeps queries and documents in the same vector space. Not "Embeddings must be regenerated for every query at index time": Document embeddings are created at ingestion; queries are embedded at query time with the same model. Not "Any embedding model can be mixed freely": Mixing models causes a vector-space mismatch and poor retrieval. Not "Queries must always use a larger embedding model than ind…": They must match, not differ by size. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team is deciding chunk size. What is the typical trade-off between very large and very small chunks?

options.text: Smaller chunks always retrieve better in every case
Large chunks preserve context but can dilute relevance and exceed limits; small chunks are precise but may lose surrounding context
Larger chunks always reduce cost
Chunk size has no effect on retrieval quality

explanation: Chunk size trades context retention against retrieval precision and token limits. Not "Smaller chunks always retrieve better in every case": Too-small chunks can lose needed context. Not "Larger chunks always reduce cost": Larger chunks can increase tokens per retrieval and cost. Not "Chunk size has no effect on retrieval quality": Chunk size materially affects relevance and context. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants chunk boundaries that follow the meaning of the text (paragraph/topic shifts) rather than arbitrary token counts. Which strategy should they pick?

options.text: Semantic chunking
Sharding
Fixed-size chunking
No chunking

explanation: Semantic chunking places boundaries at meaning shifts to keep coherent ideas intact. Not "Sharding": Sharding is storage distribution, not semantic splitting. Not "Fixed-size chunking": Fixed-size splits by counts regardless of meaning. Not "No chunking": No chunking keeps the whole document as one unit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A developer is exposing tools to an LLM-based application using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). For a lightweight, event-driven MCP server, which AWS compute pattern is recommended?

options.text: Store it as an S3 object
Run it only on a developer laptop in production
Run it on a dedicated mainframe
Run the MCP server on AWS Lambda

explanation: A common AWS pattern is hosting a lightweight MCP server on Lambda for serverless, event-driven tool exposure. Not "Store it as an S3 object": An MCP server is a running service, not a static object. Not "Run it only on a developer laptop in production": Local laptops are not a production hosting pattern. Not "Run it on a dedicated mainframe": Mainframes are not an AWS MCP hosting pattern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A complex, long-running MCP server needs more control over runtime, networking, and resources than a function provides. Which AWS pattern fits best?

options.text: Host it as a static website on S3
Use Amazon SES
Convert it to a CloudFront function
Run the MCP server on Amazon ECS (containers)

explanation: Being Python, Strands runs on Lambda and integrates into Step Functions workflows. Not "It must run inside Amazon QuickSight": QuickSight is BI; it does not host agents. Not "It can only run on bare-metal servers": It runs on serverless and managed compute, not bare metal only. Not "It runs exclusively in the browser": It is a server-side SDK, not browser-only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A "model-driven" agent framework differs from a workflow-heavy framework in what key way?

options.text: The model dynamically plans steps and decides tool use, instead of developers hand-coding complex fixed workflows
It removes the need for any model
It forbids using tools
It only supports deterministic if/else graphs

explanation: Model-driven agents let the model reason and orchestrate, reducing hand-built workflow logic. Not "It removes the need for any model": The model is central to a model-driven approach. Not "It forbids using tools": Tool use is a core capability. Not "It only supports deterministic if/else graphs": That describes the workflow-heavy approach it contrasts with. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team wants to run a Strands-built agent in a managed, secure, serverless environment at production scale without managing servers. Which is a natural fit?

options.text: Run it only on a developer's laptop
Deploy it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
Store the code in S3 and never run it
Embed it in a CloudFront cache

explanation: AgentCore Runtime hosts agents from frameworks like Strands in a managed serverless runtime. Not "Run it only on a developer's laptop": A laptop is not production-scale managed hosting. Not "Store the code in S3 and never run it": Storing code does not run the agent. Not "Embed it in a CloudFront cache": CloudFront is a CDN, not an agent runtime. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which TWO are accurate about Amazon Bedrock Agents' capabilities? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They require you to write the orchestration/reasoning loop yourself
They are only for image generation
They can invoke tools/APIs defined via an OpenAPI schema or function definitions
They can integrate a knowledge base for retrieval-augmented responses
They store vectors as a database

explanation: Agents call actions defined by OpenAPI schemas or function definitions. Bedrock Agents can use Knowledge Bases to ground answers. Not "They require you to write the orchestration/reasoning loo…": The managed agent handles the orchestration loop. Not "They are only for image generation": Agents handle reasoning and tool use, not just images. Not "They store vectors as a database": Vector storage is a separate vector-store concern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A production agent platform must provide identity/access to tools, persistent memory, tool gateways, and end-to-end observability across agents built in different frameworks. Which single AWS offering is designed to deliver all of these?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Kendra

explanation: AgentCore bundles Runtime, Identity, Gateway, Memory, and Observability for production agents across frameworks. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Registry": The registry versions models; it is not an agent operations platform. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails are safety policies only. Not "Amazon Kendra": Kendra is enterprise search, not an agent platform. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An education company built a content generation system on Amazon Bedrock that generates practice questions from a mix of curated and scraped data. Reviewers must verify content credibility, so the company wants to add source lineage. Which combination of steps meets this with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to explain model predictions
Register the curated and scraped input datasets with AWS Glue Data Catalog
Use AWS CloudTrail to log reviewer feedback actions
Tag FM outputs with metadata from the data source
Enable Amazon Bedrock invocation logging and correlate logs with the data source

explanation: The Data Catalog creates a searchable, managed inventory of sources with minimal overhead. Tagging outputs with source metadata gives reviewers direct, automated traceability between generated content and its origin. Not "Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to explain model predictions": Clarify is for explainability/bias, not source lineage. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail to log reviewer feedback actions": CloudTrail logs API actions, not content source lineage. Not "Enable Amazon Bedrock invocation logging and correlate lo…": Correlating logs to sources requires manual or custom work and does not directly establish lineage. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A company must replace a production FM only if a new model performs better, following a sequential, reviewed validation process. Which ordering of the five steps is correct?

options.text: Create test dataset → Define metrics → Analyze & report → A/B test → Quality gates
Define metrics → Create test dataset → A/B test vs production → Automated quality gates (Step Functions) → Analyze & report
A/B test → Define metrics → Create dataset → Analyze & report → Quality gates
Quality gates → A/B test → Analyze & report → Define metrics → Create dataset

explanation: Decide how to measure, get data, compare, gate the rollout, then document — the correct sequence. Not "Create test dataset → Define metrics → Analyze & report →…": You must define metrics before building the dataset and analyze after testing, not before. Not "A/B test → Define metrics → Create dataset → Analyze & re…": You cannot A/B test before defining metrics and preparing data. Not "Quality gates → A/B test → Analyze & report → Define metr…": Gates and testing cannot precede defining metrics and data. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A third-party application needs secure authentication to use Amazon Bedrock: integrate the existing IdP, keep audit logs, eliminate long-lived credentials, and provide temporary access. Which TWO solutions meet these requirements? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Create IAM users per employee and rotate keys with Secrets Manager
Use Amazon Cognito with OIDC to authenticate via the IdP and exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials
Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer validating against LDAP and issuing JWTs
Deploy AWS IAM Identity Center with SAML federation to the IdP and grant Bedrock via permission sets
Create an IAM role with STS AssumeRole but store IAM user credentials in app config

explanation: Cognito OIDC federates the IdP, issues temporary credentials, and audits via CloudTrail. IAM Identity Center with SAML federates the IdP, uses temporary credentials, and logs via CloudTrail. Not "Create IAM users per employee and rotate keys with Secret…": IAM users use long-lived keys and do not federate the IdP. Not "Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer validating against L…": Custom LDAP/JWT does not provide temporary AWS credentials or native IdP federation. Not "Create an IAM role with STS AssumeRole but store IAM user…": Storing IAM user credentials violates the no-long-lived-credentials requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security.html

prompt: A Bedrock RAG app retrieves many relevant docs, but the most relevant info often appears lower in results. Which TWO steps improve relevance ranking with MINIMAL operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Knowledge Bases with hybrid search and OpenSearch Serverless to combine vectors with keyword matching
Configure OpenSearch Serverless with Learning to Rank for relevance scoring
Create Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and a custom similarity scoring algorithm
Use SageMaker JumpStart FMs with Kendra Intelligent Ranking and custom relevancy algorithms
Use Amazon Bedrock reranker models with Amazon OpenSearch Service to reorder results by semantic relevance

explanation: Hybrid search improves retrieval relevance by blending semantic and keyword matching. Bedrock rerankers are purpose-built to reorder results so the most relevant surface first. Not "Configure OpenSearch Serverless with Learning to Rank for…": Learning to Rank requires custom trained/maintained models — more overhead. Not "Create Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and a custom simil…": Custom scoring and DB management add operational overhead. Not "Use SageMaker JumpStart FMs with Kendra Intelligent Ranki…": Bedrock built-in reranking is simpler and more integrated than custom ranking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A company must deploy existing Python agent code to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with minimal overhead, auto-managing HTTP server, endpoint routing, and health monitoring, supporting sub-second and streaming responses. Which TWO approaches fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy on Amazon ECS Fargate using a custom container image running the AgentCore SDK
Implement a FastAPI server with /invocations and /ping and container orchestration
Use the AgentCore SDK with the @app.entrypoint decorator to auto-handle server setup and endpoints
Use the AgentCore starter toolkit for automated packaging, containerization, and deployment
Deploy on Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoints with a custom inference container

explanation: The SDK auto-creates the server on port 8080, the /invocations and /ping endpoints, and handles JSON/streaming. The toolkit automates ARM64 build, ECR push, and CreateAgentRuntime deployment with minimal overhead. Not "Deploy on Amazon ECS Fargate using a custom container ima…": Custom containers/task definitions add management overhead with no auto server/health setup. Not "Implement a FastAPI server with /invocations and /ping an…": Manual FastAPI/Docker/orchestration adds overhead. Not "Deploy on Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoints with a cus…": Custom inference containers and autoscaling add infrastructure overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A diagnostic imaging app must run similarity searches across 50 million images, processed daily but searched infrequently, with a cost-effective, responsive, no-infrastructure solution. Which is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Store vectors in RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector
Store vectors in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and use vector search
Use DynamoDB to store vectors and custom similarity logic in Lambda
Create an Amazon S3 vector bucket with vector indexes to store image embeddings and perform similarity searches

explanation: S3 Vectors is serverless, scales to billions of vectors, and is cost-optimized for infrequent searches. Not "Store vectors in RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector": RDS requires managing instances and is not cost-effective for infrequent workloads. Not "Store vectors in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and use vec…": OpenSearch Serverless suits frequent low-latency search; provisioned capacity is underused for rare searches. Not "Use DynamoDB to store vectors and custom similarity logic…": DynamoDB has no native vector search; custom logic adds latency and cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A single-Region Bedrock app gets "Too many requests" at peak. The company must increase throughput without extra operational overhead, keep the same API, and use the same FM. Which is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Create a Lambda that defaults to the original Region and falls back to a secondary Region
Use cross-Region inference to distribute traffic across multiple Regions in the geography
Use prompt routing to distribute traffic across multiple FMs from the same family
Use provisioned throughput to provision higher throughput

explanation: Cross-Region inference automatically spreads load across Regions, same model and API, no extra ops. Not "Create a Lambda that defaults to the original Region and …": A custom Lambda failover adds operational overhead. Not "Use prompt routing to distribute traffic across multiple …": Prompt routing needs two different models; the requirement is the same FM. Not "Use provisioned throughput to provision higher throughput": Provisioned throughput suits steady usage, not occasional peaks. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An AI assistant must include new S3 documents ASAP and exclude deleted ones ASAP, using a Bedrock Knowledge Base with S3 as the data source. Which solution is scalable, event-driven, and resilient?

options.text: EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes → Lambda that runs StartIngestionJob
EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes → Lambda that tracks S3 changes
S3 Event Notifications → Lambda directly calling the ingest/delete APIs
S3 Event Notifications → Amazon SQS → Lambda calling IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments

explanation: SQS buffers spikes and retries between S3 events and Lambda, ensuring no updates are missed. Not "EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes → Lambda that runs …": Periodic full re-sync is inefficient and not event-driven. Not "EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes → Lambda that track…": Time-based polling is not near-real-time and is inefficient. Not "S3 Event Notifications → Lambda directly calling the inge…": Direct invocation lacks buffering/retry and can fail under load. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A RAG app returns generic "no relevant information found" after a code update. No errors, FM invokes successfully (X-Ray), OpenSearch is healthy, latency normal. What is the cause?

options.text: The FM temperature parameter was increased
The Lambda role is missing bedrock:InvokeModel
The embeddings were deleted during the update and not re-indexed
The updated Lambda uses a different version of the embedding model than was used to index documents

explanation: Embedding drift creates a vector-space mismatch between queries and stored vectors, silently breaking retrieval. Not "The FM temperature parameter was increased": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval. Not "The Lambda role is missing bedrock:InvokeModel": The model invokes successfully, so the permission exists. Not "The embeddings were deleted during the update and not re-…": Deleted embeddings would surface as errors or failed queries; none are observed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A financial services company wants a mobile app for account inquiries built from large volumes of customer-support email stored in S3 that contains PII which must not appear in search results. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to redact PII and integrate with Amazon DocumentDB for queries
Use Amazon Textract to extract text, Amazon Macie to scan for PII, integrate with Kendra
Use Amazon Kendra and a Bedrock FM system prompt to remove PII during query processing
Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from the email data, then integrate with Amazon Kendra for enterprise search

explanation: Comprehend redacts PII before indexing; Kendra provides managed enterprise search of the processed data. Not "Use Amazon Comprehend to redact PII and integrate with Am…": DocumentDB needs custom search and lacks NLP for natural-language enterprise search. Not "Use Amazon Textract to extract text, Amazon Macie to scan…": Macie discovers/classifies PII but does not redact it for GenAI; Textract targets scanned docs, not raw email. Not "Use Amazon Kendra and a Bedrock FM system prompt to remov…": System prompts cannot reliably remove PII and can be bypassed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A company must analyze videos and photos from public fashion shows to extract style elements, store results, and present a trend dashboard, with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution fits?

options.text: Use Step Functions to process media with Amazon Bedrock multimodal FMs; store results in S3; visualize with Amazon QuickSight
Use Claude for text analysis and Stable Diffusion for images, store in OpenSearch, build Managed Grafana
Use Rekognition Custom Labels (trained model), store in DynamoDB, build a Managed Grafana dashboard with custom plugins
Use EventBridge + Lambda with Amazon QuickSight Q to analyze videos/photos and a QuickSight dashboard

explanation: Bedrock multimodal FMs analyze media directly with no custom model training; Step Functions + QuickSight are serverless. Not "Use Claude for text analysis and Stable Diffusion for ima…": Managing OpenSearch, multiple FMs, and custom dashboards adds overhead, and it analyzes text rather than visuals. Not "Use Rekognition Custom Labels (trained model), store in D…": Custom model training and Grafana plugins add overhead. Not "Use EventBridge + Lambda with Amazon QuickSight Q to anal…": QuickSight Q answers questions about existing dashboard data; it cannot analyze media. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A financial company needs Bedrock prompt templates governed via approval workflows and comprehensive logging of all model invocations with 7-year retention. Which TWO steps meet this with MINIMAL overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs into CloudTrail Lake with 7-year retention
Use EventBridge to capture invocation events to CloudWatch Logs then export to S3 Object Lock
Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with multi-stage approval workflows and IAM multi-party authorization
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 with S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) for 7 years, with per-business-unit prefixes
Store prompt templates in DynamoDB with item-level permissions for approvals

explanation: Prompt Management natively handles versioned templates with multi-stage approvals. Invocation logging plus immutable Object Lock storage meets comprehensive 7-year retention with low overhead. Not "Enable CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs into C…": CloudTrail captures API metadata, not full prompt/response content. Not "Use EventBridge to capture invocation events to CloudWatc…": Custom pipelines add failure points and do not provide a complete audit trail. Not "Store prompt templates in DynamoDB with item-level permis…": Custom approval logic in DynamoDB adds development overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A company requires that all InvokeModel and Converse calls apply Bedrock guardrails, enforced in the MOST operationally efficient way. Which solution fits?

options.text: Configure IAM policies with both GuardrailIdentifier and PromptRouterArn condition keys
Store guardrail IDs in SSM Parameter Store and have a Lambda fetch them per call
Configure IAM policies for InvokeModel/Converse with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key on all roles that access Bedrock FMs
Create a Lambda that validates guardrails before proxying all requests to Bedrock

explanation: The GuardrailIdentifier condition key centrally enforces guardrail usage with no custom code. Not "Configure IAM policies with both GuardrailIdentifier and …": PromptRouterArn is unrelated to guardrail enforcement and adds needless complexity. Not "Store guardrail IDs in SSM Parameter Store and have a Lam…": Per-call lookups add latency and Lambda maintenance. Not "Create a Lambda that validates guardrails before proxying…": A proxy Lambda adds a bottleneck/failure point and custom maintenance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security.html

prompt: A virtual assistant using Anthropic Claude on Bedrock must stop generating output after a specific phrase appears in the response. Which solution meets this?

options.text: Use the temperature parameter to control the phrase likelihood
Use the top-k parameter to control token diversity
Use the stop sequences parameter in the inference call to specify the trigger phrase
Add the trigger phrase "stop at this phrase" in the user prompt

explanation: Stop sequences are a built-in, reliable API mechanism that halts generation at the specified string. Not "Use the temperature parameter to control the phrase likel…": Temperature controls randomness, not the stopping point. Not "Use the top-k parameter to control token diversity": top-k controls sampling, not stopping. Not "Add the trigger phrase "stop at this phrase" in the user …": Relying on the model to follow the instruction is unreliable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A cross-functional team wants to use Amazon Q Developer to optimize productivity, enforce integration patterns, automate performance tuning, and accelerate testing. Which TWO steps meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Q Developer for security analysis but require manual security-team approval of all changes
Configure Q Developer to auto-generate/refactor integration code, give targeted API guidance, and suggest performance optimizations across the codebase
Use Q Developer to retrospectively document integration patterns across codebases
Limit Q Developer to merge-request fixes with periodic manual refactoring cycles
Integrate Q Developer automated unit/integration test generation into the CI/CD pipelines

explanation: Real-time generation, refactoring, and optimization boost productivity and reduce integration errors. Embedding test generation in CI/CD continuously validates components and catches defects early. Not "Use Q Developer for security analysis but require manual …": Mandatory manual approval of everything creates a bottleneck. Not "Use Q Developer to retrospectively document integration p…": Reactive analysis misses real-time assistance benefits. Not "Limit Q Developer to merge-request fixes with periodic ma…": Restricting to merge time slows resolution and underuses its capabilities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A DJL-served LLM on 8-GPU instances is underutilized: real max sequence length is 10x smaller than configured, concurrency is low, and the model fits within 4 GPUs. Which TWO steps improve resource utilization? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase the number of instances and spread requests more evenly
Use tensor parallelism degree 8 to split the model across all GPUs
Use tensor parallelism with a degree of 4 to deploy two model replicas per instance
Enable speculative decoding to reduce per-request latency
Reduce the model's maximum sequence length to allow a higher rolling batch size per GPU

explanation: Since the model fits in 4 GPUs, degree 4 packs two replicas across 8 GPUs for full utilization. Freeing memory by lowering max sequence length increases batch size, throughput, and concurrency. Not "Increase the number of instances and spread requests more…": This does not raise per-instance concurrency or reduce the memory footprint. Not "Use tensor parallelism degree 8 to split the model across…": Degree 8 serves only one replica across 8 GPUs, leaving half idle since the model fits in 4. Not "Enable speculative decoding to reduce per-request latency": Speculative decoding improves latency, not utilization. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A developer must deploy a Hugging Face text-to-image model (tested in SageMaker JumpStart) for on-demand generation. It must use GPUs, handle text datasets up to 50 MB, and respond within 15 minutes. Which deployment strategy fits?

options.text: Create a SageMaker batch transform job on a GPU instance
Deploy a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint on a general-purpose instance
Deploy a SageMaker Real-Time endpoint on a GPU instance
Deploy a SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint on an accelerated (GPU) instance, invoked on demand via Lambda

explanation: Async endpoints support up to ~15-minute runtimes, large payloads (up to ~1 GB), and GPUs. Not "Create a SageMaker batch transform job on a GPU instance": Batch transform is offline, not on-demand within 15 minutes. Not "Deploy a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint on a gen…": Serverless inference does not support GPUs. Not "Deploy a SageMaker Real-Time endpoint on a GPU instance": Real-time endpoints cap payloads near 25 MB, failing the 50 MB requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A news company wants a web editor where journalists click "analyze" and immediately receive streamed style-guide revisions; articles carry content-category metadata. Which architecture meets this with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: API Gateway REST API with Lambda function URLs and chunked transfer encoding
API Gateway WebSocket API → Lambda reads the category metadata, routes to the right Bedrock model, uses Prompt Management for style rules, and streams suggestions via the Bedrock streaming API
SQS ingestion → Step Functions → Lambda → DynamoDB → API Gateway WebSocket streaming
Application Load Balancer with ECS tasks running custom routing/style containers

explanation: WebSockets give serverless real-time streaming; Prompt Management governs rules; streaming returns suggestions immediately. Not "API Gateway REST API with Lambda function URLs and chunke…": REST is poorly suited to long-lived real-time streaming. Not "SQS ingestion → Step Functions → Lambda → DynamoDB → API …": SQS polling adds latency, defeating immediate feedback on click. Not "Application Load Balancer with ECS tasks running custom r…": Custom ECS containers add infrastructure management overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A Bedrock Knowledge Base ingests documents from multiple S3 buckets, and the team needs to monitor ingestion to identify and troubleshoot document-processing issues. Which solution meets this?

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail to track API calls related to ingestion
Implement Bedrock model invocation logging to capture document processing metrics
Enable CloudWatch Application Signals to detect knowledge base performance issues
Configure knowledge base logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights to query for failed document processing

explanation: KB logging records per-file status (e.g., RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, INDEXING_FAILED) for troubleshooting. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail to track API calls related to inges…": CloudTrail logs API calls, not document-level processing status. Not "Implement Bedrock model invocation logging to capture doc…": Invocation logging captures inference calls, not ingestion. Not "Enable CloudWatch Application Signals to detect knowledge…": Application Signals monitors app performance, not KB ingestion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A customer-support solution needs to route each user query to one of several specialized agents (billing, technical, account) and keep a coherent conversation across them. Which AWS open-source framework is purpose-built for multi-agent orchestration and routing?

options.text: AWS Agent Squad (multi-agent orchestrator)
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

explanation: Agent Squad orchestrates multiple specialized agents, routing each query to the best-suited agent while maintaining unified conversation context. Not "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases provide RAG retrieval, not multi-agent routing. Not "Amazon Comprehend": Comprehend is NLP analysis, not an agent orchestration framework. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails enforce content safety; they do not orchestrate multiple agents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: In AWS Agent Squad, how is each incoming user request assigned to the right specialized agent?

options.text: Requests are assigned round-robin regardless of content
The user must manually pick an agent each turn
An LLM-powered classifier analyzes the input, agent descriptions, and conversation history to select the best-suited agent
Agents are chosen by alphabetical order of their names

explanation: Agent Squad uses a classifier (e.g., the default Bedrock Classifier) to route requests by intent. Not "Requests are assigned round-robin regardless of content": Routing is intent-based via the classifier, not blind round-robin. Not "The user must manually pick an agent each turn": Routing is automatic; users do not hand-pick agents per turn. Not "Agents are chosen by alphabetical order of their names": Selection is based on classification of intent/context, not naming order. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which TWO are accurate about AWS Agent Squad? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can only run a single agent at a time and has no routing
It is a vector database
Member agents can be different types, such as Amazon Bedrock model agents, Amazon Lex bots, or AWS Lambda functions
It requires Provisioned Throughput to classify requests
It maintains unified conversation context across agents for coherent multi-turn interactions

explanation: Agent Squad supports heterogeneous agents including Bedrock, Lex, and Lambda-backed agents. The orchestrator keeps shared context so conversations stay coherent as routing changes. Not "It can only run a single agent at a time and has no routing": Its entire purpose is routing across multiple agents. Not "It is a vector database": Agent Squad is an orchestration framework, not a vector store. Not "It requires Provisioned Throughput to classify requests": Classification uses a model/classifier; it does not mandate provisioned capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: In Agent Squad, what is the difference between the classifier's view and an individual agent's view of conversation history?

options.text: The classifier has a global view across agents, while each agent sees only its own conversation history
History is never retained anywhere
Every agent always sees the full global history
The classifier sees nothing and routes blindly

explanation: This lets the classifier route with full context while keeping each agent focused on its domain. Not "History is never retained anywhere": Agent Squad maintains conversation context. Not "Every agent always sees the full global history": Agents see only their own history; the global view belongs to the classifier. Not "The classifier sees nothing and routes blindly": The classifier specifically uses global context to route. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: How do AWS Strands Agents and AWS Agent Squad differ in purpose?

options.text: Both are vector stores
Strands is a model-driven SDK for building an individual agent; Agent Squad orchestrates and routes across multiple specialized agents
They are identical products
Strands routes between many agents and Agent Squad builds one agent

explanation: Strands builds single agents (model + prompt + tools); Agent Squad coordinates many agents. Not "Both are vector stores": Neither is a vector store. Not "They are identical products": They serve different roles: single-agent SDK vs multi-agent orchestration. Not "Strands routes between many agents and Agent Squad builds…": This reverses their roles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team wants an agent to interleave reasoning with tool actions (think, act, observe, repeat) using structured steps orchestrated on AWS. Which pattern/approach matches?

options.text: Sharding the vector index
A single one-shot prompt with no tools
The ReAct pattern, which can be implemented with AWS Step Functions to structure reasoning and tool-use steps
Provisioned Throughput scaling

explanation: ReAct (Reason + Act) interleaves reasoning and actions; Step Functions can structure these steps. Not "Sharding the vector index": Sharding is storage tuning, unrelated to agent reasoning. Not "A single one-shot prompt with no tools": One-shot prompting does not interleave reasoning and tool actions. Not "Provisioned Throughput scaling": That reserves capacity; it is not a reasoning pattern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A complex task benefits from breaking the problem into intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final answer. Which prompting technique is this?

options.text: Top-k sampling
Chain-of-thought reasoning
Hybrid search
Stop sequences

explanation: Chain-of-thought prompts the model to reason through intermediate steps, improving complex task performance. Not "Top-k sampling": top-k controls candidate tokens, not reasoning structure. Not "Hybrid search": Hybrid search is a retrieval technique, not a reasoning method. Not "Stop sequences": Stop sequences end generation; they do not elicit step-by-step reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agentic workflow must pause for a human to review and approve high-impact actions before continuing. Which approach implements this human-in-the-loop control on AWS?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a review/approval step (e.g., with a callback) before the agent proceeds
Remove all guardrails to speed approvals
Store the action in S3 and hope a human notices
Increase the model temperature so it self-approves

explanation: Step Functions can pause for human approval (task tokens/callbacks) to gate sensitive actions. Not "Remove all guardrails to speed approvals": Removing safeguards is the opposite of controlled human review. Not "Store the action in S3 and hope a human notices": Passive storage is not an orchestrated approval mechanism. Not "Increase the model temperature so it self-approves": Temperature affects randomness, not human approval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A developer calls Amazon Bedrock with the InvokeModel API across several providers and finds each model expects a different request body. What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: InvokeModel cannot be used for text models
InvokeModel uses one identical body for every model
InvokeModel request/response bodies are model-specific, so the JSON payload must match each model's schema
InvokeModel only accepts CSV

explanation: With InvokeModel you format the body to the chosen model's native request schema. Not "InvokeModel cannot be used for text models": InvokeModel is a primary API for text models. Not "InvokeModel uses one identical body for every model": Native InvokeModel bodies differ per provider/model. Not "InvokeModel only accepts CSV": Bedrock requests are JSON, and the schema is model-specific. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants a single, consistent request/response format for multi-turn chat that works across multiple Bedrock models without hand-coding each model's native schema. Which API should they use?

options.text: The Rerank API
StartIngestionJob
InvokeModel with a model-specific body for each model
The Amazon Bedrock Converse API, which provides a unified messages interface across supported models

explanation: Converse abstracts model-specific formats into a consistent messages structure with roles, simplifying portability. Not "The Rerank API": Rerank reorders retrieved documents; it is not a chat interface. Not "StartIngestionJob": That ingests data into a Knowledge Base; it is not a chat inference API. Not "InvokeModel with a model-specific body for each model": InvokeModel requires per-model formatting, which is what they want to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: When formatting input for a dialog-based application using the Bedrock Converse API, how is the conversation typically structured?

options.text: As a CSV of tokens
As a sequence of messages with roles (e.g., user and assistant), plus an optional system instruction
As a vector embedding only
As a single concatenated string with no roles

explanation: Conversation formatting uses role-tagged messages (user/assistant) and an optional system prompt. Not "As a CSV of tokens": Conversations are structured messages, not token CSVs. Not "As a vector embedding only": Embeddings are for retrieval, not the chat message structure. Not "As a single concatenated string with no roles": Dialog formatting uses structured role-tagged turns, not one undifferentiated string. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A pipeline sends requests to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. What determines the required input data format?

options.text: All SageMaker endpoints require the Bedrock Converse schema
The endpoint/container's expected content type and serializer (e.g., application/json or text/csv) per the model's contract
SageMaker endpoints accept any format without serialization
SageMaker endpoints only accept audio

explanation: SageMaker endpoints expect input matching the container's content type and the model's input contract. Not "All SageMaker endpoints require the Bedrock Converse schema": SageMaker input depends on the container, not the Bedrock Converse format. Not "SageMaker endpoints accept any format without serialization": Input must match the endpoint's expected content type/serializer. Not "SageMaker endpoints only accept audio": Format depends on the model; it is not audio-only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Inconsistent, messy text is degrading FM response quality. A team wants to normalize and reformat inputs before inference with minimal custom infrastructure. Which approach fits?

options.text: Send raw messy text directly and raise temperature
Disable all preprocessing to save cost
Use AWS Lambda functions to normalize/reformat the data (and optionally Amazon Comprehend to extract entities) before calling the FM
Provision a large GPU cluster to compensate

explanation: Lambda is a low-overhead way to clean and reformat inputs; Comprehend can enrich them prior to inference. Not "Send raw messy text directly and raise temperature": Higher temperature adds randomness and does not fix input quality. Not "Disable all preprocessing to save cost": Skipping preprocessing worsens response quality. Not "Provision a large GPU cluster to compensate": Hardware does not fix input formatting/quality issues. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Why is correct input formatting important when integrating foundation models?

options.text: Models have model-specific input requirements; malformed or mismatched formatting causes errors or poor responses
All models accept identical raw input, so formatting never matters
Formatting is only relevant for image models
Formatting only affects billing, not behavior

explanation: Matching each model's expected request/message format is necessary for valid calls and good output quality. Not "All models accept identical raw input, so formatting neve…": Input requirements vary by model/API; formatting matters. Not "Formatting is only relevant for image models": It applies to text, chat, and other modalities, not just images. Not "Formatting only affects billing, not behavior": Formatting affects whether the call succeeds and the quality of the response. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: An education company built a content generation system on Amazon Bedrock that generates practice questions to quiz end users on a topic. The system consumes a mix of curated data and scraped data in the topic domain. Reviewers must approve the generated question-response sets before end users can access them. The company wants to add source lineage so reviewers can verify the credibility of the content. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock invocation logging and correlate the logs with the data source.
Register the curated and scraped input datasets with AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Use AWS CloudTrail to log reviewer feedback actions.
Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to explain model predictions.
Tag FM outputs with metadata from the data source.

explanation: The Data Catalog creates a searchable inventory of data sources reviewers can use to verify origin and credibility, using a managed service with structured metadata and minimal overhead. Tagging the generated questions with metadata about the curated/scraped sources gives direct, automated traceability between content and its origins and immediate access to source information for reviewers. Not "Enable Amazon Bedrock invocation logging and correlate th…": Invocation logging tracks model interactions, but correlating logs to data sources requires manual work or custom automation. It captures usage data without helping reviewers verify content credibility. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail to log reviewer feedback actions.": CloudTrail logs API calls and can record approval/rejection actions, but it does not provide source lineage of the generated content. Not "Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to explain model predictions.": Clarify provides model explainability and bias detection, not source lineage tracking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A company is implementing a systematic evaluation process to replace an in-production FM in Amazon Bedrock with a new model. The change depends on the new model demonstrating better performance, and the company must follow a sequential validation process in which each step is reviewed and approved before proceeding. Which ordering of the five steps is correct?

options.text: Define evaluation metrics -> Conduct A/B testing -> Create a test dataset -> Analyze results and generate a report -> Implement automated quality gates.

Define evaluation metrics (relevance, factual accuracy, fluency) -> Create a test dataset with diverse scenarios and edge cases -> Conduct A/B testing against the production model -> Implement automated quality gates with AWS Step Functions -> Analyze results and generate an evaluation report.
Create a test dataset -> Define evaluation metrics -> Conduct A/B testing -> Analyze results and generate a report -> Implement automated quality gates with AWS Step Functions.
Conduct A/B testing -> Define evaluation metrics -> Create a test dataset -> Implement automated quality gates -> Analyze results and generate a report.

explanation: Metrics must be defined first so the dataset and tests can target them; the dataset enables A/B testing; quality gates then enforce the criteria before a final analysis and report. Not "Define evaluation metrics -> Conduct A/B testing -> Creat…": The test dataset must exist before A/B testing, and gates should precede the final report. Not "Create a test dataset -> Define evaluation metrics -> Con…": Metrics should be defined before the dataset is built, and quality gates belong before the final reporting step, not after. Not "Conduct A/B testing -> Define evaluation metrics -> Creat…": You cannot run meaningful A/B testing before metrics and a test dataset exist. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company needs secure authentication for a third-party application that uses Amazon Bedrock. The solution must integrate with the company's existing identity provider (IdP), maintain comprehensive audit logs of authentication and API calls, eliminate long-lived credentials, and provide temporary access to Amazon Bedrock. Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an IAM role and configure federation with AWS STS AssumeRole, storing the application's IAM user credentials in the application configuration.
Create IAM users for each employee, assign permissions through IAM policies, and rotate credentials with AWS Secrets Manager.
Deploy AWS IAM Identity Center with SAML federation to the IdP and configure custom permission sets that grant access to Amazon Bedrock.
Configure an Amazon API Gateway Lambda authorizer to validate credentials against LDAP and issue signed JWTs for Amazon Bedrock access.
Implement an OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration with Amazon Cognito that authenticates users through the IdP and exchanges tokens for temporary AWS credentials to access Amazon Bedrock.

explanation: IAM Identity Center with SAML integrates with the IdP, issues temporary credentials (no long-lived keys), and provides audit logging through CloudTrail. Cognito with OIDC authenticates through the existing IdP, exchanges identity tokens for temporary AWS credentials (no long-lived keys), and logs via CloudTrail. Not "Create an IAM role and configure federation with AWS STS …": Storing IAM user credentials violates the requirement to eliminate long-lived credentials and does not integrate with the IdP properly. Not "Create IAM users for each employee, assign permissions th…": IAM users rely on persistent access keys, do not integrate with the IdP, and do not provide temporary access. Not "Configure an Amazon API Gateway Lambda authorizer to vali…": This does not provide temporary AWS credentials, requires custom development, and does not use built-in identity federation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A company is developing a RAG application on Amazon Bedrock that processes customer support documents. The application retrieves many relevant documents, but users report that the most relevant information often appears lower in the results. The company wants to improve relevance ranking so the most useful information appears first. Which combination of steps will improve relevance with MINIMAL operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker JumpStart FMs with Amazon Kendra Intelligent Ranking to create custom relevancy scoring algorithms.
Use Knowledge Bases with hybrid search and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to combine vector embeddings with keyword matching.
Configure Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with the Bedrock Knowledge Bases plugin and use OpenSearch Learning to Rank for relevance scoring.
