Create an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database with pgvector and a custom similarity scoring algorithm combining vector distances with metadata.
Use Amazon Bedrock reranker models with Amazon OpenSearch Service to reorder retrieved results based on semantic relevance to the query.

explanation: Hybrid search combines semantic vector embeddings with keyword matching to improve retrieval relevance with minimal overhead. Bedrock reranker models are purpose-built to score query-document relevance and reorder results so the most relevant information appears first. Not "Use Amazon SageMaker JumpStart FMs with Amazon Kendra Int…": Bedrock already provides built-in reranking optimized for FM integration; this approach is more complex and less integrated. Not "Configure Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with the Bedrock K…": Learning to Rank is an open-source plugin that requires custom scoring and trained, maintained models — more overhead than built-in Bedrock features. Not "Create an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database with pgvector…": This requires custom development and managing the vector database — more operational overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A financial services company must deploy existing Python agent code to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime to reduce infrastructure management and operational complexity. The agent must handle quick data lookups (sub-second) and comprehensive research report generation (streaming responses over several minutes). The solution must automatically manage HTTP server configuration, endpoint routing, and health monitoring. Which deployment approaches will meet these requirements with MINIMAL operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy the agent using the AgentCore starter toolkit for automated packaging, containerization, and deployment workflows.
Deploy the agent on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate using a custom container image running the AgentCore SDK.
Implement the AgentCore SDK with the @app.entrypoint decorator to automatically handle server setup and endpoint management.
Implement a FastAPI server configured with /invocations and /ping endpoints and container orchestration.
Deploy the agent on Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints using a custom inference container.

explanation: The starter toolkit automates packaging, ARM64 container builds, ECR creation/push, and deployment via CreateAgentRuntime — minimal overhead. The SDK auto-creates an HTTP server on port 8080, implements the required /invocations and /ping endpoints, and supports both JSON and streaming responses without manual configuration. Not "Deploy the agent on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate using a cus…": This requires building and maintaining Dockerfiles, images, and task definitions with no automatic HTTP server setup or health monitoring. Not "Implement a FastAPI server configured with /invocations a…": FastAPI requires manual configuration of endpoints, JSON/streaming handling, Dockerfiles, and orchestration — more operational overhead. Not "Deploy the agent on Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoin…": This increases infrastructure overhead: building images, configuring the inference server, auto scaling, and health monitoring. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A company is building a diagnostic imaging application that performs similarity searches across 50 million images to assist with diagnosis. New images are processed daily, but similarity searches are performed infrequently, only when users need to find similar cases. The company wants a cost-effective solution with responsive search performance and no infrastructure management. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Store image vectors in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and use the pgvector extension.
Use Amazon DynamoDB to store image vectors and implement custom similarity search logic with AWS Lambda.
Store image vectors in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and use vector search for similarity searches.
Create an Amazon S3 vector bucket with vector indexes to store image embeddings and perform similarity searches.

explanation: Amazon S3 Vectors is fully managed and serverless, scales to billions of vectors, suits infrequent searches, requires no provisioning, and bills only for what you use. Not "Store image vectors in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and use …": RDS requires provisioning and managing instances (not 'no infrastructure management') and is not cost-effective for infrequent workloads. Not "Use Amazon DynamoDB to store image vectors and implement …": DynamoDB has no built-in vector similarity search; custom Lambda logic adds latency and compute cost. Not "Store image vectors in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and u…": OpenSearch Serverless is optimized for high-throughput, frequent searches; you pay for provisioned capacity that stays underutilized with infrequent searches. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An ecommerce company uses Amazon Bedrock in a single AWS Region to generate product descriptions and recommendations. During peak periods it receives "Too many requests, please wait before trying again." errors. The company must increase invocation throughput during peaks without additional operational overhead, keep compatibility with the existing Bedrock API, and use the same FM. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Use prompt routing to distribute traffic across multiple FMs from the same family.
Use provisioned throughput to provision a higher level of throughput for the FM.
Create an AWS Lambda function to invoke the model in the original Region by default and fall back to a secondary Region.
Use cross-Region inference to distribute traffic across multiple Regions within a geographic area.

explanation: Cross-Region inference automatically distributes inference requests across multiple Regions in your geography, increasing throughput with no extra infrastructure and the same API/FM. Not "Use prompt routing to distribute traffic across multiple …": Intelligent prompt routing requires at least two different models from the same family; the requirement is to use the same FM. Not "Use provisioned throughput to provision a higher level of…": Provisioned throughput suits consistent, predictable usage, not occasional peaks, and is less cost-effective here. Not "Create an AWS Lambda function to invoke the model in the …": A Lambda intermediary must be built and maintained, increasing cost and operational overhead versus a built-in feature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company uses an AI assistant that answers questions from internal documents stored in Amazon S3, using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with S3 as the data source. The company wants new documents reflected in responses as soon as possible and deleted documents excluded as soon as possible. A developer must build a scalable, event-driven, and resilient solution. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure EventBridge Scheduler to run every 5 minutes and invoke a Lambda that tracks S3 changes and calls IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments.
Configure S3 Event Notifications to send object-created/deleted events to an Amazon SQS queue, and have a Lambda poll the queue and call IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments.
Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke a Lambda on object-created/deleted events that calls IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments.
Configure EventBridge Scheduler to run every 5 minutes and invoke a Lambda that syncs S3 with the knowledge base via StartIngestionJob.

explanation: SQS buffers events between S3 and Lambda, absorbs spikes, provides automatic retries, and ensures no updates are missed — scalable and resilient. Not "Configure EventBridge Scheduler to run every 5 minutes an…": This is time-based rather than near real-time, and tracking changes in Lambda is not operationally efficient. Not "Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke a Lambda on ob…": Direct S3-to-Lambda invocation has no buffering or retry support and can fail under high load. Not "Configure EventBridge Scheduler to run every 5 minutes an…": Periodic full scanning is inefficient, introduces delays, and is not event-driven. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A financial services company runs a RAG application that answers questions from internal market analysis reports. It uses an Amazon Bedrock embedding model and an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster as the vector store; a Lambda function performs embedding and search. After a code update, the app returns generic responses such as 'no relevant information found' even for previously answerable questions. CloudWatch Logs shows no errors, X-Ray confirms successful FM invocation, the cluster is healthy, and query latency is normal. What is the cause of this issue?

options.text: The Amazon Bedrock FM temperature parameter was increased.
The Lambda function's IAM role is missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission.
The document embeddings in OpenSearch were deleted during the update and not re-indexed.
The updated Lambda function uses a different version of the embedding model.

explanation: Embedding drift: query embeddings generated by a different model than was used to index documents cause a vector-space mismatch and ineffective retrieval. Not "The Amazon Bedrock FM temperature parameter was increased.": Temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval; this is a retrieval failure. Not "The Lambda function's IAM role is missing bedrock:InvokeM…": The model is invoked successfully; a missing permission would throw an access error. Not "The document embeddings in OpenSearch were deleted during…": Deleted embeddings would surface in logs or failed queries; with no errors and normal latency, documents are still being retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A financial services company wants a mobile app to help users with account inquiries and general account information. It has a large volume of customer-support email exchanges to use as source material, stored in Amazon S3. The data contains personally identifiable information (PII) that must not appear in search results. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from the email data in S3, and integrate Comprehend with Amazon Kendra to enable enterprise search of the processed data.
Use Amazon Kendra for enterprise search and integrate with an Amazon Bedrock FM, using a system prompt to identify and remove PII during query processing.
Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII, and integrate with Amazon DocumentDB for database queries.
Use Amazon Textract to extract text, Amazon Macie to scan for PII in S3, and integrate Textract and S3 with Amazon Kendra.

explanation: Comprehend detects and redacts PII from text, and Kendra provides managed enterprise search over the processed data for conversational integration. Not "Use Amazon Kendra for enterprise search and integrate wit…": System prompts cannot reliably or consistently remove PII and can be jailbroken — not secure for sensitive financial data. Not "Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII, and integ…": DocumentDB requires custom search development and lacks NLP for natural-language interactions; it is not enterprise search. Not "Use Amazon Textract to extract text, Amazon Macie to scan…": Macie is for data discovery/security posture, not PII redaction for GenAI; Textract targets scanned documents, not raw email text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A company wants an application that analyzes videos and photos from public fashion shows to understand style elements and trends, stores the extracted information, and provides a dashboard summarizing trends. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to process videos and photos with Amazon Bedrock multimodal FMs, store results in S3, and use an Amazon QuickSight dashboard to visualize trends.

Use Amazon EventBridge to trigger Lambda functions that use Amazon QuickSight Q to analyze the videos and photos, store results in S3, and deploy a QuickSight dashboard with ML-powered trend analysis.
Use an Anthropic Claude model in Bedrock to analyze text descriptions, use Stable Diffusion for image analysis, store results in OpenSearch Service, and create a Managed Grafana dashboard.
Use Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels to train a custom model, store results in DynamoDB, and create an Amazon Managed Grafana dashboard with custom plugins.

explanation: Bedrock multimodal FMs (e.g., Amazon Nova Pro, Claude) analyze visual content directly without custom model development; Step Functions orchestrates and QuickSight builds dashboards serverlessly. Not "Use Amazon EventBridge to trigger Lambda functions that u…": QuickSight Q answers questions about data already in a dashboard; it cannot analyze videos or photos. Not "Use an Anthropic Claude model in Bedrock to analyze text …": This manages an OpenSearch cluster and multiple FMs with custom visualizations, and analyzes text descriptions rather than the visual content directly. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels to train a custom mo…": This requires custom model training/maintenance and custom Grafana plugin development — more overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A financial services company uses Amazon Bedrock to build an AI assistant for customer-support reps across multiple business units. A developer must ensure prompt templates are governed through approval workflows, and the company requires comprehensive logging of all model invocations with a 7-year retention period for regulatory compliance. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with MINIMAL operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with multi-stage approval workflows and IAM policies that require multi-party authorization.
Set up EventBridge rules to capture invocation events, route to CloudWatch Logs by business unit, export to S3, and enable S3 Object Lock compliance mode for 7 years.
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs, deliver to CloudTrail Lake with 7-year retention, tag events with business unit ID, and query with CloudTrail Lake.
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3, enable S3 Object Lock compliance mode for 7 years, and create separate prefixes per business unit.
Store prompt templates in DynamoDB tables with composite keys partitioned by business unit and use IAM item-level permissions for approvals.

explanation: Prompt Management creates, parameterizes, versions, and approves prompt templates with multi-stage approvals and access controls — built-in governance for multiple business units. Built-in invocation logging needs minimal setup; Object Lock compliance mode enforces immutable 7-year retention; prefixes segregate business units. Not "Set up EventBridge rules to capture invocation events, ro…": This requires custom configuration and maintenance, adds failure points, and does not provide the comprehensive audit trail needed. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs, d…": CloudTrail captures only API metadata, not the prompt content and model responses needed for regulatory reconstruction. Not "Store prompt templates in DynamoDB tables with composite …": This requires custom development for approval workflows and access control — more overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A company is implementing AI governance requiring all FM interactions to be secured with guardrails. After configuring Amazon Bedrock guardrails, the company must ensure that all InvokeModel and Converse API calls apply the guardrails. Which solution will enforce guardrail compliance for the API calls in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.text: Create a Lambda function that validates and enforces guardrails before proxying requests to Bedrock, used as the exclusive endpoint.
Configure IAM policies for InvokeModel/Converse with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key, applied to all IAM roles that access Bedrock FMs.
Configure IAM policies for InvokeModel/Converse with both the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier and bedrock:PromptRouterArn condition keys, requiring prompt router validation.
Store guardrail identifiers in Systems Manager Parameter Store and have a Lambda retrieve the identifier before each Bedrock call.

explanation: The GuardrailIdentifier condition key centrally and efficiently enforces guardrail compliance across all relevant API calls. Not "Create a Lambda function that validates and enforces guar…": A proxy adds a failure point and bottleneck and requires custom code maintenance — less efficient than built-in capabilities. Not "Configure IAM policies for InvokeModel/Converse with both…": PromptRouterArn filters access by prompt router and is unrelated to guardrail enforcement; it adds complexity without benefit. Not "Store guardrail identifiers in Systems Manager Parameter …": Retrieving the identifier per call adds latency and Lambda maintenance overhead. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A developer is building a virtual assistant using an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. The application sends user queries and expects conversational responses, and the developer wants the application to stop generating output after a specific phrase is produced. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use the top-k parameter to control the diversity of tokens in the output.
Use the stop sequences parameter in the inference call to specify a trigger phrase.
Use the temperature parameter to control the likelihood of the phrase appearing.
Add the trigger phrase 'stop at this phrase' in the user prompt.

explanation: Stop sequences are a built-in API mechanism that halt generation when a specified phrase is produced, directly controlling output. Not "Use the top-k parameter to control the diversity of token…": Top-k controls sampling diversity, not stopping at a phrase. Not "Use the temperature parameter to control the likelihood o…": Temperature controls randomness/creativity, not the stopping point. Not "Add the trigger phrase 'stop at this phrase' in the user …": This relies on the model following instructions, which it may not do reliably. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A cross-functional team is developing a generative AI application on AWS. The team needs to optimize developer productivity, enforce consistent integration patterns, automate performance tuning, and accelerate AI testing across multiple business units using Amazon Q Developer while maintaining application quality. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon Q Developer to retrospectively analyze and document common integration patterns across business units' code bases.
Integrate Amazon Q Developer automated unit and integration test generation into the team's CI/CD pipelines.
Incorporate Amazon Q Developer to resolve coding issues during merge requests, reserving most refactoring and optimization for periodic manual review cycles.
Use Amazon Q Developer to analyze code for security best practices, with mandatory manual security-team approval of all code changes before integration.
Configure Amazon Q Developer to automatically generate and refactor integration code, provide targeted API usage guidance, and suggest performance optimizations across the modular code base.

explanation: Embedding automated test generation into CI/CD continuously validates components, sustaining velocity and quality with early defect detection. This delivers real-time code generation, refactoring, API recommendations, and performance optimization, increasing productivity and reducing integration errors. Not "Use Amazon Q Developer to retrospectively analyze and doc…": Reactive retrospective analysis fails to use real-time assistance for generation, refactoring, and testing. Not "Incorporate Amazon Q Developer to resolve coding issues d…": Limiting use to merge/review stages and infrequent manual cycles does not optimize the core benefits. Not "Use Amazon Q Developer to analyze code for security best …": Mandatory manual approval of all changes creates a bottleneck and does not accelerate workflows or automate tuning/testing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A developer deployed a fine-tuned LLM to an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint using the default continuous-batching configuration with the Deep Java Library (DJL). The model is served on GPU instances with 8 GPUs each. As demand grows, many instances are needed and the developer wants to avoid costs from overutilization. Logs show the maximum I/O sequence length in real requests is 10x smaller than configured, concurrency per instance is low, and profiling shows the model's weights and activations fit entirely within 4 GPUs. Which combination of steps can improve resource utilization? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Split the model across all 8 GPUs using a tensor parallelism degree of 8 to improve memory efficiency.
Increase the number of SageMaker AI instances and spread requests more evenly.
Use tensor parallelism with a degree of 4 to deploy two model replicas on each instance.
Enable speculative decoding to reduce response latency for each request.
Reduce the model's maximum sequence length to allow a higher rolling batch size for each GPU.

explanation: Because the model fits within 4 GPUs, a tensor-parallel degree of 4 creates two replicas across the 8 GPUs, using the hardware fully. With DJL, reducing the max sequence length frees memory for larger batches, increasing throughput and concurrency per instance. Not "Split the model across all 8 GPUs using a tensor parallel…": A degree of 8 serves only one replica across all GPUs, leaving half the capacity underutilized since the model fits in 4 GPUs. Not "Increase the number of SageMaker AI instances and spread …": This does not improve concurrency or reduce the GPU memory footprint; serving-property configuration is the better lever. Not "Enable speculative decoding to reduce response latency fo…": Speculative decoding improves latency, not resource utilization. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A developer tested a pre-trained Hugging Face text-to-image model with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart and now needs to deploy it for on-demand image generation. The solution must use GPUs for inference, handle text datasets up to 50 MB of image descriptions, and provide responses within 15 minutes. Which deployment strategy will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a SageMaker Real-Time Inference endpoint using an accelerated computing instance type and create a Lambda for invocation.
Create a SageMaker AI batch transform job using an accelerated computing instance type and create a Lambda to start the job.
Deploy a SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint using an accelerated computing instance type and create a Lambda for on-demand invocation.
Deploy a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint using a general purpose instance type and create a Lambda for invocation.

explanation: Asynchronous inference supports long-running requests (up to ~15 minutes), GPU instances, and large payloads (up to 1 GB), and scales with usage. Not "Deploy a SageMaker Real-Time Inference endpoint using an …": Real-time endpoints cap payloads near 25 MB, which does not meet the 50 MB requirement. Not "Create a SageMaker AI batch transform job using an accele…": Batch transform is for offline batch processing, not on-demand individual requests within 15 minutes. Not "Deploy a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint using a …": Serverless inference does not support the GPU instances needed for efficient image generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A news media company wants a content-conformance tool that reviews and adjusts articles against a style guide. Journalists need a web-based editor that provides real-time analysis on request: clicking an 'analyze' button should immediately begin streaming suggested revisions into the editor. Articles carry content categories in metadata (news, sports, editorial). The company wants an Amazon Bedrock FM to analyze content and provide immediate feedback. Which architecture will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use an SQS queue for article ingestion, Step Functions to process content, a Lambda to determine category and invoke Bedrock with style-guide prompts, DynamoDB for results, and an API Gateway WebSocket API for streaming.
Configure an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS tasks running custom containers that implement routing and style checking using Bedrock streaming and WebSocket connections.
Create an API Gateway REST API with Lambda function URLs for response streaming using chunked transfer encoding.

Deploy an API Gateway WebSocket API linked to a Lambda that reads the content category from metadata, routes to the appropriate Bedrock model, uses Bedrock Prompt Management for style-guide rules, and uses the Bedrock streaming API to return suggestions in real time.

explanation: WebSocket APIs provide real-time bidirectional communication; the Lambda routes by metadata, Prompt Management manages rules, and the streaming API returns suggestions immediately with minimal infrastructure. Not "Use an SQS queue for article ingestion, Step Functions to…": SQS requires polling and introduces latency, so it does not provide immediate feedback when journalists click 'analyze'. Not "Configure an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS ta…": Running custom containers on ECS requires managing infrastructure, scaling, and deployment — more effort than serverless. Not "Create an API Gateway REST API with Lambda function URLs …": REST APIs are not suited to long-lived real-time streaming connections; size limits and timeouts produce a poor experience. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A company runs a question-answering application that uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base ingesting documents from multiple Amazon S3 buckets. The company needs to monitor the data ingestion process to identify and troubleshoot document-processing issues. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Implement Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to capture metrics about document processing and embedding generation.
Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals to automatically detect and alert on knowledge base performance issues.
Configure knowledge base logging with Amazon CloudWatch Logs as the destination and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query for failed document processing.
Enable AWS CloudTrail to track all API calls related to knowledge base operations and document ingestion.

explanation: Knowledge bases support built-in logging to CloudWatch Logs that records per-file ingestion status (ingested, ignored, failed); Logs Insights can query statuses such as RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, or INDEXING_FAILED. Not "Implement Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to capt…": Model invocation logging captures inference requests, not knowledge base ingestion processes. Not "Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals to automatic…": Application Signals monitors application performance/health and does not integrate with knowledge base ingestion monitoring. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail to track all API calls related to k…": CloudTrail tracks API calls but not the document-level processing information needed to troubleshoot ingestion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A company runs a high-volume Amazon Bedrock summarization workload with steady, predictable traffic 24 hours a day. The team wants the lowest cost per token while guaranteeing that capacity is always available during business-critical hours. Following the Cost Optimization pillar of the Generative AI Lens, which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use on-demand inference for every request.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a committed term for the model.
Increase max tokens per request so fewer calls are needed.
Run the workload as a nightly Bedrock batch inference job.

explanation: For steady, high, predictable volume, a committed Provisioned Throughput model unit lowers cost per token and guarantees dedicated capacity. Not "Use on-demand inference for every request.": On-demand pricing suits spiky or unpredictable low volume; at steady high volume it is not the lowest cost and does not reserve capacity. Not "Increase max tokens per request so fewer calls are needed.": Larger outputs raise cost per call and do not reduce the number of distinct summaries needed. Not "Run the workload as a nightly Bedrock batch inference job.": Batch inference is for offline, latency-tolerant jobs; it cannot serve steady real-time traffic. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A regulated company is applying the security and responsible-AI guidance of the Generative AI Lens to a Bedrock assistant. It needs a managed, configurable control plane to block denied topics, filter harmful content, and redact PII consistently across multiple foundation models. Which AWS capability best meets this need with the LEAST custom code?

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
A set of IAM identity-based policies on the model.
Lowering the model temperature parameter.

explanation: Guardrails provide configurable, model-agnostic policies for denied topics, content filters, word filters, and PII redaction that apply consistently across FMs. Not "CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics.": Alarms detect operational anomalies after the fact; they do not filter or redact content. Not "A set of IAM identity-based policies on the model.": IAM controls who can call the model, not what content the model may produce or must redact. Not "Lowering the model temperature parameter.": Temperature affects randomness, not topic blocking, content filtering, or PII redaction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An interactive customer assistant must minimize the latency end users perceive while keeping output quality acceptable for routine questions. Which combination best reflects the Performance Efficiency pillar for a Bedrock workload?

options.text: Always use the largest available model for every request.
Increase max tokens to ensure complete answers.
Route all interactive traffic through batch inference.
Select a smaller, latency-optimized (or distilled) model and stream tokens to the client.

explanation: Right-sizing to a smaller/distilled model reduces inference time, and response streaming lowers perceived latency by showing tokens as they are generated. Not "Always use the largest available model for every request.": The largest model maximizes capability but adds latency and cost that routine questions do not require. Not "Increase max tokens to ensure complete answers.": Larger outputs increase generation time, worsening perceived latency. Not "Route all interactive traffic through batch inference.": Batch inference is asynchronous and offline; it is unsuitable for interactive latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A platform team wants to operationalize quality assurance for a deployed generative AI feature so regressions are caught automatically as models and prompts change. Which practice best reflects the Operational Excellence pillar?

options.text: Establish automated evaluation pipelines with continuous monitoring of output quality and drift, feeding results back into release decisions.
Monitor only infrastructure metrics such as CPU and memory.
Run a single manual quality check before the initial launch.
Rely on end-user complaints to surface quality problems.

explanation: Operational Excellence emphasizes automating evaluation and observability so quality is measured continuously and improvements are driven by data. Not "Monitor only infrastructure metrics such as CPU and memory.": Infrastructure health says nothing about generation quality or drift. Not "Run a single manual quality check before the initial launch.": A one-time check does not catch regressions introduced by later model or prompt changes. Not "Rely on end-user complaints to surface quality problems.": Waiting for complaints is reactive and lets defects reach users undetected. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A security team is hardening a Bedrock workload according to the Security pillar of the Generative AI Lens. Which TWO practices should they adopt? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send prompts to a public endpoint without TLS to reduce overhead.
Embed long-lived IAM access keys in the application package.
Encrypt data at rest with AWS KMS and reach Bedrock through VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS network.
Apply least-privilege IAM with condition keys (for example, requiring a specific bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier) for model access.
Disable all logging to minimize the data footprint.

explanation: Customer-managed encryption and private connectivity protect data confidentiality and reduce exposure of prompts and outputs. Least-privilege identity-based policies with condition keys restrict who can call models and can enforce that guardrails are applied. Not "Send prompts to a public endpoint without TLS to reduce o…": Unencrypted transport exposes sensitive prompt and response data. Not "Embed long-lived IAM access keys in the application package.": Long-lived embedded keys are a major security risk and violate credential best practices. Not "Disable all logging to minimize the data footprint.": Disabling logging removes the audit trail needed for security monitoring and compliance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A company must classify tens of millions of archived documents with a foundation model. Results are consumed by an analytics team the next day, so real-time latency is unnecessary. Which approach best satisfies the Cost Optimization and Sustainability pillars?

options.text: Provision dedicated throughput and keep it running 24/7.
Use Amazon Bedrock batch inference with a right-sized model.
Invoke the model in real time, one document per request, as fast as possible.
Use the largest available model for every document in real time.

explanation: Batch inference processes large datasets asynchronously at lower cost, and a right-sized model avoids over-provisioning compute for a latency-tolerant job. Not "Provision dedicated throughput and keep it running 24/7.": A continuously provisioned endpoint wastes capacity for a once-daily, latency-tolerant job. Not "Invoke the model in real time, one document per request, …": High-volume real-time invocation is more expensive and unnecessary when results are needed only the next day. Not "Use the largest available model for every document in rea…": This maximizes cost and energy use with no benefit for a non-interactive workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A RAG chatbot resends a large, static system prompt plus a lengthy policy document with every request. Token costs and latency are climbing because the same context is reprocessed each time. Which Bedrock capability reduces cost and latency for the repeated context with the LEAST change to the application?

options.text: Enable prompt caching so the static portion of the prompt is reused across requests.
Increase the temperature parameter.
Switch the workload to Provisioned Throughput.
Move to a model with a larger context window.

explanation: Prompt caching stores and reuses repeated prompt prefixes, cutting both the tokens billed and the latency for the unchanging context. Not "Increase the temperature parameter.": Temperature changes output randomness and has no effect on cost or latency of repeated context. Not "Switch the workload to Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity but still reprocesses the repeated context on every call and changes the pricing model significantly. Not "Move to a model with a larger context window.": A larger context window does not reduce the cost of reprocessing the same tokens each request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A company needs a high-quality, human-labeled dataset to support supervised fine-tuning of a model. It wants managed labeling workflows, the option of a private or vendor workforce, and built-in quality controls, with minimal infrastructure to manage. Which service is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth.
AWS Glue DataBrew.

explanation: Ground Truth provides managed data-labeling workflows, workforce options (private, vendor, or Mechanical Turk), and quality features such as annotation consolidation. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data; it does not label datasets for training. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend performs automated NLP such as entity and PII detection, not managed human labeling. Not "AWS Glue DataBrew.": DataBrew cleans and normalizes tabular data; it does not run human annotation workflows. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A data scientist must clean, transform, and engineer features from large tabular datasets before training, and wants a mostly visual, low-code flow that exports prepared data to Amazon S3. Which service fits best?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight.
Amazon Kendra.
Amazon Athena.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

explanation: Data Wrangler offers a visual, low-code interface for importing, cleaning, transforming, and exporting tabular data for ML, reducing custom preprocessing code. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is for business-intelligence dashboards, not ML data preparation. Not "Amazon Kendra.": Kendra is an enterprise search service, not a data-prep tool. Not "Amazon Athena.": Athena queries data in S3 with SQL but is not a guided data-preparation and feature-engineering tool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Thousands of raw JSON and CSV documents land in Amazon S3 daily and must be cleaned, normalized, and partitioned at scale before being ingested into a knowledge base. The team wants a serverless solution with the LEAST operational overhead. Which service should they use?

options.text: An Amazon EMR cluster running Spark.
AWS Glue serverless ETL jobs.
A fleet of EC2 instances running batch scripts.
One AWS Lambda invocation per file with custom parsing.

explanation: Glue runs serverless Apache Spark ETL that cleans, transforms, and partitions large datasets without provisioning or managing clusters. Not "An Amazon EMR cluster running Spark.": EMR is powerful but requires provisioning and managing cluster capacity, adding operational overhead. Not "A fleet of EC2 instances running batch scripts.": Self-managed EC2 batch processing maximizes operational overhead. Not "One AWS Lambda invocation per file with custom parsing.": Per-file Lambda parsing is hard to coordinate at scale and hits timeout and orchestration limits for large ETL. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Before building a training corpus, a company must discover and classify where sensitive data and PII reside across hundreds of Amazon S3 buckets. Which service is purpose-built for this discovery task?

options.text: Amazon Inspector.
Amazon GuardDuty.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon Comprehend.

explanation: Macie uses managed data identifiers and machine learning to discover and classify sensitive data and PII across S3 at scale. Not "Amazon Inspector.": Inspector assesses workloads for software vulnerabilities, not sensitive-data classification. Not "Amazon GuardDuty.": GuardDuty is a threat-detection service for accounts and workloads, not data classification. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend detects and can redact PII within individual text inputs but is not designed to inventory sensitive data across many buckets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A company plans to fine-tune a model on customer chat transcripts but must programmatically remove personally identifiable information from the free text before training. Which service should it use to detect and redact the PII?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend PII detection and redaction.
Amazon Textract.
Amazon Rekognition.
Amazon Macie.

explanation: Comprehend can detect PII entities in text and redact or mask them, producing sanitized transcripts suitable for training. Not "Amazon Textract.": Textract extracts text from scanned documents; it does not specialize in PII redaction of conversational text. Not "Amazon Rekognition.": Rekognition analyzes images and video, not text PII. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies and reports on sensitive data in S3 but does not redact PII inside text for downstream training. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Before fine-tuning, a team wants to measure class imbalance and representation bias in the training dataset so they can correct it. Which capability is designed for pre-training bias analysis?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon CloudWatch.

explanation: Clarify computes pre-training bias metrics on datasets (and post-training bias and feature-attribution explanations on models). Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.": Model Monitor detects drift on a deployed endpoint, not bias in a training dataset before training. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend performs NLP tasks, not dataset bias measurement. Not "Amazon CloudWatch.": CloudWatch monitors operational metrics, not dataset bias. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A developer is assembling a dataset to fine-tune an Amazon Bedrock model for a supervised task. What is the correct way to provide the training data?

options.text: Point the job at a DynamoDB table of records.
Provide only unlabeled raw text with no prompt/response pairs.
Upload a single large PDF of reference material.
Upload a JSONL file of prompt/completion (or messages) examples to Amazon S3 in the format the model expects.

explanation: Bedrock customization expects labeled examples as JSONL records in S3 that match the target model's schema. Not "Point the job at a DynamoDB table of records.": Fine-tuning reads training data from S3 in the required file format, not from DynamoDB. Not "Provide only unlabeled raw text with no prompt/response p…": Unlabeled text is for continued pre-training, not supervised fine-tuning, which needs labeled pairs. Not "Upload a single large PDF of reference material.": An unstructured PDF is not a labeled training dataset; that pattern suits RAG ingestion, not supervised fine-tuning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A governance team must document each model's intended use, training data, evaluation results, and risk ratings in a standardized, auditable form, with the least custom build. Which AWS feature should they use?

options.text: AWS Config.
A free-form README stored in S3.
Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.
AWS CloudTrail.

explanation: Model Cards capture intended use, training details, evaluation, and risk information in a standardized, versioned, auditable document. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not model documentation. Not "A free-form README stored in S3.": A custom README lacks the standardized structure, versioning, and governance integration of Model Cards. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API activity, not model documentation and governance metadata. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team is preparing a dataset to fine-tune a foundation model and wants to maximize resulting quality while avoiding overfitting and data leakage. Which TWO data-preparation steps best support these goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Include duplicate records to increase the dataset size.
Increase the number of training epochs regardless of validation loss.
Include PII in the examples to add more signal.
Hold out a separate validation/test split that does not overlap the training data.
Deduplicate and clean/normalize the examples.

explanation: A non-overlapping evaluation split prevents train/test leakage and gives an honest measure of generalization. Removing duplicates and normalizing inconsistent text reduces bias toward repeated samples and improves the signal the model learns from. Not "Include duplicate records to increase the dataset size.": Duplication inflates size artificially and encourages overfitting to repeated examples. Not "Increase the number of training epochs regardless of vali…": Blindly adding epochs is a training hyperparameter choice, not data preparation, and risks overfitting. Not "Include PII in the examples to add more signal.": Including PII creates privacy and compliance risk and does not improve task quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A real-time chat router must classify incoming messages into a small set of intents. The task is simple, but volume is very high and the team wants the lowest latency and cost. Which Amazon Nova model is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Nova Reel.
Amazon Nova Canvas.
Amazon Nova Pro.
Amazon Nova Micro.

explanation: Nova Micro is the text-only, lowest-latency, lowest-cost Nova model, well suited to high-volume, simple text tasks such as intent classification. Not "Amazon Nova Reel.": Nova Reel generates video and is irrelevant to text intent classification. Not "Amazon Nova Canvas.": Nova Canvas generates images and is not used for text classification. Not "Amazon Nova Pro.": Nova Pro is the most capable multimodal Nova model, with higher cost and latency than a simple classification task requires. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company is satisfied with the accuracy of a large foundation model but needs lower inference cost and latency in production for a well-defined task. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed to transfer the larger model's quality to a smaller, cheaper model?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput.
Model distillation, training a smaller student model from the larger teacher model.
Cross-Region inference.
Prompt caching.

explanation: Bedrock model distillation generates data from a teacher model to fine-tune a smaller student that approximates its quality at lower cost and latency. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for a chosen model but does not create a smaller, cheaper model. Not "Cross-Region inference.": Cross-Region inference distributes load across Regions for throughput; it does not reduce per-call model size or cost. Not "Prompt caching.": Prompt caching reuses repeated prompt prefixes but does not change the model used for inference. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An assistant must answer using internal documents that change frequently, and answers must always reflect the latest content. Which approach meets this with the LOWEST ongoing maintenance?

options.text: Paste all documents into every prompt.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation with a knowledge base over the documents.
Fine-tune the model nightly on the latest documents.
Use continued pre-training whenever documents change.

explanation: RAG retrieves the current documents at query time, so updated content is reflected immediately without retraining the model. Not "Paste all documents into every prompt.": Stuffing all documents into the prompt is costly, hits context limits, and does not scale as the corpus grows. Not "Fine-tune the model nightly on the latest documents.": Repeated fine-tuning is costly and operationally heavy and still lags behind document changes between runs. Not "Use continued pre-training whenever documents change.": Continued pre-training is even heavier than fine-tuning and is not how you keep answers current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Prompt engineering has not reliably produced a company's required brand voice and a strict, consistent output format. The underlying domain knowledge is stable and does not change often. Which customization approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Add a knowledge base and use RAG.
Increase the temperature parameter.
Fine-tune the model on labeled examples that demonstrate the desired tone and format.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: Fine-tuning teaches consistent style and formatting from examples and is appropriate when the behavior, not freshness of facts, is the gap. Not "Add a knowledge base and use RAG.": RAG supplies fresh facts but does not reliably enforce tone and output formatting. Not "Increase the temperature parameter.": Higher temperature increases variability, working against a consistent voice and format. Not "Purchase Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput affects capacity and cost, not the model's style or formatting behavior. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A firm wants a model to deeply absorb specialized domain vocabulary and patterns from a very large corpus of unlabeled internal text. Which Amazon Bedrock customization method fits this goal?

options.text: Continued pre-training on the unlabeled corpus.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Model distillation.
Supervised fine-tuning on labeled prompt/completion pairs.

explanation: Continued pre-training adapts a model to domain language using large volumes of unlabeled text. Not "Retrieval-Augmented Generation.": RAG injects retrieved context at inference time but does not change what the model has learned. Not "Model distillation.": Distillation compresses a larger model into a smaller one; it is not a method for absorbing a domain corpus. Not "Supervised fine-tuning on labeled prompt/completion pairs.": Fine-tuning needs labeled examples and targets specific task behavior rather than broad domain-language adaptation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A compliance summarizer must produce highly consistent, low-variability output and avoid creative phrasing. Which TWO inference-parameter adjustments best support more deterministic, focused responses? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower the temperature.
Greatly increase top-k to consider many tokens.
Lower top-p (nucleus sampling).
Increase max tokens.
Raise the temperature substantially.

explanation: A low temperature reduces randomness, making outputs more deterministic and repeatable. A lower top-p narrows the token pool to the most probable tokens, reducing variability. Not "Greatly increase top-k to consider many tokens.": A large top-k widens the candidate pool and increases variability. Not "Increase max tokens.": Max tokens controls output length, not determinism. Not "Raise the temperature substantially.": Higher temperature increases randomness, the opposite of the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must run sentiment analysis over 10 million archived product reviews. The results are needed for a weekly report, so latency does not matter, and cost should be minimized. Which Amazon Bedrock option fits best?

options.text: Increase max tokens to process more reviews per call.
A loop of real-time InvokeModel calls.
Provisioned Throughput running continuously.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference.

explanation: Batch inference processes large datasets asynchronously at a lower price point, ideal for latency-tolerant, high-volume jobs. Not "Increase max tokens to process more reviews per call.": Max tokens does not batch records and would not reduce overall cost for this workload. Not "A loop of real-time InvokeModel calls.": Per-record real-time calls are more expensive and unnecessary for a weekly, offline report. Not "Provisioned Throughput running continuously.": Reserved capacity running 24/7 wastes money for a once-weekly job. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A startup's Bedrock usage is spiky and unpredictable, with long idle periods between bursts. They want to pay only for what they use and avoid paying for idle capacity. Which pricing/inference choice is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Batch inference for all traffic.
On-demand inference.
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment.
A dedicated SageMaker endpoint kept always on.

explanation: On-demand pricing charges per request with no commitment, which is most cost-effective for spiky, unpredictable, low-utilization traffic. Not "Batch inference for all traffic.": Batch is offline and cannot serve interactive, bursty requests. Not "Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment.": A commitment pays for reserved capacity that sits idle during the long quiet periods. Not "A dedicated SageMaker endpoint kept always on.": An always-on endpoint incurs cost during idle periods, defeating the goal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must compare two candidate foundation models for a summarization use case across relevance and coherence at scale, without standing up a human rating panel. Which approach has the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Spot-check a handful of outputs manually in a notebook.
Compare CloudWatch latency metrics for the two models.
Use an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job with an LLM-as-a-judge (automatic) evaluator.
Recruit and manage a human evaluation panel for all outputs.

explanation: Bedrock model evaluation supports automatic LLM-as-a-judge scoring across quality dimensions at scale with minimal setup. Not "Spot-check a handful of outputs manually in a notebook.": Ad hoc manual review is not systematic or scalable for a reliable comparison. Not "Compare CloudWatch latency metrics for the two models.": Latency metrics do not measure summarization relevance or coherence. Not "Recruit and manage a human evaluation panel for all outputs.": Human-only evaluation is accurate but operationally heavy and slow at scale. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A developer wants one consistent API to hold multi-turn conversations and use tool calling across several different Bedrock models, without writing model-specific request and response handling. Which API should they use?

options.text: A separate InvokeModel integration per model with custom payloads.
Custom adapter code in front of each model.
The Amazon Bedrock Converse API.
Amazon API Gateway request mapping templates.

explanation: Converse provides a unified, model-agnostic interface for multi-turn messages and tool use across supported Bedrock models. Not "A separate InvokeModel integration per model with custom …": Per-model InvokeModel payloads require model-specific request/response handling, which Converse abstracts away. Not "Custom adapter code in front of each model.": Building adapters reinvents what the Converse API already standardizes. Not "Amazon API Gateway request mapping templates.": API Gateway mapping does not normalize differing model message and tool-use formats. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An application already calls a supported Bedrock model and the team wants to reduce token-generation latency with the smallest possible application change. Which option should they evaluate first?

options.text: Switch to a larger, more capable model.
Move the workload to batch inference.
Enable latency-optimized inference for the supported model.
Add more retries to the client.

explanation: Latency-optimized inference reduces response latency for supported models without an application rewrite. Not "Switch to a larger, more capable model.": A larger model typically increases latency rather than reducing it. Not "Move the workload to batch inference.": Batch inference is asynchronous and increases, not decreases, time-to-response. Not "Add more retries to the client.": Retries handle failures; they do not lower per-request latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company has a fine-tuned open-weights model (a supported architecture) trained outside AWS and wants to serve it through the standard Amazon Bedrock APIs on demand, without operating its own inference servers. Which capability should it use?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.
A container on Amazon ECS.
A self-managed Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint.

explanation: Custom Model Import lets you bring supported custom model weights into Bedrock and invoke them through the standard on-demand Bedrock APIs without managing servers. Not "Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for Bedrock models, not for importing your own weights. Not "A container on Amazon ECS.": Running the model on ECS means operating your own inference infrastructure. Not "A self-managed Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint.": A SageMaker endpoint can serve the model but requires managing the endpoint and does not expose it through the Bedrock APIs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An application must accept product photos from users and answer natural-language questions about what is in each image. Which choice is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use Amazon Textract to read the image.
Invoke a Bedrock multimodal foundation model (such as Claude or Amazon Nova Pro) through the Converse API.
Use Amazon Rekognition to return object labels.
Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings.

explanation: A multimodal FM can reason over image inputs and produce natural-language answers about their content. Not "Use Amazon Textract to read the image.": Textract extracts text from documents and forms; it does not answer visual questions about general photos. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition to return object labels.": Rekognition returns labels and detections but does not hold a natural-language Q&A about an image. Not "Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings.": Text embeddings represent text for search; they do not analyze image content or answer questions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team is building semantic search and wants a text embedding model that lets them choose smaller output dimensions to cut vector-storage cost while retaining strong retrieval quality. Which model fits?

options.text: Anthropic Claude.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, which supports configurable output dimensions.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon Titan Image Generator.

explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 lets you select among multiple output dimension sizes to trade storage/cost against accuracy. Not "Anthropic Claude.": Claude is a text-generation model, not a dedicated embeddings model. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend provides NLP analyses, not configurable embedding vectors for a vector store. Not "Amazon Titan Image Generator.": An image generation model does not produce text embeddings for search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team is creating an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and wants a fully managed vector store that integrates natively with Bedrock, supports frequent low-latency similarity queries, and requires no cluster sizing or management. Which option fits best?

options.text: Amazon S3 with objects named by embedding.
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store.
A self-managed Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster you size and patch.
Amazon DynamoDB with a custom similarity function.

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless is a natively integrated, fully managed vector store for Bedrock knowledge bases that scales automatically for frequent low-latency queries. Not "Amazon S3 with objects named by embedding.": Plain S3 has no vector index or similarity search capability. Not "A self-managed Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster you size…": A provisioned cluster requires capacity planning, scaling, and maintenance, adding operational overhead. Not "Amazon DynamoDB with a custom similarity function.": DynamoDB has no native vector similarity search and would require custom, slower logic. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A knowledge base serves several departments, and each user must only retrieve documents tagged for their department. The team wants to enforce this at retrieval time without maintaining separate copies of the corpus. Which capability should they use?

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model is less literal.
Retrieve everything and truncate the results in the client.
Apply metadata filtering on the Retrieve call using the document's department attribute.
Add an instruction in the prompt asking the model to ignore other departments.

explanation: Bedrock knowledge bases support metadata attributes and filter expressions so retrieval returns only chunks matching the user's department. Not "Raise the temperature so the model is less literal.": Temperature has nothing to do with which documents are retrieved. Not "Retrieve everything and truncate the results in the client.": Truncation does not enforce department-level access and may still expose other departments' content. Not "Add an instruction in the prompt asking the model to igno…": Prompt instructions cannot reliably prevent irrelevant or unauthorized chunks from being retrieved and used. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An application must show end users the exact source passages that support each generated answer, with the least custom development. Which Amazon Bedrock approach provides this?

options.text: Use InvokeModel with the whole corpus pasted into the prompt.
Use the RetrieveAndGenerate API, which returns generated answers with citations to the source chunks.
Enable model invocation logging and show users the logs.
Increase max tokens so the model lists its sources.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate produces a grounded answer and returns citations identifying the retrieved passages used, with no custom attribution code. Not "Use InvokeModel with the whole corpus pasted into the pro…": Stuffing the corpus into the prompt does not produce reliable citations and does not scale. Not "Enable model invocation logging and show users the logs.": Invocation logs are for operators and do not provide user-facing source citations. Not "Increase max tokens so the model lists its sources.": Asking the model to self-report sources is unreliable; max tokens does not create verifiable citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A developer wants to fetch the most relevant chunks from a Bedrock knowledge base and then run them through their own custom prompt and a model of their choosing. Which API is appropriate?

options.text: The RetrieveAndGenerate API exclusively.
The CreateModelCustomizationJob API.
The StartIngestionJob API.
The Retrieve API, which returns ranked chunks for the developer to use in a custom generation step.

explanation: Retrieve returns the relevant passages only, letting the developer control the prompt and generation model themselves. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerate API exclusively.": RetrieveAndGenerate performs the generation for you, which removes the custom prompt/model control the developer wants. Not "The CreateModelCustomizationJob API.": That API runs fine-tuning, unrelated to retrieving chunks. Not "The StartIngestionJob API.": StartIngestionJob ingests data into the knowledge base; it does not retrieve chunks for a query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A RAG assistant occasionally produces answers that are not supported by the retrieved passages. The team wants a managed way to detect and block responses that are not grounded in the source context. Which capability helps MOST?

options.text: Increase the model temperature.
Remove the retrieved context from the prompt.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check.
Switch to on-demand pricing.

explanation: The contextual grounding (and relevance) check scores whether a response is grounded in the provided source and can block ungrounded answers. Not "Increase the model temperature.": Higher temperature increases variability and tends to worsen, not reduce, ungrounded output. Not "Remove the retrieved context from the prompt.": Removing context guarantees the answer cannot be grounded, the opposite of the goal. Not "Switch to on-demand pricing.": Pricing mode has no effect on grounding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS uses one shared knowledge base and must guarantee that one tenant can never retrieve another tenant's documents. Which design is the MOST secure and reliable?

options.text: Tag each document with its tenant ID and apply a metadata filter derived from the authenticated tenant on every Retrieve request (or use a separate knowledge base per tenant).
Store all tenants together with no filter and rely on ranking.
Let the client pass the tenant filter and trust it as-is.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to only answer about the current tenant.

explanation: Enforcing a server-side metadata filter bound to the verified tenant identity (or full isolation via per-tenant knowledge bases) reliably prevents cross-tenant retrieval. Not "Store all tenants together with no filter and rely on ran…": Relevance ranking can still surface another tenant's documents; it is not an isolation mechanism. Not "Let the client pass the tenant filter and trust it as-is.": A client-supplied, untrusted filter can be tampered with to access other tenants' data. Not "Instruct the model in the system prompt to only answer ab…": Prompt instructions do not control retrieval and can be bypassed, so other tenants' chunks can still be retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An analyst tool must answer questions that require reasoning over relationships among connected entities (people, companies, and the links between them), not just similarity to text passages. Which Amazon Bedrock knowledge base option is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon Athena queries over CSV files.
An Amazon DynamoDB table of entities.
A standard vector-only knowledge base.
A knowledge base using GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics.

explanation: GraphRAG with Neptune Analytics builds a graph of entities and relationships, enabling retrieval that reasons over connections rather than only vector similarity. Not "Amazon Athena queries over CSV files.": Athena runs SQL over files and is not a graph-aware retrieval system for RAG. Not "An Amazon DynamoDB table of entities.": DynamoDB stores items but provides no graph reasoning or managed RAG integration. Not "A standard vector-only knowledge base.": Pure vector similarity does not capture explicit relationships among connected entities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Business users want to ask natural-language analytical questions (sums, trends, comparisons) over data in an Amazon Redshift warehouse, and have the system generate and run the appropriate queries. Which Amazon Bedrock capability fits?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to read the question.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with structured data retrieval, which generates SQL from natural language.
Fine-tune a model on the warehouse schema.
Embed every table row as a vector and do similarity search.

explanation: Structured-data knowledge bases translate natural-language questions into SQL against the connected warehouse, returning accurate analytical results. Not "Use Amazon Comprehend to read the question.": Comprehend analyzes text but does not generate SQL or query a warehouse. Not "Fine-tune a model on the warehouse schema.": Fine-tuning does not give live, accurate query results over changing data the way text-to-SQL retrieval does. Not "Embed every table row as a vector and do similarity search.": Vector similarity over rows cannot perform aggregations or precise analytical queries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A company keeps 200 million archived document embeddings that are queried only a few times per month for occasional investigations. They want the lowest-cost durable vector storage with no capacity to manage. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: A provisioned OpenSearch Service cluster sized for the full corpus.
OpenSearch Serverless kept warm at all times.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: S3 Vectors offers serverless, low-cost vector storage and search at massive scale, ideal for large corpora queried infrequently with pay-for-use pricing. Not "A provisioned OpenSearch Service cluster sized for the fu…": A continuously provisioned cluster is expensive for data queried only a few times a month. Not "OpenSearch Serverless kept warm at all times.": Keeping high-performance serverless capacity ready is more expensive than needed for rare queries. Not "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector.": RDS requires running instances and is not the lowest-cost option for rarely queried, very large vector sets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team has standardized on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for its application data and wants to store and query embeddings alongside related relational records using familiar tooling, while keeping the vector store as a managed Bedrock knowledge base option. Which choice fits best?

options.text: Use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store.
Store vectors in Amazon DynamoDB.
Adopt a brand-new self-managed search cluster instead.
Keep embeddings only in application memory.

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector is a supported Bedrock vector store and lets the team keep vectors next to relational data using PostgreSQL tooling. Not "Store vectors in Amazon DynamoDB.": DynamoDB is not a supported vector store and lacks native similarity search. Not "Adopt a brand-new self-managed search cluster instead.": Introducing a separate self-managed system adds operational overhead the team is trying to avoid. Not "Keep embeddings only in application memory.": In-memory storage is not durable and cannot serve as a knowledge base vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Source content lives in Amazon S3, Confluence, and a SharePoint site. The team wants to ingest all of it into one Bedrock knowledge base with the LEAST custom code. What should they do?

options.text: Use the built-in Bedrock knowledge base data source connectors for S3, Confluence, and SharePoint.
Manually export everything to S3 on a schedule.
Write custom crawlers for each system and push to S3 only.
Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.

explanation: Bedrock knowledge bases provide managed connectors for sources such as S3, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and web crawlers, avoiding custom ingestion code. Not "Manually export everything to S3 on a schedule.": Manual exports are brittle and lag behind source changes compared with managed connectors. Not "Write custom crawlers for each system and push to S3 only.": Custom crawlers add development and maintenance overhead that the built-in connectors remove. Not "Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.": Fine-tuning is not how you ingest changing documents for retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A chat experience built on RetrieveAndGenerate must keep context across follow-up questions in a conversation with the least custom state management. Which approach should the developer use?

options.text: Increase the model context window only.
Re-embed the entire chat history into the vector store each turn.
Pass a session identifier to RetrieveAndGenerate so Bedrock maintains the conversation context.
Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt manually each turn.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate supports a session ID that preserves multi-turn context without the developer building custom conversation state. Not "Increase the model context window only.": A larger window does not automatically carry prior turns into each RetrieveAndGenerate call. Not "Re-embed the entire chat history into the vector store ea…": Re-embedding the conversation each turn is unnecessary and costly and is not how session context is maintained. Not "Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt ma…": Manual state assembly adds development overhead compared with built-in session support. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Users ask complex, multi-part questions, and the knowledge base often retrieves passages for only one part of the question, producing incomplete answers. Which built-in capability best addresses this?

options.text: Enable query decomposition (query reformulation) so the knowledge base breaks complex questions into sub-queries.
Reduce the number of retrieved results.
Increase the model temperature.
Switch to a larger generation model only.

explanation: Query decomposition splits a multi-part question into focused sub-queries, retrieving relevant passages for each part and improving completeness. Not "Reduce the number of retrieved results.": Returning fewer results would make incomplete coverage worse, not better. Not "Increase the model temperature.": Temperature affects generation randomness, not how queries are retrieved. Not "Switch to a larger generation model only.": A larger model cannot answer using passages that retrieval never returned. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team wants to add retrieval-augmented answers over their documents but does not want to build and operate an embedding pipeline, a vector database, and custom retrieval code. Which option provides managed RAG with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which manages embedding, storage, and retrieval as a service.
Fine-tune a model on the documents instead of retrieving.
Paste documents into prompts at request time.
Build a custom pipeline with Lambda, a self-managed vector database, and bespoke retrieval code.

explanation: Knowledge Bases provide fully managed RAG, handling chunking, embeddings, the vector store, and retrieval so the team avoids building the pipeline. Not "Fine-tune a model on the documents instead of retrieving.": Fine-tuning does not keep answers current as documents change and is not managed RAG. Not "Paste documents into prompts at request time.": Prompt stuffing does not scale and is not a managed retrieval solution. Not "Build a custom pipeline with Lambda, a self-managed vecto…": A hand-built pipeline maximizes operational overhead, which the team is trying to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Long policy documents have distinct topical sections. With the default fixed-size chunking, related ideas are split across chunks and retrieval quality suffers. Which chunking strategy is MOST likely to improve relevance?

options.text: Use larger fixed-size chunks only.
Increase the model temperature.
Disable chunking and embed each whole document as one vector.
Semantic chunking, which splits on semantic boundaries so each chunk holds a coherent idea.

explanation: Semantic chunking groups text by meaning rather than a fixed token count, keeping related content together and improving retrieval relevance. Not "Use larger fixed-size chunks only.": Bigger fixed chunks still ignore topic boundaries and can mix unrelated content. Not "Increase the model temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not how documents are chunked or retrieved. Not "Disable chunking and embed each whole document as one vec…": Embedding an entire long document dilutes the vector and harms precise retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team needs precise matching on small text units but also wants the language model to receive surrounding context when a small unit matches. Which chunking approach provides both?

options.text: A single fixed chunk size for everything.
Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.
No chunking at all.
Switching to a larger embedding dimension.

explanation: Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks for precision and supplies the larger parent chunk as context for generation. Not "A single fixed chunk size for everything.": One fixed size cannot simultaneously optimize for precise matching and broad context. Not "No chunking at all.": Treating each document as one chunk loses the precision of small-unit matching. Not "Switching to a larger embedding dimension.": Dimension size does not provide the parent-context behavior hierarchical chunking gives. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Answers are frequently cut off because relevant sentences fall right at the boundary between two chunks. Which adjustment most directly addresses this?

options.text: Remove all overlap to keep chunks distinct.
Add chunk overlap so adjacent chunks share boundary text.
Use a larger generation model.
Increase the temperature.
