explanation: Overlap repeats text across chunk boundaries so information spanning a boundary is captured in at least one chunk. Not "Remove all overlap to keep chunks distinct.": Removing overlap makes boundary loss worse, not better. Not "Use a larger generation model.": A larger model cannot recover content that retrieval split across boundaries. Not "Increase the temperature.": Temperature does not affect chunk boundaries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team decides to upgrade to a newer embedding model for better retrieval. What must they do to keep retrieval working correctly?

options.text: Lower the temperature on the generation model.
Do nothing; existing vectors remain compatible.
Re-embed (re-index) the entire document corpus with the new model so document and query vectors share the same space.
Re-embed only the queries, not the documents.

explanation: Query and document embeddings must come from the same model; changing the model requires re-embedding the whole corpus to avoid vector-space mismatch. Not "Lower the temperature on the generation model.": Temperature is unrelated to embedding compatibility. Not "Do nothing; existing vectors remain compatible.": Vectors from a different model live in a different space and will not match new query embeddings. Not "Re-embed only the queries, not the documents.": Mismatched query and document embeddings produce poor or empty retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A vector store is becoming expensive as the corpus grows. The team wants to cut storage and query cost while keeping acceptable retrieval accuracy. Which embedding choice helps MOST?

options.text: Store each chunk twice for redundancy.
Always use the maximum available embedding dimension.
Raise the generation temperature.
Use an embedding model that supports smaller output dimensions (for example, Titan Text Embeddings V2) and select a smaller dimension.

explanation: Smaller-dimension embeddings reduce index size and query cost, and V2 lets you trade some accuracy for substantial storage savings. Not "Store each chunk twice for redundancy.": Duplicating vectors increases cost without improving accuracy. Not "Always use the maximum available embedding dimension.": Maximum dimensions increase storage and cost, the opposite of the goal. Not "Raise the generation temperature.": Temperature does not affect embedding storage or cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Evaluation shows the correct passage exists in the store but is sometimes not returned for a query, so the model lacks the information to answer. Which retrieval-setting change should the team try FIRST?

options.text: Shorten the user's question automatically.
Increase the temperature.
Decrease the number of results returned.
Increase the number of results (top-k) returned for each query.

explanation: Returning more candidate chunks raises recall so the correct passage is more likely to be included for generation. Not "Shorten the user's question automatically.": Arbitrarily shortening the query can remove signal needed for retrieval. Not "Increase the temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not which chunks are retrieved. Not "Decrease the number of results returned.": Returning fewer results lowers recall and makes misses more likely. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Chunks were configured to be very large, and retrieval now returns passages where the relevant sentence is buried among unrelated text, weakening match quality. Which change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Raise the temperature.
Increase the chunk size further.
Reduce the chunk size so each chunk represents a more focused unit of meaning.
Embed the whole document as one chunk.

explanation: Smaller, focused chunks produce embeddings that better represent specific content, improving match precision. Not "Raise the temperature.": Temperature is unrelated to chunk granularity. Not "Increase the chunk size further.": Even larger chunks dilute the embedding more and worsen precision. Not "Embed the whole document as one chunk.": A single document-level vector is the extreme case of dilution and reduces precision. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A knowledge base ingests a large set of short, self-contained FAQ entries, where each file already represents one complete question-and-answer. Which chunking choice is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Apply aggressive small fixed-size chunking to every file.
Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.
Increase embedding dimensions to compensate.
Use a no-chunking strategy so each short file is treated as a single chunk.

explanation: When each file is already an atomic, self-contained unit, no chunking preserves the complete meaning per entry without splitting it. Not "Apply aggressive small fixed-size chunking to every file.": Splitting already-atomic FAQ entries fragments coherent answers and harms retrieval. Not "Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.": Combining unrelated entries into one chunk dilutes each entry's embedding. Not "Increase embedding dimensions to compensate.": Dimension size does not fix inappropriately split or merged atomic entries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: An application must retrieve relevant items from a combined catalog of product images and text descriptions using a single query that may be text or an image. Which embedding approach supports this?

options.text: Use Amazon Rekognition labels as the only index.
Store images as base64 strings and embed the strings as text.
Use a multimodal embedding model (such as Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings) so images and text share one vector space.
Use a text-only embedding model for everything.

explanation: Multimodal embeddings place images and text in a shared space, enabling cross-modal similarity search from either input type. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition labels as the only index.": Label detection is not a shared embedding space for semantic text-and-image retrieval. Not "Store images as base64 strings and embed the strings as t…": Embedding raw base64 as text does not capture visual semantics for retrieval. Not "Use a text-only embedding model for everything.": A text-only model cannot embed images for similarity search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants to raise the overall quality of what their RAG system retrieves and ultimately answers. Which TWO techniques are most effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a reranking step to reorder retrieved candidates by query relevance.
Choose a chunking strategy (semantic or hierarchical) aligned to the documents' structure.
Always return the fewest possible results.
Increase max tokens on the response.
Raise the generation temperature to add variety.

explanation: A reranker reorders the initial candidate set so the most relevant passages are used for generation. Chunking that respects document structure produces more coherent, relevant chunks and better retrieval. Not "Always return the fewest possible results.": Minimizing results can drop relevant passages and reduce answer quality. Not "Increase max tokens on the response.": Output length does not change which passages are retrieved or how relevant they are. Not "Raise the generation temperature to add variety.": Higher temperature increases randomness and does not improve retrieval quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants to A/B test two wordings of a production prompt and roll back instantly if one underperforms, without redeploying application code. Which Amazon Bedrock capability supports this?

options.text: Hard-code both prompts in the application and redeploy to switch.
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with versioned prompts and variants.
Store prompts in environment variables only.
Change the temperature parameter to switch prompts.

explanation: Prompt Management stores prompts as versioned, parameterized resources with variants, so teams can compare wordings and switch or roll back without code changes. Not "Hard-code both prompts in the application and redeploy to…": Hard-coding requires a code change and redeploy for every switch or rollback. Not "Store prompts in environment variables only.": Environment variables lack versioning, variants, and managed rollback for prompts. Not "Change the temperature parameter to switch prompts.": Temperature does not select between prompt wordings. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer must cap the length of model responses to control cost and prevent overly long outputs in a chat feature. Which inference setting should they use?

options.text: Set the maxTokens (maximum output tokens) parameter.
Add more stop sequences for unrelated phrases.
Increase top-k.
Raise the temperature.

explanation: maxTokens bounds the number of tokens the model can generate, directly limiting response length and cost. Not "Add more stop sequences for unrelated phrases.": Unrelated stop sequences do not reliably cap general response length. Not "Increase top-k.": Top-k widens token choice diversity; it does not bound length. Not "Raise the temperature.": Temperature changes randomness, not output length or cost ceiling. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: An assistant must consistently follow durable behavior rules (role, tone, safety constraints) across every turn of a conversation, separate from each user's question. Where should these durable instructions be placed?

options.text: Appended to each user message by the user.
In the temperature setting.
In the stop sequences list.
In the system prompt.

explanation: The system prompt sets persistent instructions and context that govern the model's behavior across the conversation, distinct from per-turn user messages. Not "Appended to each user message by the user.": Relying on users to repeat rules is unreliable and inconsistent. Not "In the temperature setting.": Temperature is a sampling parameter, not a place for behavior instructions. Not "In the stop sequences list.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not encode behavior rules. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Outputs must follow a precise structured format, and instructions alone have not produced consistent results. Which prompt-engineering technique most improves format adherence?

options.text: Provide a few worked examples (few-shot exemplars) demonstrating the exact desired format.
Shorten the prompt to a single sentence.
Increase the temperature for more creative formatting.
Remove all instructions and let the model decide.

explanation: Few-shot examples show the model the precise structure to imitate, improving consistency beyond instructions alone. Not "Shorten the prompt to a single sentence.": Over-shortening removes the structure cues the model needs. Not "Increase the temperature for more creative formatting.": Higher temperature increases variability and undermines consistent formatting. Not "Remove all instructions and let the model decide.": Removing guidance reduces, not improves, format adherence. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Several applications reuse the same prompt with only a few values changing per request (customer name, product, locale). The team wants to manage this prompt centrally and inject values at runtime. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.
Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management templates with input variables.
Concatenate strings ad hoc in every service.
Copy the prompt text into each application and edit by hand.

explanation: Prompt Management supports parameterized templates with input variables, so a single managed prompt is reused and values are supplied at invocation time. Not "Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.": Temperature does not parameterize or manage prompts. Not "Concatenate strings ad hoc in every service.": Ad hoc concatenation gives no central governance, versioning, or reuse. Not "Copy the prompt text into each application and edit by hand.": Duplicated, hand-edited prompts drift apart and are hard to maintain or update centrally. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer needs to orchestrate a multi-step generative workflow (classify input, retrieve context, then generate a response) with branching, and wants a managed, low-code way to build and version it. Which Amazon Bedrock feature is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Flows (prompt flows).
Manually wiring Lambda functions for every step from scratch.
A single InvokeModel call.
Increasing max tokens.

explanation: Bedrock Flows let you visually build and version multi-step, branching generative workflows that chain prompts, knowledge bases, and other components with little code. Not "Manually wiring Lambda functions for every step from scra…": Hand-built orchestration adds development and maintenance overhead versus a managed flow builder. Not "A single InvokeModel call.": One model call cannot orchestrate a multi-step, branching workflow. Not "Increasing max tokens.": Output length has nothing to do with workflow orchestration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: For a regression test suite, a team needs the same prompt to return as close to the same output as possible on each run. Which single inference parameter change most increases determinism?

options.text: Increase max tokens.
Set the temperature to 0 (or very near 0).
Raise the temperature to 1.
Set a very high top-k.

explanation: A temperature at or near 0 makes sampling effectively greedy, producing the most consistent, repeatable outputs. Not "Increase max tokens.": Output length does not control run-to-run consistency. Not "Raise the temperature to 1.": A high temperature maximizes randomness, the opposite of determinism. Not "Set a very high top-k.": A high top-k widens the sampling pool and increases variability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the team wants to reduce fabricated answers by making the model rely only on the supplied context and admit when the answer is not present. Which prompt technique helps MOST?

options.text: Instruct the model to answer only from the provided context and to say it does not know when the context lacks the answer.
Tell the model to always produce an answer no matter what.
Remove the retrieved context to keep prompts short.
Raise the temperature so answers are more creative.

explanation: Explicit grounding instructions plus an allowed 'I don't know' response reduce fabrication when the retrieved context does not contain the answer. Not "Tell the model to always produce an answer no matter what.": Forcing an answer encourages fabrication when information is missing. Not "Remove the retrieved context to keep prompts short.": Without context the model must guess, increasing hallucination. Not "Raise the temperature so answers are more creative.": More creativity increases the chance of fabricated content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer wants to prevent unbounded, runaway generations that drive up cost and sometimes ramble past the intended answer. Which TWO inference controls directly help? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set a sensible maxTokens limit.
Define stop sequences that end generation at a known marker.
Enlarge the context window.
Increase top-k substantially.
Increase the temperature.

explanation: maxTokens caps how many tokens can be generated, bounding cost and preventing runaway length. Stop sequences halt generation when a defined phrase appears, preventing the model from rambling past the answer. Not "Enlarge the context window.": A bigger input window does not constrain how long the output can be. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": A larger top-k affects token diversity, not output length. Not "Increase the temperature.": Higher temperature does not limit length and can make output more verbose and variable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer is building an Amazon Bedrock agent that must call an internal order-management API to look up and update orders. What is the standard way to give the agent this capability?

options.text: Paste the API documentation into the agent's instructions and hope it calls the API.
Increase the model's temperature so it can reach the API.
Define an action group backed by an AWS Lambda function, described with an API (OpenAPI) or function schema the agent can call.
Store the API responses in the prompt as static text.

explanation: Bedrock agents use action groups: a schema declares the available operations and a Lambda function executes them when the agent decides to call the API. Not "Paste the API documentation into the agent's instructions…": Instructions alone do not give the agent an executable tool; action groups provide the actual invocation path. Not "Increase the model's temperature so it can reach the API.": Temperature has nothing to do with tool or API access. Not "Store the API responses in the prompt as static text.": Static text cannot perform live lookups or updates against the order system. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: For compliance, an organization wants its own application to execute tool/API calls rather than letting the Bedrock agent invoke a Lambda directly, while still letting the agent decide which action to take. Which agent capability supports this?

options.text: Hard-code the action in the system prompt.
Disable the agent's reasoning entirely.
Lower the temperature to 0.
Configure the action group to return control to the caller so the application performs the action and returns results to the agent.

explanation: Return of control hands the chosen action and parameters back to the calling application to execute, instead of the agent invoking a Lambda directly. Not "Hard-code the action in the system prompt.": A hard-coded action removes the agent's dynamic decision-making and is not the return-of-control mechanism. Not "Disable the agent's reasoning entirely.": Disabling reasoning would remove the agent's ability to decide which action to take. Not "Lower the temperature to 0.": Temperature does not control where tool execution happens. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent should ground its answers in the company's policy documents in addition to taking actions. With the LEAST custom code, how should the developer add this knowledge?

options.text: Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent.
Fine-tune the agent's model on the policies each week.
Embed the entire policy library into the agent's instructions.
Store policies in DynamoDB and query them with custom code.

explanation: Associating a knowledge base lets the agent retrieve and ground responses on the documents without custom retrieval code. Not "Fine-tune the agent's model on the policies each week.": Repeated fine-tuning is heavy and unnecessary when a knowledge base provides current grounding. Not "Embed the entire policy library into the agent's instruct…": Instructions have limited size and cannot scale to a full document library or stay current. Not "Store policies in DynamoDB and query them with custom code.": A custom store and retrieval code adds work that the built-in knowledge base association avoids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team is deploying agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and wants each user's agent to remember preferences and prior context across separate sessions, as a managed capability. Which AgentCore component should they use?

options.text: AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: AgentCore Memory provides managed short-term and long-term memory so agents can persist and recall context across sessions. Not "AgentCore Browser.": The Browser tool provides managed web browsing, not persistent agent memory. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter runs code in a sandbox; it does not store cross-session memory. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes APIs as tools; it is not the memory store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A company already has many internal REST APIs and Lambda functions and wants to expose them to its agents as secure, governed tools without writing custom integration code for each one. Which AgentCore capability is designed for this?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway.
AgentCore Observability.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Memory.

explanation: AgentCore Gateway turns existing APIs, Lambda functions, and services into agent-ready tools (for example via MCP) with built-in authentication and governance. Not "AgentCore Observability.": Observability provides tracing and monitoring, not tool integration. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter executes code, not API-to-tool exposure. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context; it does not expose APIs as tools. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An analytics agent must run user-provided Python to perform calculations and data transformations safely, isolated from other workloads. Which AgentCore capability should the developer use?

options.text: AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: Code Interpreter gives the agent a secure, isolated sandbox to execute code for calculations and data processing. Not "AgentCore Browser.": Browser automates web interactions, not arbitrary code execution. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory stores context and does not execute code. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes external tools; it is not a code execution sandbox. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent needs to navigate websites and interact with web pages to complete tasks, in a managed and secure environment rather than self-hosted browser infrastructure. Which AgentCore capability fits?

options.text: AgentCore Identity.
AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Browser.

explanation: The AgentCore Browser tool provides a managed, secure, cloud-based browser the agent can use to navigate and interact with web pages. Not "AgentCore Identity.": Identity manages secure access to resources, not browser automation. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context, not web interaction. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter runs code; it is not a managed browser. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Agents must securely access third-party SaaS services on behalf of users, including handling tokens and consent, without the developer building a custom credential broker. Which AgentCore capability addresses this?

options.text: AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Identity.
AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.

explanation: AgentCore Identity provides secure identity and access management for agents, including authenticating to and accessing AWS and third-party services on a user's behalf. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context, not credentials and consent flows. Not "AgentCore Browser.": Browser automates web pages; it is not an identity and access broker. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter executes code and does not manage outbound identity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A complex workflow needs one coordinating agent to delegate subtasks to several specialized agents (billing, shipping, returns) and combine their results. Which Amazon Bedrock approach supports this?

options.text: Run unrelated agents with no coordination.
Increase max tokens so one agent can do everything.
Use multi-agent collaboration with a supervisor agent coordinating specialized sub-agents.
Put all capabilities into a single prompt and hope the model separates them.

explanation: Bedrock multi-agent collaboration lets a supervisor agent route subtasks to specialized agents and aggregate their outputs. Not "Run unrelated agents with no coordination.": Without coordination there is no way to combine sub-agent results into one workflow. Not "Increase max tokens so one agent can do everything.": Output length does not provide multi-agent delegation. Not "Put all capabilities into a single prompt and hope the mo…": One monolithic prompt does not provide structured delegation or specialization. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A developer wants an open-source, model-driven framework to build agents with tools and reasoning in a few lines of Python, and then deploy them to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Which option fits?

options.text: The Strands Agents SDK.
AWS Glue.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon QuickSight.

explanation: Strands Agents is AWS's open-source, model-driven agent SDK for building tool-using agents that can be deployed to AgentCore Runtime. Not "AWS Glue.": Glue is an ETL service and is unrelated to building agents. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is an NLP service, not an agent-building SDK. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is a business-intelligence service, not an agent framework. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An operations team must debug why an agent chose a particular tool and trace each step, tool call, and latency in production. Which AgentCore capability provides this visibility?

options.text: AgentCore Observability, which provides tracing and metrics for agent steps and tool calls (integrating with CloudWatch/OpenTelemetry).
AgentCore Memory.
Raising the temperature.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: AgentCore Observability captures detailed traces of an agent's reasoning steps and tool invocations for debugging and monitoring. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory stores context; it is not a tracing and monitoring tool. Not "Raising the temperature.": Temperature is unrelated to observability. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes tools; it does not provide step-level tracing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent can issue refunds, and the business requires a human to approve before any refund is executed. Which Bedrock agent feature enforces this in the action flow?

options.text: Enable user confirmation (require confirmation) on the sensitive action so the agent must obtain approval before executing it.
Disable the action group entirely.
Set temperature to 0 so the agent never makes mistakes.
Rely on the system prompt to ask the model to be careful.

explanation: Bedrock agents can require user confirmation for an action, pausing for explicit approval before the operation runs. Not "Disable the action group entirely.": Disabling the action removes the capability rather than gating it with approval. Not "Set temperature to 0 so the agent never makes mistakes.": Temperature does not create an approval step. Not "Rely on the system prompt to ask the model to be careful.": A prompt request does not enforce a hard approval gate before execution. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An application needs synchronous, low-latency predictions for small payloads with steady, predictable traffic. Which Amazon SageMaker AI deployment option is the best fit?

options.text: A SageMaker Ground Truth job.
A real-time inference endpoint.
An asynchronous inference endpoint.
A batch transform job.

explanation: Real-time endpoints provide persistent, low-latency synchronous inference, ideal for steady traffic with small payloads. Not "A SageMaker Ground Truth job.": Ground Truth is for data labeling, not model serving. Not "An asynchronous inference endpoint.": Asynchronous endpoints suit long-running requests and large payloads, adding queueing latency unnecessary for small, fast requests. Not "A batch transform job.": Batch transform is for offline, asynchronous scoring of datasets, not low-latency synchronous requests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A model serves intermittent traffic with idle periods, does not require a GPU, and the team can tolerate occasional cold starts. They want to avoid paying for idle capacity. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: A large always-on real-time endpoint.
SageMaker Serverless Inference.
An asynchronous endpoint sized for peak.
A 24/7 multi-GPU instance.

explanation: Serverless Inference automatically provisions and scales (including to zero) for intermittent CPU workloads, so you pay only when serving requests. Not "A large always-on real-time endpoint.": An always-on endpoint incurs cost during the long idle periods. Not "An asynchronous endpoint sized for peak.": Provisioning for peak wastes capacity for intermittent traffic. Not "A 24/7 multi-GPU instance.": A continuously running GPU instance is the most expensive and is unnecessary for a CPU workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A company must host hundreds of small, similar models (one per customer) cost-effectively behind as few endpoints as possible, loading each model on demand. Which SageMaker feature fits best?

options.text: One dedicated real-time endpoint per model.
A multi-model endpoint (MME).
Serverless inference with one function per model and no sharing.
A batch transform job per model.

explanation: Multi-model endpoints host many models behind a single endpoint, loading them on demand and sharing resources to reduce cost. Not "One dedicated real-time endpoint per model.": Hundreds of separate endpoints multiply cost and management overhead. Not "Serverless inference with one function per model and no s…": This does not provide the on-demand shared hosting that multi-model endpoints are designed for. Not "A batch transform job per model.": Batch transform is for offline scoring, not on-demand hosting of many models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A team deploys several large language models to GPU instances and wants to pack multiple models and copies onto shared accelerators, scale each independently, and scale unused ones to zero to cut cost. Which capability supports this?

options.text: SageMaker inference components.
A single-model real-time endpoint per model only.
Batch transform.
Ground Truth.

explanation: Inference components let you deploy multiple models/copies on shared instances, allocate resources per component, scale them independently, and scale to zero. Not "A single-model real-time endpoint per model only.": Single-model endpoints cannot pack multiple models onto shared accelerators with independent scaling. Not "Batch transform.": Batch transform is offline scoring, not GPU packing of online models. Not "Ground Truth.": Ground Truth labels data and is unrelated to serving. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Traffic to a real-time endpoint varies widely between business hours and nights. The team wants the endpoint to add and remove instances automatically based on load. What should they configure?

options.text: Automatic scaling (for example, target-tracking on invocations per instance) for the endpoint.
Raise the model temperature during peak hours.
Switch to batch transform during the day.
A fixed, manually chosen instance count sized for peak.

explanation: SageMaker endpoint auto scaling adjusts instance count based on a target metric such as invocations per instance, matching capacity to demand. Not "Raise the model temperature during peak hours.": Temperature does not affect endpoint capacity. Not "Switch to batch transform during the day.": Batch transform is offline and cannot serve real-time daytime traffic. Not "A fixed, manually chosen instance count sized for peak.": A fixed peak size wastes money at night and cannot adapt automatically. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Before promoting a new model version, a team wants to send a copy of live production traffic to it and compare results without affecting users. Which SageMaker capability provides this?

options.text: Increasing max tokens on the new version.
Batch transform on yesterday's data.
Shadow testing (shadow variants).
Deleting the old endpoint first.

explanation: Shadow testing mirrors live traffic to a shadow variant so you can validate a new version against real requests without impacting production responses. Not "Increasing max tokens on the new version.": Output length settings are unrelated to safely comparing versions on live traffic. Not "Batch transform on yesterday's data.": Offline batch scoring does not exercise the new version against live production traffic. Not "Deleting the old endpoint first.": Removing the current endpoint would disrupt users and provides no safe comparison. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A developer wants to quickly deploy a popular open foundation model with minimal setup, including a tested container and example notebooks, to get an endpoint running fast. Which option is best?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend.
Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.
Deploy the model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
Build a custom container from scratch and write all serving code.

explanation: JumpStart offers prebuilt, deployable foundation and task models with curated containers and example notebooks for fast, low-effort deployment. Not "Use Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is a managed NLP service, not a way to deploy an arbitrary foundation model. Not "Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.": Batch transform does not create an online endpoint. Not "Build a custom container from scratch and write all servi…": Building everything yourself is the slowest, highest-effort path. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A team must score a large, fixed dataset that already sits in Amazon S3 in a single offline run, with no need for a persistent endpoint. Which SageMaker option is MOST appropriate and cost-effective?

options.text: An asynchronous endpoint for each record.
A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.
A serverless endpoint with manual paging.
A batch transform job.

explanation: Batch transform processes a whole dataset from S3 in one offline run and tears down compute afterward, with no persistent endpoint to pay for. Not "An asynchronous endpoint for each record.": Per-record async calls add unnecessary overhead versus one batch transform over the dataset. Not "A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.": Looping requests over a persistent endpoint is more expensive and complex than a single batch job. Not "A serverless endpoint with manual paging.": Serverless endpoints target intermittent online requests, not bulk offline scoring of a fixed dataset. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: When updating a production endpoint to a new model, a team wants a controlled rollout that shifts a small percentage of traffic first and automatically rolls back if errors spike. Which SageMaker feature provides this?

options.text: Batch transform validation only.
Deleting and recreating the endpoint in place.
Raising the instance count during the switch.
Deployment guardrails with a canary (or linear) traffic-shifting strategy and automatic rollback.

explanation: SageMaker deployment guardrails shift traffic gradually (canary/linear), monitor alarms, and roll back automatically if the new version misbehaves. Not "Batch transform validation only.": Offline batch validation does not control live traffic shifting or rollback. Not "Deleting and recreating the endpoint in place.": An in-place replace gives no gradual shift or automatic rollback and risks downtime. Not "Raising the instance count during the switch.": More instances does not provide controlled traffic shifting or automatic rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Developers want inline, context-aware code suggestions and the ability to generate functions from natural-language comments directly inside their IDE to speed up routine coding. Which capability provides this?

options.text: Amazon Kendra.
Amazon Q Developer in-IDE code suggestions and generation.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon QuickSight Q.

explanation: Amazon Q Developer integrates with the IDE to provide real-time inline completions and generate code from natural-language prompts. Not "Amazon Kendra.": Kendra is enterprise search, not an IDE coding assistant. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is an NLP analysis service, not a coding assistant. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers natural-language questions about BI data, not IDE code generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team wants an assistant that can take a natural-language feature request, plan the change, and implement it across multiple files in their project. Which Amazon Q Developer capability is designed for this?

options.text: Increasing the model temperature.
The Amazon Q Developer feature-development agent (/dev), which plans and applies multi-file changes.
Single-line autocomplete only.
A CloudWatch dashboard.

explanation: The Q Developer agent for software development analyzes the codebase, proposes a plan, and generates coordinated changes across multiple files. Not "Increasing the model temperature.": Temperature does not provide multi-file feature implementation. Not "Single-line autocomplete only.": Basic autocomplete cannot plan and implement a multi-file feature. Not "A CloudWatch dashboard.": Dashboards visualize metrics; they do not implement code features. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: An enterprise must upgrade many applications from an old Java version to a current LTS release and wants to automate the repetitive code changes at scale. Which Amazon Q Developer capability helps MOST?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon Q Developer code transformation (automated language/framework upgrades).
Manually editing each file by hand.

explanation: Q Developer's transformation capability automates large-scale upgrades, such as moving codebases to a newer Java version, reducing manual effort. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails govern model output content, not code transformations. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data and has nothing to do with code upgrades. Not "Manually editing each file by hand.": Manual edits across many applications are slow and error-prone, which automation avoids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A security-conscious team wants their assistant to scan code for vulnerabilities and suggest remediations as part of development. Which Amazon Q Developer capability provides this?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer security scanning, which detects vulnerabilities and suggests fixes.
Raising the temperature parameter.
Amazon GuardDuty agent on the laptop.
Amazon Athena queries.

explanation: Q Developer can scan code for security issues and recommend remediations directly in the developer workflow. Not "Raising the temperature parameter.": Temperature is unrelated to code security scanning. Not "Amazon GuardDuty agent on the laptop.": GuardDuty monitors AWS accounts and workloads for threats, not in-IDE source code scanning for developers. Not "Amazon Athena queries.": Athena queries data in S3 and does not scan code for vulnerabilities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: To improve coverage and velocity, a team wants to automatically generate unit tests for existing functions. Which capability supports this with the least manual effort?

options.text: Writing every test by hand with no tooling.
Amazon QuickSight.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon Q Developer unit test generation.

explanation: Q Developer can generate unit tests for existing code, increasing coverage with minimal manual effort. Not "Writing every test by hand with no tooling.": Hand-writing all tests is the slowest option and is what the team wants to avoid. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is for dashboards, not test generation. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend performs NLP analysis, not unit test generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team must retain the full request and response content of every Amazon Bedrock model call for troubleshooting and audit. Which capability captures this with the LEAST custom code?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie on the application logs.
Enable AWS CloudTrail only.
Add print statements in the application and hope they are captured.
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3 (and/or CloudWatch Logs).

explanation: Model invocation logging is a built-in feature that records full prompts, responses, and metadata to S3 and/or CloudWatch with no custom instrumentation. Not "Use Amazon Macie on the application logs.": Macie classifies sensitive data; it does not capture model request/response content. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail only.": CloudTrail records API activity metadata, not the full prompt and response content. Not "Add print statements in the application and hope they are…": Ad hoc logging is incomplete and unreliable compared with built-in invocation logging. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A finance team needs to attribute Amazon Bedrock usage and cost to specific applications and teams that share the same models. Which approach is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Guess each team's share from total spend.
Disable logging to lower the bill.
Use Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles with cost allocation tags to track usage and cost per application.
Raise the temperature to reduce cost.

explanation: Application inference profiles let you route and tag invocations so usage and cost can be tracked and attributed per application or team. Not "Guess each team's share from total spend.": Estimation without tagging is inaccurate and not auditable. Not "Disable logging to lower the bill.": Disabling logging removes visibility and does not attribute cost. Not "Raise the temperature to reduce cost.": Temperature does not attribute or reduce cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: An application intermittently receives throttling errors from Amazon Bedrock, and operators want to be alerted automatically when throttling rises. What should they configure?

options.text: Nothing; throttling cannot be monitored.
Lower the temperature to reduce throttling.
A CloudWatch alarm on the Bedrock throttling metric for the model.
Increase max tokens to avoid throttling.

explanation: Bedrock publishes CloudWatch metrics (including throttling), so an alarm on the throttle metric notifies operators when throttling increases. Not "Nothing; throttling cannot be monitored.": Throttling is observable through CloudWatch metrics and can be alarmed on. Not "Lower the temperature to reduce throttling.": Temperature has no effect on throttling or its monitoring. Not "Increase max tokens to avoid throttling.": Output length does not address request-rate throttling or provide alerting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A generative AI request flows through API Gateway, several Lambda functions, a knowledge base, and Bedrock, and the team needs to find which component causes high end-to-end latency. Which service provides distributed tracing to localize the bottleneck?

options.text: AWS X-Ray.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon Macie.
AWS Glue.

explanation: X-Ray traces requests across distributed components, producing a service map and segment timings that pinpoint the slow part of the chain. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend analyzes text and is not a tracing tool. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data and does not trace request latency. Not "AWS Glue.": Glue is for ETL, not distributed tracing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: Invocation logs are being written to CloudWatch Logs, and an engineer needs to interactively query them to find error patterns and aggregate failures. Which tool should they use?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition.
Amazon QuickSight Q on raw log files.
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Increasing the log retention period only.

explanation: Logs Insights provides an interactive query language to search, filter, and aggregate log data such as invocation logs to surface error patterns. Not "Amazon Rekognition.": Rekognition analyzes images and video, not logs. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q on raw log files.": QuickSight Q answers questions over prepared BI datasets, not ad hoc CloudWatch log querying. Not "Increasing the log retention period only.": Longer retention stores logs but does not provide query and aggregation capabilities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A model deployed on a SageMaker real-time endpoint must be monitored for data drift and degradation in input/prediction quality over time, with automated alerts. Which capability is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
Amazon Athena.

explanation: Model Monitor continuously checks deployed endpoints for data quality, drift, and other issues against a baseline and can raise alerts. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not model data drift. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails filter content; they do not monitor endpoint data drift. Not "Amazon Athena.": Athena is a query service and does not monitor model drift. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: After launch, a team wants to continuously assure the quality of a generative feature in production, catching regressions as prompts and models change. Which practice is MOST effective?

options.text: Log responses and run periodic automated evaluations on sampled production traffic, alerting on quality regressions.
Run a single pre-launch test and never re-check.
Only watch CPU and memory metrics.
Wait for users to report problems.

explanation: Combining response logging with scheduled automated evaluation on samples provides ongoing, data-driven quality monitoring and early regression detection. Not "Run a single pre-launch test and never re-check.": A one-time test misses regressions introduced by later changes. Not "Only watch CPU and memory metrics.": Infrastructure metrics do not reveal degradations in generation quality. Not "Wait for users to report problems.": Relying on complaints is reactive and lets defects reach users. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A mobile app must let many end users call Amazon Bedrock without embedding AWS credentials in the app. The team wants each user to receive scoped, temporary AWS credentials after signing in. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Embed a shared IAM access key in the mobile app.
Give every user the root account credentials.
Store one IAM user's secret in the app config for everyone.
Use Amazon Cognito identity pools to exchange a sign-in for temporary, scoped AWS credentials.

explanation: Cognito identity pools federate authenticated users to temporary AWS credentials tied to an IAM role, avoiding embedded long-lived keys. Not "Embed a shared IAM access key in the mobile app.": Embedding long-lived keys in a distributed app is a serious security risk. Not "Give every user the root account credentials.": Sharing root credentials is never acceptable and grossly violates least privilege. Not "Store one IAM user's secret in the app config for everyone.": A shared long-lived secret cannot be scoped per user and is easily compromised. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A regulated company must call Amazon Bedrock from workloads in its VPC without traversing the public internet. Which solution provides private connectivity?

options.text: Create VPC interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock.
Route all Bedrock calls through a public NAT gateway only.
Use the model temperature to control routing.
Disable encryption to simplify networking.

explanation: Interface VPC endpoints via PrivateLink keep traffic to Bedrock on the AWS network, avoiding the public internet. Not "Route all Bedrock calls through a public NAT gateway only.": A NAT gateway still sends traffic over the public internet, not a private path. Not "Use the model temperature to control routing.": Temperature is unrelated to network connectivity. Not "Disable encryption to simplify networking.": Disabling encryption weakens security and does not provide private connectivity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A company must encrypt its Bedrock custom model artifacts and knowledge base data at rest using keys it controls and can audit and rotate. Which approach should it use?

options.text: Hard-code an encryption passphrase in the app.
Store the data in a public S3 bucket.
Rely on no encryption to reduce latency.
Encrypt with an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).

explanation: A customer managed KMS key gives the company control over key policies, rotation, and CloudTrail auditing of key usage for data at rest. Not "Hard-code an encryption passphrase in the app.": A hard-coded passphrase is insecure and is not a managed, auditable key. Not "Store the data in a public S3 bucket.": Public exposure is the opposite of the security requirement. Not "Rely on no encryption to reduce latency.": Operating without encryption fails the data-protection requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An application in Account A must call Amazon Bedrock resources governed by Account B, using temporary credentials and no long-lived keys. Which mechanism is appropriate?

options.text: Make all Bedrock resources public.
Email an IAM access key from Account B to Account A.
Create an IAM role in Account B and have Account A assume it with AWS STS AssumeRole.
Use the same root user for both accounts.

explanation: Cross-account IAM roles assumed via STS provide temporary credentials and scoped permissions without sharing long-lived keys. Not "Make all Bedrock resources public.": Public access removes the access control the requirement depends on. Not "Email an IAM access key from Account B to Account A.": Sharing long-lived access keys is insecure and unmanageable. Not "Use the same root user for both accounts.": Sharing root credentials across accounts is a severe security violation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An agent's AWS Lambda function must call a third-party API that requires a secret API key, which must be stored securely and rotated without code changes. Which service should hold the key?

options.text: A hard-coded constant in the Lambda code.
AWS Secrets Manager.
An unencrypted object in a public S3 bucket.
A plaintext environment variable committed to source control.

explanation: Secrets Manager securely stores credentials, controls access via IAM, and supports rotation without changing application code. Not "A hard-coded constant in the Lambda code.": Hard-coded secrets cannot be rotated safely and risk exposure. Not "An unencrypted object in a public S3 bucket.": Public, unencrypted storage of a secret is a serious vulnerability. Not "A plaintext environment variable committed to source cont…": Committing secrets to source control exposes them and provides no rotation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: Security policy requires that a given IAM role be allowed to invoke only one specific approved foundation model in Amazon Bedrock and no others. How is this BEST enforced?

options.text: Lower the temperature on the disallowed models.
Write a least-privilege IAM policy that allows invoke actions only on the approved model's resource ARN.
Rely on the application code to choose the right model.
Allow all Bedrock models and remind developers to use only the approved one.

explanation: Scoping the IAM policy to the specific model ARN enforces that the role can invoke only the approved model, following least privilege. Not "Lower the temperature on the disallowed models.": Temperature does not restrict which models a role may call. Not "Rely on the application code to choose the right model.": Application-side selection is not an access control and can be bypassed. Not "Allow all Bedrock models and remind developers to use onl…": A broad allow with a verbal reminder does not technically restrict access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A compliance team must ensure that customer prompts are processed only within an approved AWS Region and are not used to train the base foundation models. Which statement and configuration are correct?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock in the approved Region; Bedrock processes data in that Region and does not use your prompts or outputs to train the base models.
You must file a support ticket or it will train on your data by default.
Only running your own self-hosted model can prevent base-model training on your data.
Data is always processed globally regardless of Region.

explanation: Bedrock keeps inference data within the Region you call and does not use customer inputs/outputs to train base models, so selecting the approved Region meets the requirement. Not "You must file a support ticket or it will train on your d…": Bedrock does not use your inputs/outputs to train base models, so no opt-out ticket is required for that. Not "Only running your own self-hosted model can prevent base-…": Using Bedrock already prevents your data from training the base models; self-hosting is not required for that guarantee. Not "Data is always processed globally regardless of Region.": Bedrock processes your inference data in the Region where you invoke the model, not globally. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A team needs to filter harmful content (hate, insults, violence, sexual content, and misconduct) in both prompts and responses, with adjustable strictness per category. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature provides this?

options.text: Lowering the temperature.
Content filters with configurable strength thresholds per harmful category.
Provisioned Throughput.
Stop sequences.

explanation: Guardrails content filters detect and block harmful categories in input and output, with adjustable filter strengths per category. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not filter harmful content. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput is a capacity feature, unrelated to content filtering. Not "Stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation at a phrase; they do not classify or block harmful categories. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A banking assistant must never discuss a specific prohibited subject (for example, giving individualized investment advice), even when users phrase the request in new ways. Which Guardrails feature is designed for this?

options.text: A larger context window.
Denied topics, defined with a description and examples so the guardrail blocks that subject.
Increasing max tokens.
A higher temperature.

explanation: Denied topics let you define subjects to block by description and examples, so the guardrail refuses related requests regardless of phrasing. Not "A larger context window.": Context size does not prevent a prohibited topic from being discussed. Not "Increasing max tokens.": Output length does not block a subject. Not "A higher temperature.": Temperature does not enforce topic restrictions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: An assistant must ensure that any personally identifiable information appearing in model responses is masked or blocked before reaching users. Which Guardrails capability addresses this?

options.text: A custom font in the UI.
Stop sequences on names.
The sensitive information (PII) filter, which can mask or block PII in inputs and outputs.
Lowering the temperature.

explanation: Guardrails can detect PII and either mask it (for example, redact) or block the response, protecting users from exposure. Not "A custom font in the UI.": Presentation styling does not remove PII from the content. Not "Stop sequences on names.": Stop sequences cannot reliably detect and redact varied PII entities. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not detect or mask PII. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A public chatbot is targeted by users trying to override its instructions and extract restricted behavior. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails capability specifically helps detect these attempts?

options.text: Adding more few-shot examples of jokes.
The prompt attack filter, which detects prompt injection and jailbreak attempts.
Increasing the temperature to confuse attackers.
Switching to batch inference.

explanation: Guardrails include a prompt attack filter that flags prompt injection and jailbreak inputs so they can be blocked. Not "Adding more few-shot examples of jokes.": Unrelated examples do not provide injection detection. Not "Increasing the temperature to confuse attackers.": Temperature does not detect or stop prompt attacks. Not "Switching to batch inference.": Batch inference is a serving mode and does not detect prompt attacks. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A company runs a self-managed RAG pipeline and even calls a model hosted outside Amazon Bedrock, but it wants to apply the same Bedrock guardrail policies to arbitrary text at chosen points in the flow. Which capability enables this?

options.text: The ApplyGuardrail API, which evaluates text against a guardrail independently of a model invocation.
Raising the temperature.
Provisioned Throughput.
Only inline guardrails on Bedrock InvokeModel.

explanation: ApplyGuardrail lets you assess input or output text against a guardrail at any point, including content from models not hosted in Bedrock. Not "Raising the temperature.": Temperature is unrelated to applying guardrail policies. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput is a capacity feature, not a guardrail evaluation API. Not "Only inline guardrails on Bedrock InvokeModel.": Inline-only guardrails would not cover text from external models or arbitrary pipeline points, which ApplyGuardrail handles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the team wants the guardrail itself to block responses that are not supported by the retrieved source or that stray from the user's query, using a tunable threshold. Which Guardrails capability fits?

options.text: The contextual grounding and relevance checks, with configurable thresholds.
Denied topics only.
A larger model temperature.
Stop sequences.

explanation: Guardrails contextual grounding and relevance checks score whether a response is grounded in the source and relevant to the query, and can block low-scoring responses based on thresholds you set. Not "Denied topics only.": Denied topics block subjects but do not measure grounding in the retrieved source. Not "A larger model temperature.": Temperature does not assess or enforce grounding. Not "Stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation and cannot assess grounding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A regulated insurer needs strong assurance that policy-related answers conform to its written rules, with verifiable checks rather than only probabilistic filtering. Which newer Amazon Bedrock Guardrails capability is designed to mathematically verify outputs against encoded policies?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput.
Automated Reasoning checks.
Stop sequences.
Increasing the temperature.

explanation: Automated Reasoning checks use formal, logic-based verification against an encoded policy to validate whether responses are consistent with the rules, reducing factual errors in regulated domains. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput is a capacity feature, not a verification capability. Not "Stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not verify policy conformance. Not "Increasing the temperature.": Temperature does not verify outputs against policy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A financial firm must store generated compliance records so they cannot be altered or deleted for a mandated retention period, even by administrators. Which configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: Use S3 versioning alone without Object Lock.
Keep records only in application memory.
Store records in Amazon S3 with Object Lock in compliance mode for the required retention period.
Store records in a standard S3 bucket and ask staff not to delete them.

explanation: S3 Object Lock compliance mode enforces write-once-read-many (WORM) immutability so objects cannot be modified or deleted, even by the root user, until retention expires. Not "Use S3 versioning alone without Object Lock.": Versioning preserves prior versions but does not prevent deletion or enforce a compliance retention lock. Not "Keep records only in application memory.": In-memory storage is volatile and provides no durable, immutable retention. Not "Store records in a standard S3 bucket and ask staff not t…": A policy request does not technically prevent modification or deletion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: An auditor must determine which IAM principals called which Amazon Bedrock APIs, and when, across the account. Which service provides this audit trail?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards only.
AWS CloudTrail.

explanation: CloudTrail records API calls including the principal, action, time, and source, providing the management/audit trail of who did what. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data; it does not record API caller identity and actions. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend analyzes text and is not an API audit service. Not "Amazon CloudWatch dashboards only.": Dashboards visualize metrics but do not provide the per-call identity and action audit trail. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: For regulatory reconstruction, a company must retain the actual prompt content and model responses (not just API metadata) for every Bedrock call, in immutable storage. Which combination meets this?

options.text: Rely on CloudWatch metrics for content.
Print prompts to the application console only.
Enable AWS CloudTrail alone.
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and apply S3 Object Lock for the retention period.

explanation: Invocation logging captures full prompt and response content, and Object Lock makes the stored logs immutable for the mandated retention. Not "Rely on CloudWatch metrics for content.": Metrics are numeric aggregates and do not store prompt or response text. Not "Print prompts to the application console only.": Console output is not durable, complete, or immutable for compliance. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail alone.": CloudTrail captures API metadata, not the full prompt and response content required for reconstruction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A company wants to keep customer chat transcripts for analytics but must comply with privacy rules that prohibit retaining personally identifiable information. What is the BEST approach before storing the transcripts?

options.text: Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII indefinitely.
Redact PII from the transcripts with Amazon Comprehend before storing the sanitized text.
Store the raw transcripts unchanged for completeness.
Raise the model temperature to obscure PII.

explanation: Detecting and redacting PII with Comprehend before storage lets the company keep useful analytics data while complying with privacy requirements. Not "Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII indefinitely.": Encryption protects data at rest but does not satisfy a rule against retaining PII at all. Not "Store the raw transcripts unchanged for completeness.": Storing raw PII violates the privacy requirement. Not "Raise the model temperature to obscure PII.": Temperature does not remove PII from stored text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: Stored embeddings and invocation logs contain sensitive business data, and the security team must control and audit the encryption keys used to protect them at rest. Which approach should they adopt?

options.text: Leave the data unencrypted to simplify access.
Use a single shared password stored in code.
Encrypt the data with AWS KMS customer managed keys and restrict and audit key usage via key policies and CloudTrail.
Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.

explanation: Customer managed KMS keys give the team control over rotation and access, and CloudTrail records key usage for auditing. Not "Leave the data unencrypted to simplify access.": Unencrypted sensitive data fails the data-protection requirement. Not "Use a single shared password stored in code.": A hard-coded shared secret is insecure and not an auditable managed key. Not "Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.": Public storage exposes the sensitive data and is the opposite of the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A production Bedrock workload has steady, high, predictable demand for 12 business hours and near-zero traffic overnight. The team must guarantee dedicated capacity during business hours (no throttling) at the lowest total cost, keeping the same model and API. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput without a long-term commitment, creating model units for business hours and deleting them overnight.
Use on-demand inference for all traffic.
Use Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment sized for peak.
Use cross-Region inference to add capacity during business hours.

explanation: No-commitment Provisioned Throughput guarantees dedicated capacity while active and is billed only while provisioned, so releasing units overnight avoids paying for the idle period. Not "Use on-demand inference for all traffic.": On-demand has no idle cost but cannot guarantee dedicated capacity during peak hours, so it fails the no-throttling requirement. Not "Use Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment size…": A committed term is cheapest per hour but you pay for the reserved units overnight too, so with near-zero overnight traffic it is not the lowest total cost. Not "Use cross-Region inference to add capacity during busines…": Cross-Region inference spreads on-demand traffic for throughput/availability but does not reserve guaranteed capacity, and it is still on-demand priced. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A synchronous, customer-facing Bedrock feature must become more resilient to transient errors and to a single-Region impairment, per the Reliability pillar. Which TWO measures are MOST effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase maxTokens so fewer requests are needed.
Place a single-Region Amazon SQS queue in front of the model call.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for throttling and transient 5xx errors.
Use cross-Region inference (or multi-Region failover) so requests can be served if one Region is impaired.
Lower the temperature for more consistent outputs.

explanation: Backoff with jitter recovers from transient throttling/5xx without synchronized retry storms, directly improving reliability. Spreading or failing over across Regions keeps the feature available during a regional impairment. Not "Increase maxTokens so fewer requests are needed.": Output length has no effect on resilience to errors or regional failure. Not "Place a single-Region Amazon SQS queue in front of the mo…": A queue in one Region is itself a regional single point of failure and adds latency to a synchronous, user-facing path, so it does not address regional resilience here. Not "Lower the temperature for more consistent outputs.": Temperature controls randomness, not reliability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An interactive assistant must reduce the latency users perceive on long answers, WITHOUT changing which model is used and without a training step. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: Enable response streaming and turn on latency-optimized inference for the model.
Buy Provisioned Throughput at high model units.
Distill to a smaller student model.
Switch to a model with a larger context window.

explanation: Streaming shows tokens as they are generated (cutting perceived latency) and latency-optimized inference speeds generation, both without changing the model or training anything. Not "Buy Provisioned Throughput at high model units.": Provisioned Throughput reduces throttling/queueing but does not lower the per-token generation time that dominates perceived latency on long answers. Not "Distill to a smaller student model.": Distillation reduces latency but changes the model and requires a training step, which the scenario forbids. Not "Switch to a model with a larger context window.": A bigger context window does not reduce generation latency and can increase it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A team must roll out a new prompt version to production with the ability to revert instantly if quality regresses, measure both versions, and avoid redeploying application code. Which approach best fits Operational Excellence?

options.text: Manage the prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with versions/variants, run automated evaluations, and switch or revert by changing the active version.
Hard-code the new prompt behind an application feature flag.
Raise the temperature so the new prompt is more robust.
Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt, and split traffic.

explanation: Managed prompt versions/variants plus automated evaluation let you compare, switch, and roll back without any code deploy. Not "Hard-code the new prompt behind an application feature flag.": A feature flag enables reverting but still requires a code deploy to ship the prompt and provides no managed versioning or evaluation. Not "Raise the temperature so the new prompt is more robust.": Temperature does not provide rollout control, measurement, or rollback. Not "Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt,…": This is custom, requires code deploys, and lacks managed prompt versioning and built-in evaluation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A workload classifies tens of millions of documents per day in rolling waves; results must be available within about two hours of each submission (not real time). Cost must be minimized. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput sized for the wave peaks.
On-demand real-time invocation for each document.
Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs.

explanation: The work is high-volume and latency-tolerant (about two hours), which is exactly what Bedrock batch inference is priced and designed for. Not "Provisioned Throughput sized for the wave peaks.": Reserved capacity guarantees throughput but costs more than batch for latency-tolerant bulk work. Not "On-demand real-time invocation for each document.": Per-document real-time calls work but are the most expensive option at this volume and are unnecessary given the two-hour tolerance. Not "Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.": Asynchronous inference serves SageMaker-hosted models, not Bedrock foundation models, so it does not apply. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A team building a Bedrock RAG application wants AWS prescriptive best practices created specifically for generative AI concerns such as RAG accuracy, responsible AI, and model selection. Which resource is the BEST fit?

options.text: The AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens.
The AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens.
The AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens.
The six core Well-Architected pillars alone.

explanation: The Generative AI Lens provides design principles and best practices tailored to generative AI workloads, including RAG and responsible AI. Not "The AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens.": The SaaS Lens targets SaaS business/architecture concerns, not generative AI design. Not "The AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens.": The ML Lens covers the traditional ML lifecycle and is not focused on generative-AI-specific concerns like RAG accuracy and responsible AI for FMs. Not "The six core Well-Architected pillars alone.": The core pillars are general guidance; the GenAI-specific practices live in the Generative AI Lens. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A RAG chatbot includes a 6,000-token static policy preamble in every request. The team wants to cut the cost and latency of that repeated context with minimal change and using the SAME model. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Enable prompt caching for the static preamble so the repeated prefix is reused across requests.
Store the preamble in a knowledge base and retrieve it each call.
Fine-tune the model so the policy is implicit and can be dropped from prompts.
Reduce maxTokens on the response.

explanation: Prompt caching reuses the unchanging prefix, reducing both billed tokens and latency for the repeated context with no model change. Not "Store the preamble in a knowledge base and retrieve it ea…": Retrieval still injects the preamble tokens every call and adds a retrieval step, so it does not cut the repeated-token cost. Not "Fine-tune the model so the policy is implicit and can be …": Fine-tuning changes the model, adds maintenance, and is not a minimal change; it also makes policy updates harder. Not "Reduce maxTokens on the response.": Lowering output length does not reduce the cost of the repeated input preamble. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A customer-facing RAG assistant occasionally produces confident but unsupported answers. The team wants to reduce hallucinations while keeping a good user experience, aligned with the GenAI Lens responsible-AI guidance. Which combination is BEST?

options.text: Add a Guardrails contextual grounding check and instruct the model to answer only from the retrieved context and to say it does not know when the answer is absent.
Switch to a larger model.
Set temperature to 0.
Add a denied-topics policy for the subject area.

explanation: Combining a grounding check with an explicit grounding/abstention instruction is defense-in-depth that targets ungrounded answers directly. Not "Switch to a larger model.": A larger model still hallucinates without grounding controls; size is not a grounding mechanism. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Lower randomness alone does not make an answer grounded in the sources; the model can still confidently fabricate. Not "Add a denied-topics policy for the subject area.": Denied topics block whole subjects; they do not detect or prevent ungrounded answers within an allowed subject. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A bank's assistant must always cite the LATEST internal regulations (which change weekly) AND must CONSISTENTLY emit a strict report template. Which approach meets BOTH with the least ongoing effort?

options.text: Fine-tune the model every week on both the regulations and the template.
Use RAG only, relying on a detailed prompt to enforce the template.
Use continued pre-training on the regulations and a prompt for the template.
Use RAG for the frequently changing regulations and fine-tune the model for the fixed report template/style.

explanation: RAG keeps regulatory content current without retraining, while fine-tuning reliably enforces a rigid output format; each technique handles the part it is best at. Not "Fine-tune the model every week on both the regulations an…": Weekly fine-tuning is operationally heavy and still lags between runs; RAG handles freshness far more cheaply. Not "Use RAG only, relying on a detailed prompt to enforce the…": RAG fixes freshness, but prompt-only formatting is not reliably consistent, which the scenario explicitly requires. Not "Use continued pre-training on the regulations and a promp…": Continued pre-training is for absorbing domain language from large corpora, is heavy, and does not keep weekly content current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team has a very large corpus of UNLABELED specialized legal text and wants the base model to internalize the domain's vocabulary and patterns. Which customization method is appropriate?

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Continued pre-training on the unlabeled corpus.
Supervised fine-tuning.
Model distillation.
