explanation: Continued pre-training adapts a model to domain language using large volumes of unlabeled text. Not "Retrieval-Augmented Generation.": RAG retrieves text at inference time but does not make the model internalize domain language. Not "Supervised fine-tuning.": Fine-tuning requires labeled prompt/response pairs; the corpus is unlabeled, so it does not apply. Not "Model distillation.": Distillation compresses a larger model into a smaller one; it is not a method for absorbing a domain corpus. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Latency and cost of a large model are too high, but the team must KEEP its accuracy on their specific task and can accept an upfront training step. Which option BEST fits?

options.text: Enable latency-optimized inference on the large model.
Lower top-k to make the large model cheaper.
Model distillation, training a smaller student from the large teacher on the task.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model.

explanation: Distillation produces a smaller, cheaper, faster model that retains much of the teacher's task accuracy, and it explicitly involves an upfront training step. Not "Enable latency-optimized inference on the large model.": Latency-optimized inference speeds responses but does not meaningfully cut the large model's cost and involves no training step. Not "Lower top-k to make the large model cheaper.": Sampling parameters do not change model cost or latency materially. Not "Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model.": Provisioned Throughput stabilizes capacity but does not reduce the per-call cost or size of the large model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Throughput must increase for a steady, predictable, high baseline load running 24/7, at the lowest per-token cost, using the same model and API. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with a committed term.
On-demand inference with client retries.
Bedrock batch inference.
Cross-Region inference.

explanation: For steady 24/7 high volume, a committed Provisioned Throughput model unit gives the lowest per-token cost and guaranteed capacity. Not "On-demand inference with client retries.": On-demand at constant high volume costs more and risks throttling versus committed reserved capacity. Not "Bedrock batch inference.": Batch inference is offline and cannot serve steady real-time throughput. Not "Cross-Region inference.": Cross-Region inference adds throughput but is on-demand priced, so it is not the lowest per-token cost for steady 24/7 load. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: To make a model's outputs maximally deterministic for snapshot tests, which TWO inference settings TOGETHER are most effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set temperature to 0.
Add several stop sequences.
Use a high temperature with a low maxTokens.
Increase top-k substantially.
Constrain sampling with a low top-p (and avoid a large top-k).

explanation: A temperature of 0 makes sampling effectively greedy, the primary lever for deterministic output. Narrowing the nucleus to the most probable tokens removes residual variability that temperature alone may leave. Not "Add several stop sequences.": Stop sequences control where generation ends, not how deterministic the tokens are. Not "Use a high temperature with a low maxTokens.": High temperature maximizes randomness; capping length does not make content deterministic. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": A larger top-k widens the candidate pool and increases variability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A pipeline expects the model to stop generating exactly when it produces the marker END_JSON, and that marker must not appear in the output to keep downstream parsing clean. Which solution is BEST?

options.text: Configure END_JSON as a stop sequence in the inference request.
Set maxTokens to an estimated length.
Instruct the model in the prompt to stop after END_JSON.
Lower the temperature.

explanation: A stop sequence halts generation when the phrase is produced and the stop text itself is not included in the returned output, which keeps parsing clean. Not "Set maxTokens to an estimated length.": A length guess does not stop at the marker and risks cutting content or leaving the marker in. Not "Instruct the model in the prompt to stop after END_JSON.": Prompt instructions are not a reliable stopping mechanism and would leave the marker in the text. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature does not control stopping at a specific phrase. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A high-volume pipeline must caption product IMAGES with short text at the lowest cost and latency while still supporting vision. Which Amazon Nova model is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Nova Pro.
Amazon Nova Micro.
Amazon Nova Canvas.
Amazon Nova Lite.

explanation: Nova Lite is the low-cost multimodal model, the cheapest/fastest Nova option that still understands images. Not "Amazon Nova Pro.": Nova Pro understands images but at higher cost and latency than this simple, high-volume captioning needs. Not "Amazon Nova Micro.": Nova Micro is the lowest-cost model overall but is text-only and cannot process images. Not "Amazon Nova Canvas.": Nova Canvas generates images; it does not caption or understand existing images. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must cut vector-storage cost for a TEXT-ONLY semantic search while keeping good recall, with minimal re-architecture. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and select a smaller output dimension.
Increase the embedding dimension to improve accuracy.
Use a text-generation model to produce the embeddings.
Switch to Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.

explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports configurable, smaller dimensions that cut index size and cost while keeping acceptable recall, with no architecture change. Not "Increase the embedding dimension to improve accuracy.": Larger dimensions increase storage and cost, the opposite of the goal. Not "Use a text-generation model to produce the embeddings.": Generative models are not embedding models and would not provide a proper vector index. Not "Switch to Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.": Multimodal embeddings target image+text retrieval and do not reduce storage for a text-only search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must compare two models on SUMMARY quality (coherence and relevance) over thousands of documents, automatically, with NO human raters and NO reference summaries available. Which evaluation approach fits?

options.text: Compare the two models' CloudWatch latency metrics.
A human evaluation workflow.
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation with an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator.
Bedrock evaluation using reference-based metrics such as BERTScore or exact match.

explanation: LLM-as-a-judge scores open-ended quality dimensions at scale without humans and without needing reference answers. Not "Compare the two models' CloudWatch latency metrics.": Latency does not measure summary coherence or relevance. Not "A human evaluation workflow.": Human evaluation is excluded by the no-human-raters constraint. Not "Bedrock evaluation using reference-based metrics such as …": Reference-based metrics require ground-truth reference summaries, which are not available here. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must build ONE codebase that does multi-turn chat WITH tool calling across both Anthropic Claude and Amazon Nova models, minimizing model-specific request/response code. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Build a custom abstraction layer over each model's API.
Use InvokeModelWithResponseStream per model.
Call InvokeModel with each model's native JSON body.
Use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API.

explanation: Converse provides a unified, model-agnostic interface for multi-turn messages and tool use across supported models, minimizing per-model code. Not "Build a custom abstraction layer over each model's API.": A custom layer reinvents what Converse already standardizes. Not "Use InvokeModelWithResponseStream per model.": This still needs model-specific bodies and only adds streaming, not unification. Not "Call InvokeModel with each model's native JSON body.": InvokeModel requires model-specific payloads and parsing, which is exactly the per-model code to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company fine-tuned open-weights Llama models OUTSIDE AWS (a supported architecture) and wants them callable through the Amazon Bedrock runtime API, on demand, with no servers to run. Which option is correct?

options.text: Buy Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.
Deploy the weights to a SageMaker real-time endpoint.
Run continued pre-training in Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.

explanation: Custom Model Import brings supported external weights into Bedrock so they are invoked through the standard on-demand Bedrock APIs with no managed infrastructure. Not "Buy Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for Bedrock models; it does not serve your own imported weights. Not "Deploy the weights to a SageMaker real-time endpoint.": A SageMaker endpoint can serve the model but is not the Bedrock runtime API and requires managing the endpoint. Not "Run continued pre-training in Bedrock.": Continued pre-training customizes a Bedrock base model; it does not import your externally trained weights. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team wants to grow throughput using cross-Region inference, but compliance requires that all inference data remain within one approved Region. What is the CORRECT stance?

options.text: Enable cross-Region inference; it always keeps data within the source Region's country.
Enable cross-Region inference; the data never leaves the source Region.
Do not use a cross-Region profile that can route outside the approved Region; stay on in-Region on-demand or Provisioned Throughput.
Switch to batch inference to keep data in Region.

explanation: Cross-Region inference can route requests to other Regions in the geography, which would violate single-Region data residency, so it must be avoided for this requirement. Not "Enable cross-Region inference; it always keeps data withi…": Routing targets depend on the profile's geography and are not guaranteed to stay in one country/Region. Not "Enable cross-Region inference; the data never leaves the …": Cross-Region inference can process requests in other Regions, so this statement is incorrect. Not "Switch to batch inference to keep data in Region.": Batch versus real-time is unrelated to the residency guarantee and does not address the throughput requirement correctly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Users upload SCREENSHOTS OF CHARTS and ask analytical questions about the trends shown. Which approach BEST answers them?

options.text: Use Amazon Textract to extract the chart.
Use Amazon Rekognition to analyze the image.
Send the image to a Bedrock multimodal foundation model via the Converse API.
Use Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.

explanation: A multimodal FM can interpret the chart's visuals and answer natural-language analytical questions about the trends. Not "Use Amazon Textract to extract the chart.": Textract extracts text and tables from documents but does not reason about a chart's visual trends. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition to analyze the image.": Rekognition returns labels/objects, not analytical answers about chart trends. Not "Use Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.": Multimodal embeddings support retrieval/similarity, not question answering about an image. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A Bedrock foundation model must process a very large OFFLINE job over millions of prompts at the lowest cost; turnaround of tens of minutes is fine. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput.
Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference (a model invocation job).
A loop of on-demand InvokeModel calls.

explanation: Batch inference is purpose-built for large, latency-tolerant offline workloads on Bedrock FMs at the lowest cost. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Reserved online capacity is not the cheapest way to run a one-off offline bulk job. Not "Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.": Asynchronous inference serves SageMaker-hosted models, not Bedrock foundation models, so it does not apply. Not "A loop of on-demand InvokeModel calls.": Real-time calls in a loop are more expensive and slower for millions of prompts than a batch job. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team has only about 30 examples of a desired behavior and needs better adherence quickly; collecting thousands of labeled examples is not feasible. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use few-shot prompting that includes the example demonstrations.
Distill the model.
Run continued pre-training.
Fine-tune the model on the 30 examples.

explanation: Few-shot prompting leverages a handful of examples immediately and is the right tool when labeled data is scarce. Not "Distill the model.": Distillation addresses cost/latency, not teaching a behavior from a few examples. Not "Run continued pre-training.": Continued pre-training needs a large unlabeled corpus, not 30 examples. Not "Fine-tune the model on the 30 examples.": Roughly 30 examples are generally too few to fine-tune effectively and risk overfitting with little gain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A summarizer sometimes truncates mid-sentence, but the team also wants to prevent runaway, overly long outputs. Which TWO settings TOGETHER best address both? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a stop sequence at the natural end-of-answer marker.
Lower the temperature.
Increase maxTokens enough to fit a complete answer.
Increase top-k.
Enlarge the model's context window.

explanation: A stop sequence ends generation cleanly at the intended boundary, preventing runaway length. Mid-sentence truncation means the output is hitting the token cap, so raising maxTokens to a sufficient size lets answers complete. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature affects randomness, not truncation or maximum length. Not "Increase top-k.": Top-k changes token diversity, not output length. Not "Enlarge the model's context window.": The context window governs input size, not how long the output may be. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Before fine-tuning on customer chat transcripts, a team must programmatically REMOVE PII from the free text across a large dataset. Which service is the right tool?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-information filter.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection and redaction.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon Textract.

explanation: Comprehend detects and redacts PII entities within text, producing sanitized transcripts for training. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-information filter.": Guardrails apply at inference time to a model's prompts/responses; they are not a batch redaction tool for preparing a training corpus. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data across S3 but does not redact PII inside text for downstream training. Not "Amazon Textract.": Textract extracts text from documents; it does not detect or redact PII. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A governance team must INVENTORY where PII resides across 500 Amazon S3 buckets before deciding how to process it. Which service fits BEST?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon S3 Inventory.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

explanation: Macie is built to discover and classify sensitive data and PII across S3 at scale, producing the inventory the team needs. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend analyzes and redacts PII within individual text inputs but is not a bucket-scale discovery/classification inventory tool. Not "Amazon S3 Inventory.": S3 Inventory lists objects and metadata but does not classify which contain PII. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails govern model I/O at inference; they do not scan storage for sensitive data. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team needs human-labeled instruction/response pairs with a managed workforce option and built-in quality controls (annotation consolidation). Which service is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend custom classification.
Raw Amazon Mechanical Turk tasks.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth.

explanation: Ground Truth provides managed labeling workflows, workforce options, and quality features such as annotation consolidation. Not "Amazon Comprehend custom classification.": Comprehend automates classification; it is not a human-labeling service for creating new pairs. Not "Raw Amazon Mechanical Turk tasks.": Mechanical Turk supplies a crowd but lacks the managed labeling workflow, templates, and consolidation that Ground Truth adds. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.": Data Wrangler transforms tabular data; it does not run human annotation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Millions of raw JSON documents must be cleaned, normalized, and partitioned every night as a repeatable, serverless production pipeline with the least operational overhead. Which service is BEST?

options.text: An Amazon EMR Spark cluster.
AWS Glue serverless ETL jobs.
One AWS Lambda invocation per file.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

explanation: Glue runs scheduled, serverless Spark ETL for large-scale cleaning/partitioning with no clusters to manage. Not "An Amazon EMR Spark cluster.": EMR is capable but requires provisioning and managing cluster capacity. Not "One AWS Lambda invocation per file.": Per-file Lambda processing is hard to orchestrate at this scale and hits timeout limits. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.": Data Wrangler is an interactive, notebook-oriented prep tool, not a hands-off serverless nightly production pipeline at this scale. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A developer must provide a SUPERVISED fine-tuning dataset to Amazon Bedrock. What is the correct format and location?

options.text: An Amazon DynamoDB table of examples.
A JSONL file of prompt/completion (or messages) examples in Amazon S3 matching the model's schema.
A CSV export of raw documents in S3.
A folder of PDFs in S3.

explanation: Bedrock customization reads labeled examples as JSONL records from S3 in the required schema. Not "An Amazon DynamoDB table of examples.": Fine-tuning reads from S3 in the required file format, not from DynamoDB. Not "A CSV export of raw documents in S3.": Raw documents are not labeled prompt/response pairs; this is not a supervised fine-tuning dataset. Not "A folder of PDFs in S3.": An unstructured PDF corpus suits RAG ingestion, not supervised fine-tuning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team must measure representation imbalance in the TRAINING DATASET before any training begins. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics.
Amazon Comprehend.

explanation: Clarify computes pre-training bias metrics directly on the dataset before training. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.": Model Monitor detects drift on a deployed endpoint, not dataset bias before training. Not "Amazon SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics.": Post-training metrics evaluate a trained model's predictions, not the dataset before training. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend performs NLP tasks, not dataset bias measurement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A governance team must publish a standardized, human-readable record of each model's intended use, training data, evaluation, and risk rating for audits. Which feature is BEST?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.
AWS Config.

explanation: Model Cards capture intended use, training details, evaluation, and risk in a standardized, versioned, auditable document. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail logs API activity, not model governance documentation. Not "Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.": Lineage tracking records artifact/step graphs automatically; it is not the human-readable governance document of intended use and risk. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not model documentation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team must AUTOMATICALLY track which dataset version and which processing job produced a given model artifact, as a queryable lineage graph. Which capability is correct?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.
Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.
AWS CloudTrail.

explanation: ML Lineage Tracking automatically records the entities and relationships (datasets, jobs, models) as a queryable lineage graph. Not "AWS Glue Data Catalog.": The Data Catalog inventories data sources; it does not track model-artifact lineage. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.": Model Cards are a manually authored governance document, not an automatic artifact-lineage graph. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not a model-artifact lineage graph. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team is preparing a fine-tuning dataset and wants to minimize overfitting and train/test leakage. Which TWO steps best support this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Include the evaluation questions in the training set for coverage.
Increase the number of training epochs.
Deduplicate near-duplicate examples.
Create a held-out test split that does not overlap the training data.
Oversample the majority class to grow the dataset.

explanation: Removing duplicates prevents the model from overweighting repeated samples and reduces overfitting. A non-overlapping evaluation split prevents leakage and gives an honest generalization estimate. Not "Include the evaluation questions in the training set for …": Putting test items into training is textbook data leakage. Not "Increase the number of training epochs.": Epoch count is a training hyperparameter, not a data-preparation step, and more epochs can overfit. Not "Oversample the majority class to grow the dataset.": Oversampling the majority worsens imbalance and encourages overfitting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A Bedrock knowledge base needs a fully managed vector store for HIGH query-per-second, LOW-latency similarity search with no capacity planning. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.
Amazon S3 Vectors.

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless is the natively integrated, auto-scaling managed vector store suited to frequent, low-latency queries without capacity planning. Not "Amazon Neptune Analytics.": Neptune Analytics powers GraphRAG over relationships, not general high-QPS vector search. Not "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": Aurora pgvector is supported but you size and manage the database instance; it is not the auto-scaling serverless choice for high QPS. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors.": S3 Vectors optimizes cost for infrequent queries at huge scale, not high-QPS low-latency search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A corpus of billions of embeddings is queried only a few times per month for occasional investigations. The team wants the lowest-cost durable vector storage with no capacity to manage. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: S3 Vectors gives serverless, pay-for-use vector storage and search at massive scale, ideal for infrequent queries. Not "Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.": OpenSearch Serverless keeps warm capacity you pay for, which is wasteful for queries a few times a month. Not "Amazon DynamoDB.": DynamoDB has no native vector similarity search. Not "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": Aurora requires running instances and is not the lowest-cost option for rarely queried, very large vector sets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Embeddings must live ALONGSIDE existing relational records in the SAME managed PostgreSQL database for transactional consistency, with minimal new technology. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps vectors next to relational data in one transactional database with familiar tooling. Not "Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.": OpenSearch Serverless is excellent for vectors but is a separate system with no transactional co-location with the relational data. Not "Amazon Neptune Analytics.": Neptune is a graph store, not a relational+vector database. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors.": S3 Vectors is a separate, non-transactional store and cannot co-locate with relational records. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Answering a question requires MULTI-HOP reasoning over relationships among connected entities, not just similarity to text. Which knowledge base option is BEST?

options.text: A vector-only knowledge base with more results returned.
A structured-data (text-to-SQL) knowledge base.
A knowledge base using GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: GraphRAG builds an entity-relationship graph that supports multi-hop reasoning over connections. Not "A vector-only knowledge base with more results returned.": Returning more similar chunks does not provide explicit multi-hop relationship traversal. Not "A structured-data (text-to-SQL) knowledge base.": Structured-data retrieval handles tabular aggregation, not entity-to-entity multi-hop reasoning. Not "Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": pgvector does similarity search, not graph multi-hop reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Business users ask natural-language questions that require SUMS and aggregations over an Amazon Redshift warehouse, and the assistant should generate and run the queries. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight Q.
A GraphRAG knowledge base on Neptune Analytics.
Embed each table row as a vector and use similarity search.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with structured data retrieval (text-to-SQL).

explanation: Structured-data retrieval translates natural language into SQL against the warehouse, returning accurate aggregations. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers over prepared BI datasets in a dashboard; it is not the Bedrock RAG generation path the assistant needs. Not "A GraphRAG knowledge base on Neptune Analytics.": GraphRAG reasons over relationships, not tabular aggregation. Not "Embed each table row as a vector and use similarity search.": Vector similarity over rows cannot compute sums or precise aggregations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A developer must fetch the top relevant chunks and then run them through their OWN prompt and a model NOT wired into the knowledge base. Which API is correct?

options.text: The RetrieveAndGenerate API.
The Retrieve API.
The RetrieveAndGenerateStream API.
The StartIngestionJob API.

explanation: Retrieve returns ranked chunks only, leaving the prompt and generation model fully under the developer's control. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerate API.": RetrieveAndGenerate performs the generation for you, removing the custom prompt/model control required here. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerateStream API.": This also performs generation (streamed), so it does not give custom prompt/model control. Not "The StartIngestionJob API.": StartIngestionJob ingests data; it does not retrieve chunks for a query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An app must show end users the exact source passages behind each answer with the LEAST custom development. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Ask the model in the prompt to list its sources.
Use Retrieve, then build custom generation and citation-mapping code.
Use RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns the answer with citations to the source chunks.
Enable model invocation logging and surface the logs.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate produces a grounded answer plus citations with no custom attribution code. Not "Ask the model in the prompt to list its sources.": Self-reported sources are unreliable and not verifiable citations. Not "Use Retrieve, then build custom generation and citation-m…": This works but adds the custom generation and citation code the requirement wants to avoid. Not "Enable model invocation logging and surface the logs.": Invocation logs are operator data, not user-facing citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS uses one shared knowledge base and must GUARANTEE that a tenant can never retrieve another tenant's documents. Which design is the most secure and reliable?

options.text: Pass the tenant filter from the client and trust it.
Rely on relevance ranking to keep tenants separate.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to stay within the tenant.
Tag documents with tenant ID and apply a metadata filter derived from the authenticated tenant on every Retrieve call (or use a separate knowledge base per tenant).

explanation: A server-side filter bound to the verified identity (or full per-tenant isolation) reliably prevents cross-tenant retrieval. Not "Pass the tenant filter from the client and trust it.": A client-supplied, untrusted filter can be tampered with to reach other tenants' data. Not "Rely on relevance ranking to keep tenants separate.": Ranking can still surface another tenant's documents; it is not an isolation control. Not "Instruct the model in the system prompt to stay within th…": Prompt instructions do not control retrieval and can be bypassed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Relevant passages ARE being retrieved but appear LOW in the result list, so answers miss them. The team wants to fix the ordering with the least overhead. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Increase the number of results returned.
Re-ingest with semantic chunking.
Switch to hybrid search.
Add a Bedrock reranker model to reorder the retrieved candidates by query relevance.

explanation: A reranker reorders already-retrieved candidates so the most relevant passages move to the top. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": Returning more results does not move the relevant ones to the top. Not "Re-ingest with semantic chunking.": Re-chunking is a heavier ingestion change and does not directly reorder results. Not "Switch to hybrid search.": Hybrid search improves whether relevant items are retrieved (recall); the problem here is ordering of items already retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Queries that contain exact product codes and acronyms are frequently MISSED by pure semantic search. Which change BEST fixes retrieval?

options.text: Enable hybrid search that combines semantic vectors with keyword matching.
Raise the generation temperature.
Add a reranker model.
Increase the embedding dimensions.

explanation: Hybrid search adds keyword matching so exact tokens like product codes are found alongside semantic matches. Not "Raise the generation temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval of exact terms. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker reorders retrieved items but cannot surface an exact-keyword match that the vector search failed to retrieve. Not "Increase the embedding dimensions.": Higher dimensions do not reliably solve exact-token matching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Content must be ingested into one knowledge base from Amazon S3, Confluence, and SharePoint with the LEAST custom code. What should the team do?

options.text: Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.
Use the built-in Bedrock knowledge base data source connectors for each source.
Write custom crawlers that copy everything to S3 first.
Manually export each source to S3 on a schedule.

explanation: Managed connectors for S3, Confluence, SharePoint, and others ingest the content without custom code. Not "Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.": Fine-tuning is not ingestion and does not keep content current. Not "Write custom crawlers that copy everything to S3 first.": Custom crawlers add development and maintenance the connectors remove. Not "Manually export each source to S3 on a schedule.": Manual exports are brittle and lag behind source changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A RetrieveAndGenerate chat must keep context across follow-up questions with the LEAST custom state management. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window.
Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt each turn.
Pass a session identifier to RetrieveAndGenerate so Bedrock maintains the conversation context.
Re-embed the chat history into the vector store each turn.

explanation: The session ID preserves multi-turn context without the developer building custom conversation state. Not "Use a model with a larger context window.": A larger window does not automatically carry prior turns into each call. Not "Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt ea…": Manual state assembly is more work than the built-in session support. Not "Re-embed the chat history into the vector store each turn.": Re-embedding history is costly and is not how session context is maintained. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Complex, multi-part questions retrieve passages for only ONE part, yielding incomplete answers. Which built-in capability BEST addresses this?

options.text: Enable query decomposition (reformulation) so the knowledge base splits the question into sub-queries.
Increase the number of results returned.
Add a reranker model.
Switch to a larger generation model.

explanation: Decomposition retrieves passages for each sub-question, improving coverage and completeness. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": More results add noise but do not ensure each sub-question is covered. Not "Add a reranker model.": Reranking reorders retrieved items but cannot fetch passages for an unaddressed sub-question. Not "Switch to a larger generation model.": A larger model cannot use passages that were never retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: New and deleted documents in Amazon S3 must be reflected in a Bedrock knowledge base quickly, WITHOUT re-scanning the entire source each time, in a scalable and resilient way. Which design is BEST?

options.text: Run an EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to diff the bucket.
Send S3 object-created/deleted events to an SQS queue, and have a Lambda call the incremental IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments APIs.
On every change, call StartIngestionJob to sync the whole data source.
Invoke a Lambda directly from S3 events with no queue.

explanation: Event-driven SQS buffering with the incremental document APIs updates only changed items and adds retries/resilience. Not "Run an EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to diff the …": Polling on a timer is not near-real-time and is less efficient than event-driven updates. Not "On every change, call StartIngestionJob to sync the whole…": StartIngestionJob re-scans the source, which is inefficient and not incremental. Not "Invoke a Lambda directly from S3 events with no queue.": Direct invocation lacks buffering and retries and can fail under load. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team wants grounded answers WITH citations over their documents, with the least operational overhead and no retrieval pipeline to build. Which option is BEST?

options.text: A custom pipeline with Lambda and a self-managed vector database.
Amazon Kendra by itself.
Fine-tune a model on the documents.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (managed RAG).

explanation: Knowledge Bases manage chunking, embeddings, the vector store, retrieval, and citations as a service. Not "A custom pipeline with Lambda and a self-managed vector d…": A hand-built pipeline maximizes operational overhead. Not "Amazon Kendra by itself.": Kendra is enterprise search; on its own it does not provide the managed FM generation-with-citations RAG flow. Not "Fine-tune a model on the documents.": Fine-tuning is not RAG and does not provide citations or freshness. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A RAG assistant returns confident answers that the retrieved passages do not actually support. The team wants a MANAGED, tunable way to block ungrounded responses. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Switch to a larger model.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check with a tuned threshold.
Lower the temperature.
Add a reranker model.

explanation: The contextual grounding check scores whether a response is supported by the source and can block low-scoring answers. Not "Switch to a larger model.": A larger model can still produce ungrounded answers without a grounding control. Not "Lower the temperature.": Lower randomness does not guarantee grounding in the retrieved context. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker improves ordering of retrieved passages but does not verify or block ungrounded generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Retrieval must MATCH on small, precise text units but then give the language model the BROADER surrounding context for those matches. Which chunking strategy is BEST?

options.text: Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.
Large fixed-size chunking.
Semantic chunking.
No chunking.

explanation: Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks for precision and supplies the larger parent chunk as context for generation. Not "Large fixed-size chunking.": Large fixed chunks sacrifice precise matching on small units. Not "Semantic chunking.": Semantic chunking yields coherent chunks but does not provide the parent-context-on-child-match behavior required here. Not "No chunking.": Treating each document as one chunk loses the precise small-unit matching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Long documents mix several topics. Each chunk must hold ONE coherent topic for precise matching; there is no need to also pass a larger parent context. Which strategy is BEST?

options.text: Only increasing chunk overlap.
Semantic chunking.
Fixed-size chunking.
Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.

explanation: Semantic chunking splits on meaning so each chunk is one coherent topic, which fixes topic bleed without an extra parent layer. Not "Only increasing chunk overlap.": Overlap helps boundary continuity but does not make each chunk a single coherent topic. Not "Fixed-size chunking.": Fixed sizes cut across topic boundaries, the root problem. Not "Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.": Hierarchical adds a parent-context layer that is unnecessary here and does not specifically fix topic boundaries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Answers are frequently cut off because relevant sentences fall right at the boundary between two chunks. Which adjustment most directly fixes this?

options.text: Reduce the chunk size.
Increase the number of results returned.
Switch to hierarchical chunking.
Add chunk overlap so adjacent chunks share boundary text.

explanation: Overlap repeats boundary text so information spanning a boundary is captured in at least one chunk. Not "Reduce the chunk size.": Smaller chunks create MORE boundaries and can make boundary loss worse. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": Returning more chunks does not fix content split across a boundary. Not "Switch to hierarchical chunking.": Hierarchical chunking is heavier than needed and does not specifically target boundary cut-offs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: After upgrading to a newer embedding model, retrieval quality collapsed even though documents are present. What must the team do?

options.text: Clear the application cache.
Lower the generation temperature.
Re-embed only the queries with the new model.
Re-embed (re-index) the entire corpus with the new model so document and query vectors share the same space.

explanation: Query and document embeddings must come from the same model; switching models requires re-embedding the whole corpus. Not "Clear the application cache.": Caching is unrelated to embedding-space mismatch. Not "Lower the generation temperature.": Temperature does not affect embedding compatibility. Not "Re-embed only the queries with the new model.": Mismatched query and document spaces still produce poor retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A growing vector index is too expensive. The team wants to cut storage and query cost while keeping acceptable recall. Which change helps MOST?

options.text: Switch to a multimodal embedding model.
Use an embedding model with smaller output dimensions (for example, Titan Text Embeddings V2) and pick a smaller dimension.
Store each chunk twice for redundancy.
Use the maximum embedding dimension available.

explanation: Smaller-dimension embeddings shrink the index and query cost while keeping acceptable recall. Not "Switch to a multimodal embedding model.": Multimodal embeddings are for image+text retrieval and do not reduce text storage cost. Not "Store each chunk twice for redundancy.": Duplication increases cost without improving accuracy. Not "Use the maximum embedding dimension available.": Maximum dimensions increase storage and cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Evaluation shows the correct passage EXISTS in the store but is sometimes NOT returned, so the model lacks the facts to answer. Which change should the team try FIRST?

options.text: Reduce the chunk overlap.
Add a reranker model.
Increase the number of results (top-k) returned per query.
Lower the temperature.

explanation: Returning more candidates raises recall so the correct passage is more likely included. Not "Reduce the chunk overlap.": Less overlap does not improve whether the missing passage is retrieved. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker reorders retrieved results but cannot rank a passage that was never retrieved. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval recall. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Chunks were configured very large, so retrieval returns passages where the relevant sentence is buried among unrelated text and match quality is weak. Which change is BEST?

options.text: Increase the embedding dimensions.
Add more chunk overlap.
Reduce the chunk size to more focused units of meaning.
Increase the chunk size further.

explanation: Smaller, focused chunks produce embeddings that better represent specific content, improving match precision. Not "Increase the embedding dimensions.": Dimension size does not fix oversized, diluted chunks. Not "Add more chunk overlap.": Overlap addresses boundaries, not the dilution caused by oversized chunks. Not "Increase the chunk size further.": Larger chunks dilute the embedding more and worsen precision. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A knowledge base ingests many short, self-contained FAQ entries, where each file is already one complete question-and-answer. Which chunking choice is BEST?

options.text: Apply small fixed-size chunking to every file.
Use hierarchical chunking.
Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.
Use a no-chunking strategy so each short file is one chunk.

explanation: When each file is already atomic, no chunking preserves the complete meaning per entry. Not "Apply small fixed-size chunking to every file.": Splitting atomic FAQ entries fragments coherent answers. Not "Use hierarchical chunking.": Hierarchical structure is unnecessary for already-atomic entries. Not "Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.": Merging unrelated entries dilutes each entry's embedding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A catalog must be searchable by EITHER a text query or an image query against the same items. Which embedding approach supports this?

options.text: Use a multimodal embedding model (such as Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings) so images and text share one vector space.
Index Amazon Rekognition labels only.
Use a text-only embedding model for everything.
Embed base64 image strings as text.

explanation: Multimodal embeddings place images and text in a shared space, enabling cross-modal similarity search. Not "Index Amazon Rekognition labels only.": Label detection is not a shared semantic embedding space for text-and-image retrieval. Not "Use a text-only embedding model for everything.": A text-only model cannot embed images for similarity search. Not "Embed base64 image strings as text.": Embedding base64 as text does not capture visual semantics. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants to raise the overall quality of what their RAG system retrieves and answers. Which TWO techniques are most effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choose a chunking strategy (semantic or hierarchical) aligned to the documents' structure.
Raise the generation temperature for variety.
Add a reranking step to reorder retrieved candidates by relevance.
Increase maxTokens on the response.
Always return only the single top result.

explanation: Structure-aligned chunking produces more coherent, relevant chunks and better retrieval. A reranker moves the most relevant passages to the top for generation. Not "Raise the generation temperature for variety.": Higher temperature increases randomness and does not improve retrieval quality. Not "Increase maxTokens on the response.": Output length does not change which passages are retrieved. Not "Always return only the single top result.": Returning just one result can drop relevant passages and reduce answer quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team must A/B test two wordings of a production prompt and revert instantly if one underperforms, WITHOUT redeploying application code. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Hard-code both prompts behind an application feature flag.
Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt.
Adjust the temperature to switch behavior.
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with versioned prompts and variants.

explanation: Managed prompt versions/variants allow comparison and instant switch/rollback with no code deploy. Not "Hard-code both prompts behind an application feature flag.": A feature flag still requires a code deploy to ship the prompts and lacks managed versioning/evaluation. Not "Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt.": This is custom, requires code deploys, and has no managed prompt versioning. Not "Adjust the temperature to switch behavior.": Temperature does not select between prompt wordings. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer must cap response length to control cost and avoid overly long chat outputs. Which inference setting is correct?

options.text: Increase top-k.
Set the maxTokens (maximum output tokens) parameter.
Raise the temperature.
Add unrelated stop sequences.

explanation: maxTokens directly bounds output length and cost. Not "Increase top-k.": Top-k changes token diversity, not length. Not "Raise the temperature.": Temperature changes randomness, not maximum length. Not "Add unrelated stop sequences.": Unrelated stop sequences do not reliably cap general length. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Durable behavior rules (role, tone, safety constraints) must govern EVERY turn of a conversation, separate from each user question. Where should they go?

options.text: Appended by the user to each message.
In the system prompt.
In the stop sequences list.
In the temperature setting.

explanation: The system prompt sets persistent instructions that apply across the conversation, separate from per-turn user messages. Not "Appended by the user to each message.": Relying on users to repeat rules is inconsistent and unreliable. Not "In the stop sequences list.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not encode behavior rules. Not "In the temperature setting.": Temperature is a sampling parameter, not a place for rules. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Outputs must follow a precise structured format, instructions alone have not worked, and the team needs a fix QUICKLY without a training step. Which technique is BEST?

options.text: Increase the temperature.
Fine-tune the model on formatting examples.
Shorten the prompt to one sentence.
Add a few worked examples (few-shot exemplars) of the exact format to the prompt.

explanation: Few-shot examples show the model the precise structure to imitate and require no training. Not "Increase the temperature.": Higher temperature increases variability and undermines format consistency. Not "Fine-tune the model on formatting examples.": Fine-tuning is heavier and slower than needed when few-shot prompting can fix formatting quickly. Not "Shorten the prompt to one sentence.": Over-shortening removes the structure cues the model needs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Several applications reuse the same prompt with only a few values changing per request, and the team wants central management with runtime value injection. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Copy the prompt into each application and edit by hand.
Concatenate strings ad hoc in each service.
Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management templates with input variables.

explanation: Parameterized managed templates are reused centrally and take values at invocation time. Not "Copy the prompt into each application and edit by hand.": Duplicated prompts drift and are hard to govern centrally. Not "Concatenate strings ad hoc in each service.": Ad hoc concatenation has no central governance or versioning. Not "Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.": Temperature does not parameterize or manage prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer needs a MANAGED, low-code way to build and version a multi-step generative workflow with branching (classify, then retrieve, then generate). Which Amazon Bedrock feature is BEST?

options.text: Hand-built AWS Step Functions wiring each step.
Amazon Bedrock Agents.
A single InvokeModel call.
Amazon Bedrock Flows (prompt flows).

explanation: Bedrock Flows visually build and version multi-step, branching workflows chaining prompts, knowledge bases, and other components with little code. Not "Hand-built AWS Step Functions wiring each step.": Step Functions can orchestrate but require more custom build than a managed flow builder. Not "Amazon Bedrock Agents.": Agents provide autonomous tool-using reasoning, which is heavier and different from a defined, branching prompt-chain workflow. Not "A single InvokeModel call.": One call cannot orchestrate a multi-step, branching workflow. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A regression suite needs the same prompt to produce as close to identical output as possible on each run. Which SINGLE parameter change most increases determinism?

options.text: Set a very high top-k.
Increase maxTokens.
Set the temperature to 0.
Raise the temperature to 1.

explanation: A temperature of 0 makes decoding effectively greedy, maximizing run-to-run consistency. Not "Set a very high top-k.": A high top-k widens sampling and increases variability. Not "Increase maxTokens.": Output length does not control determinism. Not "Raise the temperature to 1.": A high temperature maximizes randomness. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the team wants to reduce fabricated answers by making the model rely only on the supplied context and admit when the answer is absent. Which prompt technique helps MOST?

options.text: Instruct the model to always produce an answer.
Raise the temperature for more creative answers.
Remove the retrieved context to shorten prompts.
Instruct the model to answer only from the provided context and to say it does not know when the context lacks the answer.

explanation: Explicit grounding plus an allowed abstention reduces fabrication when the context does not contain the answer. Not "Instruct the model to always produce an answer.": Forcing an answer encourages fabrication when information is missing. Not "Raise the temperature for more creative answers.": More creativity increases fabrication. Not "Remove the retrieved context to shorten prompts.": Without context the model must guess, increasing hallucination. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer must prevent unbounded, runaway generations that drive up cost and ramble past the answer. Which TWO controls directly help? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set a sensible maxTokens limit.
Enlarge the context window.
Define stop sequences that end generation at a known marker.
Increase the temperature.
Increase top-k substantially.

explanation: maxTokens caps how many tokens can be generated, bounding cost and runaway length. Stop sequences halt generation at a defined boundary so the model does not ramble on. Not "Enlarge the context window.": The context window governs input size, not output length. Not "Increase the temperature.": Higher temperature does not limit length and can make output more verbose. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": Top-k affects diversity, not length. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A model's outputs occasionally include bizarre, very low-probability words. The team wants to remove that long tail of unlikely tokens while keeping SOME variety. Which single adjustment is BEST?

options.text: Lower top-p (nucleus sampling) so only the most probable tokens are eligible.
Increase top-k substantially.
Add stop sequences.
Set temperature to 0.

explanation: A lower top-p trims the low-probability tail while still allowing variety among the top tokens, directly removing bizarre word choices. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": A larger top-k widens the candidate pool, making rare tokens more likely, not less. Not "Add stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not filter the token probability distribution. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Temperature 0 removes the tail but also eliminates the variety the team wants to keep. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: An Amazon Bedrock agent must call an internal order-management API to look up and update orders. What is the standard way to give it that capability?

options.text: Put the API documentation in the agent's instructions.
Associate a knowledge base with the agent.
Define an action group backed by a Lambda function, described with an API or function schema.
Raise the agent model's temperature.

explanation: Action groups declare callable operations via a schema and execute them through a Lambda when the agent decides to act. Not "Put the API documentation in the agent's instructions.": Instructions describe behavior but provide no executable tool to call the API. Not "Associate a knowledge base with the agent.": A knowledge base grounds answers in documents; it does not execute API actions. Not "Raise the agent model's temperature.": Temperature has nothing to do with tool or API access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: For compliance, the company's OWN application must execute tool calls, while the agent still decides which action to take. Which capability supports this?

options.text: Configure the action group to return control to the caller, which executes the action and returns the result.
Use an action group with a Lambda the agent invokes directly.
Disable the agent's reasoning.
Associate a knowledge base.

explanation: Return of control hands the chosen action and parameters back to the calling application to execute, rather than the agent invoking a Lambda. Not "Use an action group with a Lambda the agent invokes direc…": With a Lambda action group the agent executes the action, which is exactly what the compliance rule forbids. Not "Disable the agent's reasoning.": That would remove the agent's ability to decide which action to take. Not "Associate a knowledge base.": A knowledge base is for retrieval, not for delegating execution to the caller. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent must ground its answers in company policy documents, with the least custom code. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add an action group to fetch documents from S3.
Fine-tune the agent's model weekly on the policies.
Paste the entire policy library into the agent instructions.
Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent.

explanation: Associating a knowledge base lets the agent retrieve and ground responses without custom retrieval code. Not "Add an action group to fetch documents from S3.": Action groups execute operations; grounding from a corpus is what a knowledge base provides. Not "Fine-tune the agent's model weekly on the policies.": Repeated fine-tuning is heavy and unnecessary versus a knowledge base. Not "Paste the entire policy library into the agent instructions.": Instructions cannot scale to a full library or stay current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Each user's agent must remember preferences and prior context ACROSS separate sessions, as a managed AgentCore capability. Which component is correct?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway.
A custom DynamoDB table you build and maintain.
AgentCore Memory.
Per-invocation session state only.

explanation: AgentCore Memory provides managed short-term and long-term memory that persists across sessions. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes APIs as tools; it is not a memory store. Not "A custom DynamoDB table you build and maintain.": That works but is not the managed AgentCore capability the scenario asks for. Not "Per-invocation session state only.": Session state lasts within a single session; it does not persist across sessions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A company wants to expose its MANY existing internal REST APIs and Lambda functions to agents as secure, governed tools without writing per-API integration code. Which AgentCore capability fits?

options.text: AgentCore Identity.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Gateway.
Defining a separate action group for each API in every agent.

explanation: Gateway turns existing APIs/Lambdas into agent-ready tools (for example via MCP) with built-in authentication and governance. Not "AgentCore Identity.": Identity manages access/credentials, not exposure of APIs as tools. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter executes code; it is not an API-to-tool exposure layer. Not "Defining a separate action group for each API in every ag…": Per-agent action groups require wiring each API repeatedly; Gateway centralizes existing APIs as managed tools. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An analytics agent must safely execute Python to perform calculations and data transformations, isolated from other workloads, as a managed capability. Which AgentCore component is correct?

options.text: AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
A self-built Lambda action group for code execution.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: Code Interpreter gives the agent a managed, isolated sandbox to run code. Not "AgentCore Browser.": Browser automates web pages, not arbitrary code execution. Not "A self-built Lambda action group for code execution.": You would have to build and secure the sandbox yourself; Code Interpreter is the managed option. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes external tools; it is not a code-execution sandbox. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent must NAVIGATE websites and interact with web pages to complete tasks, in a managed, secure environment. Which AgentCore capability fits?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway.
AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.

explanation: The Browser tool provides a managed, secure cloud browser the agent uses to navigate and interact with pages. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes APIs as tools; it does not provide interactive web browsing. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context, not web interaction. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter runs code; it is not a browser. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Agents must securely access third-party SaaS services ON BEHALF OF users, handling tokens and consent, without a custom credential broker. Which AgentCore capability addresses this?

options.text: Amazon Cognito user pools alone.
AgentCore Identity.
AWS Secrets Manager.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: AgentCore Identity manages secure identity and access for agents, including authenticating to and accessing third-party services on a user's behalf. Not "Amazon Cognito user pools alone.": Cognito authenticates end users to your app; it is not the agent's outbound identity to third-party services. Not "AWS Secrets Manager.": Secrets Manager stores secrets but is not the agent identity/consent broker for acting on a user's behalf. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes tools; it is not the identity/consent layer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A research agent has long-running, multi-minute sessions and must be deployed serverlessly with per-session isolation, regardless of the framework it was built in. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.
A self-managed Amazon ECS on Fargate service.
A SageMaker real-time endpoint.
AWS Lambda.

explanation: AgentCore Runtime hosts agents from any framework serverlessly with session isolation and support for long-running, streaming workloads. Not "A self-managed Amazon ECS on Fargate service.": ECS works but requires building and operating the serving infrastructure. Not "A SageMaker real-time endpoint.": SageMaker endpoints serve models, not framework-agnostic agent runtimes. Not "AWS Lambda.": Lambda's execution time limit and lack of per-session agent isolation make it unsuitable for long, stateful agent sessions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An operations team must trace WHY an agent chose a tool and inspect each reasoning step, tool call, and latency in production. Which AgentCore capability provides this?

options.text: AgentCore Memory.
AWS CloudTrail.
AgentCore Observability.
Bedrock model invocation logging.

explanation: Observability captures detailed traces of the agent's reasoning steps and tool invocations for debugging and monitoring. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context; it is not a tracing tool. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not the agent's internal reasoning steps and tool decisions. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model prompts/responses, not the agent's step-by-step tool orchestration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A workflow needs ONE coordinating agent to dynamically delegate subtasks to several specialized agents (billing, shipping, returns) and combine results. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Run independent agents with no coordination.
Put every capability in one agent's prompt.
Use multi-agent collaboration with a supervisor agent coordinating specialized sub-agents.
Build the workflow in Amazon Bedrock Flows.

explanation: Multi-agent collaboration lets a supervisor route subtasks to specialized agents and aggregate their outputs dynamically. Not "Run independent agents with no coordination.": Without a supervisor there is no way to combine sub-agent results. Not "Put every capability in one agent's prompt.": A single monolithic agent provides no structured delegation or specialization. Not "Build the workflow in Amazon Bedrock Flows.": Flows is a fixed, low-code orchestration of steps; it is not dynamic agent-to-agent delegation and reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent can issue refunds, and a human must approve before any refund executes. Which Bedrock agent feature enforces this directly?

options.text: Use return of control for the action.
Enable user confirmation (require confirmation) on the sensitive action.
Set temperature to 0.
Add a note in the system prompt to confirm first.

explanation: User confirmation pauses the agent for explicit human approval before the action runs. Not "Use return of control for the action.": Return of control changes WHERE execution happens (the caller), but it is not itself a built-in human-approval gate. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Temperature does not create an approval step. Not "Add a note in the system prompt to confirm first.": Prompt instructions do not enforce a hard approval gate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A developer wants an OPEN-SOURCE, code-first, model-driven framework to build tool-using agents in a few lines of Python and then deploy them to AgentCore Runtime. Which option fits?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents configured in the console.
AWS Glue.
The Strands Agents SDK.
Amazon Q Developer.

explanation: Strands Agents is AWS's open-source, model-driven SDK for building agents in code and deploying them to AgentCore Runtime. Not "Amazon Bedrock Agents configured in the console.": Bedrock Agents is a managed, configuration-driven service, not the open-source code-first SDK described. Not "AWS Glue.": Glue is an ETL service, unrelated to building agents. Not "Amazon Q Developer.": Q Developer is a coding assistant, not an agent-building runtime SDK. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent's responses must be filtered for harmful content and PII regardless of which tools or knowledge bases it uses. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Lower the agent's temperature.
Write the safety rules into the agent's instructions.
Filter content inside each action group Lambda.
Attach an Amazon Bedrock Guardrail to the agent.

explanation: A guardrail attached to the agent applies content filtering and PII handling consistently across the agent's interactions. Not "Lower the agent's temperature.": Temperature does not filter harmful content or PII. Not "Write the safety rules into the agent's instructions.": Instructions are not a reliable, enforced safety control and can be bypassed. Not "Filter content inside each action group Lambda.": Per-tool custom filtering is inconsistent and misses responses that do not go through that Lambda. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An application needs synchronous, low-latency predictions for SMALL payloads with steady, predictable traffic. Which SageMaker AI option is BEST?

options.text: A real-time inference endpoint.
Batch transform.
Serverless Inference.
Asynchronous Inference.

explanation: Real-time endpoints give persistent, low-latency synchronous inference, ideal for steady small-payload traffic. Not "Batch transform.": Batch transform is offline; it cannot serve synchronous requests. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless can cold-start and does not support GPUs, adding latency variability not wanted for steady low-latency traffic. Not "Asynchronous Inference.": Async adds queueing latency meant for long-running or large requests, not small fast ones. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A CPU model serves intermittent traffic with long idle gaps, can tolerate occasional cold starts, and must not incur idle cost. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: An always-on real-time endpoint.
Asynchronous Inference sized for peak.
SageMaker Serverless Inference.
Provisioned, always-on GPU instance.

explanation: Serverless scales (including to zero) for intermittent CPU workloads, billing only while serving. Not "An always-on real-time endpoint.": An always-on endpoint pays for the long idle periods. Not "Asynchronous Inference sized for peak.": Provisioning for peak wastes capacity for intermittent traffic. Not "Provisioned, always-on GPU instance.": A continuously running GPU is the most expensive and unnecessary for a CPU workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Requests carry payloads up to ~1 GB and take several minutes on a GPU; responses can be delivered asynchronously. Which SageMaker option is BEST?

options.text: Asynchronous Inference.
Serverless Inference.
Batch transform.
Real-time Inference.

explanation: Async supports large payloads (up to ~1 GB), long processing, and GPU instances with queued, asynchronous responses. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless does not support GPUs and has small payload limits. Not "Batch transform.": Batch transform is for bulk offline scoring, not on-demand per-request handling. Not "Real-time Inference.": Real-time endpoints cap payloads near 25 MB and target short synchronous calls, so large/long requests fail. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A team deploys several large language models to GPU instances and wants to pack multiple models/copies onto shared accelerators, scale each independently, and scale unused ones to ZERO. Which capability fits?

options.text: SageMaker inference components.
Serverless Inference.
One real-time endpoint per model.
A multi-model endpoint (MME).

explanation: Inference components place multiple models/copies on shared instances, allocate resources per component, scale independently, and can scale to zero. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless does not support the GPUs these LLMs need. Not "One real-time endpoint per model.": Separate endpoints cannot pack models onto shared accelerators with independent scaling. Not "A multi-model endpoint (MME).": MME loads many (typically smaller) models on demand behind one endpoint but is not designed for GPU-packing LLMs with independent per-model scaling and scale-to-zero. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A company must host HUNDREDS of small, similar models (one per customer) behind as few endpoints as possible, loading each on demand to save cost. Which option is BEST?

options.text: A multi-model endpoint (MME).
SageMaker inference components.
One dedicated endpoint per model.
Batch transform per model.

explanation: MME hosts many models behind one endpoint, loading them on demand and sharing resources to cut cost. Not "SageMaker inference components.": Inference components target packing and independently scaling (often larger) models, not the classic many-small-models-on-demand pattern. Not "One dedicated endpoint per model.": Hundreds of endpoints multiply cost and management. Not "Batch transform per model.": Batch transform is offline scoring, not on-demand hosting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Real-time endpoint traffic swings widely between day and night, and the team wants instances added and removed automatically based on load. What should they configure?

options.text: Switch to batch transform during the day.
A fixed instance count sized for peak.
Use a larger instance type only.
Automatic scaling (for example, target tracking on invocations per instance).

explanation: Endpoint auto scaling adjusts instance count against a target metric, matching capacity to demand. Not "Switch to batch transform during the day.": Batch transform is offline and cannot serve real-time daytime traffic. Not "A fixed instance count sized for peak.": A fixed peak size wastes money at night and cannot adapt automatically. Not "Use a larger instance type only.": A bigger instance does not automatically scale with demand. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Before promoting a new model version, the team wants to send a COPY of live production traffic to it and compare results WITHOUT affecting any users. Which capability is correct?

options.text: A blue/green switch all at once.
Shadow testing (shadow variants).
Batch transform on yesterday's data.
A canary deployment with deployment guardrails.

explanation: Shadow testing mirrors live traffic to a shadow variant so you validate against real requests with no impact on user-facing responses. Not "A blue/green switch all at once.": An all-at-once cutover exposes all users immediately and is not a no-impact comparison. Not "Batch transform on yesterday's data.": Offline scoring does not exercise the new version against live traffic. Not "A canary deployment with deployment guardrails.": Canary routes a slice of REAL user traffic to the new version, so some users are affected, unlike shadow testing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: When updating a production endpoint, the team wants to shift a small percentage of REAL traffic first and automatically roll back if errors spike. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Shadow testing.
Deployment guardrails with a canary (or linear) traffic-shifting strategy and automatic rollback.
Recreate the endpoint in place.
Increase the instance count during the switch.

explanation: Deployment guardrails gradually shift live traffic, watch alarms, and roll back automatically if the new version misbehaves. Not "Shadow testing.": Shadow testing mirrors traffic without serving users, so it does not perform a controlled production rollout. Not "Recreate the endpoint in place.": An in-place replace has no gradual shift or automatic rollback and risks downtime. Not "Increase the instance count during the switch.": More instances does not provide controlled traffic shifting or rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A developer wants to deploy a popular open foundation model fast, with a tested container and example notebooks. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Deploy the model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.
Build a custom serving container from scratch.
Use AWS Glue to host the model.

explanation: JumpStart provides prebuilt, deployable models with curated containers and notebooks for fast deployment. Not "Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.": Batch transform does not create an online endpoint. Not "Build a custom serving container from scratch.": Building everything yourself is the slowest path. Not "Use AWS Glue to host the model.": Glue is an ETL service and cannot host a model endpoint. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A fixed dataset already in Amazon S3 must be scored in a SINGLE offline run with no persistent endpoint, at the lowest cost. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Asynchronous Inference per record.
A batch transform job.
Serverless Inference.
A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.

explanation: Batch transform scores a whole S3 dataset in one offline run and releases compute afterward, with no endpoint to pay for. Not "Asynchronous Inference per record.": Per-record async adds overhead versus a single batch over the dataset. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless targets intermittent online requests, not bulk offline scoring. Not "A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.": Looping over a persistent endpoint is more expensive and complex than one batch job. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Profiling a model served with DJL on an 8-GPU instance shows the model fits entirely within 4 GPUs and per-instance concurrency is low. Which change BEST improves GPU utilization?

options.text: Enable speculative decoding.
Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8.
Add more instances and spread requests.
Use a tensor parallelism degree of 4 so two model replicas run on each 8-GPU instance.

explanation: Since the model fits in 4 GPUs, a tensor-parallel degree of 4 places two replicas per instance, using all 8 GPUs. Not "Enable speculative decoding.": Speculative decoding reduces latency, not GPU utilization. Not "Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8.": Degree 8 serves a single replica across all GPUs, leaving half the capacity idle since the model fits in 4. Not "Add more instances and spread requests.": More instances does not raise per-instance utilization or concurrency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html
