prompt: Logs show the real maximum sequence length is about 10x smaller than the configured value and concurrency per GPU is low on a DJL-served model. Which change BEST increases throughput per GPU?

options.text: Increase the maximum sequence length.
Enable speculative decoding.
Lower the rolling batch size.
Reduce the configured maximum sequence length to allow a larger rolling batch size.

explanation: Lowering the max sequence length frees memory so more requests fit in each rolling batch, increasing throughput and concurrency. Not "Increase the maximum sequence length.": A larger max sequence length reserves more memory per request and reduces batch size. Not "Enable speculative decoding.": Speculative decoding targets latency, not batch-size-driven throughput. Not "Lower the rolling batch size.": A smaller batch reduces throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: An enterprise must upgrade many applications from an old Java version to a current LTS release, automating the repetitive code changes at scale. Which Amazon Q Developer capability is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer code transformation.
Amazon Macie.
Manually editing each project.
Amazon Q Developer inline code suggestions.

explanation: Code transformation automates large-scale upgrades such as moving codebases to a newer Java version. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data and is unrelated to code upgrades. Not "Manually editing each project.": Manual edits across many applications are slow and error-prone, which automation avoids. Not "Amazon Q Developer inline code suggestions.": Inline suggestions speed typing in the editor but do not perform an automated, repository-wide upgrade. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team wants an assistant that takes a natural-language feature request, plans it, and implements the change across MULTIPLE files. Which Amazon Q Developer capability fits?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend.
Single-line inline completion.
Amazon QuickSight Q.
The Amazon Q Developer feature-development agent (/dev).

explanation: The /dev agent analyzes the codebase, proposes a plan, and applies coordinated multi-file changes. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is an NLP service, not a coding agent. Not "Single-line inline completion.": Inline completion helps at the cursor but cannot plan and implement a multi-file feature. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers questions over BI data, not multi-file code changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: Developers want their assistant to scan SOURCE CODE for vulnerabilities and suggest fixes inside the IDE. Which option is correct?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon GuardDuty.
Amazon Inspector.
Amazon Q Developer security scanning.

explanation: Q Developer scans code for vulnerabilities and suggests remediations in the developer workflow. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data, not code vulnerabilities. Not "Amazon GuardDuty.": GuardDuty detects account/workload threats, not source-code vulnerabilities. Not "Amazon Inspector.": Inspector assesses workloads and software for vulnerabilities operationally, not in-IDE source-code scanning for developers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: To raise coverage quickly, a team wants to automatically GENERATE unit tests for existing functions. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Single-line inline completion only.
AWS CodeBuild.
Amazon Q Developer unit test generation.
Amazon QuickSight.

explanation: Q Developer generates unit tests for existing code with minimal manual effort. Not "Single-line inline completion only.": Inline completion does not systematically generate a test suite for existing functions. Not "AWS CodeBuild.": CodeBuild runs builds/tests but does not author tests. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is for dashboards, not test generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team wants automated test generation and quality checks to run CONTINUOUSLY as code is merged, not ad hoc. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Integrate Amazon Q Developer automated test generation into the CI/CD pipeline.
Run Amazon Q Developer only manually in the IDE when remembered.
Hold periodic manual review cycles instead.
Add Amazon Inspector to the pipeline for unit tests.

explanation: Embedding Q Developer test generation in CI/CD continuously validates changes and catches defects early. Not "Run Amazon Q Developer only manually in the IDE when reme…": Ad hoc IDE use is not continuous and misses merges. Not "Hold periodic manual review cycles instead.": Manual cycles are slow and not continuous. Not "Add Amazon Inspector to the pipeline for unit tests.": Inspector finds vulnerabilities; it does not generate unit tests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team must retain the FULL prompt and response content of every Bedrock model call for troubleshooting and audit, with the least custom code. Which capability is correct?

options.text: AWS X-Ray.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.
Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: Invocation logging records full prompts, responses, and metadata to S3 and/or CloudWatch with no custom instrumentation. Not "AWS X-Ray.": X-Ray traces request flow and timing, not full model content. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API metadata, not the full prompt/response content. Not "Amazon CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics are numeric aggregates, not request/response content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: An auditor needs to know WHICH IAM principal called WHICH Bedrock API and WHEN, across the account. Which service provides this?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch dashboards.
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS CloudTrail.
AWS Config.

explanation: CloudTrail records API calls with principal, action, time, and source, the audit trail of who did what. Not "Amazon CloudWatch dashboards.": Dashboards visualize metrics, not per-call caller identity. Not "Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model prompt/response content, not a full account-wide API caller audit trail. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not API caller activity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A team must identify and troubleshoot per-DOCUMENT failures during knowledge base ingestion (ingested, ignored, or failed). Which solution is correct?

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging.
Enable CloudWatch Application Signals.
Use AWS CloudTrail.
Configure knowledge base logging to CloudWatch Logs and query with Logs Insights.

explanation: Knowledge base logging records per-file ingestion status, which Logs Insights can query for failures. Not "Enable Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model calls, not the document ingestion process. Not "Enable CloudWatch Application Signals.": Application Signals monitors application performance, not knowledge base ingestion. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not document-level ingestion status. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A request flows through API Gateway, several Lambdas, a knowledge base, and Bedrock, and the team must find WHICH component causes high end-to-end latency. Which service is BEST?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch alarms on total latency.
Amazon Macie.
Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS X-Ray.

explanation: X-Ray traces requests across components and shows segment timings that pinpoint the bottleneck. Not "Amazon CloudWatch alarms on total latency.": Alarms detect that latency is high but do not localize which component is responsible. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies data and has no tracing capability. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model content, not cross-service timing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: Invocation logs are stored in CloudWatch Logs, and an engineer must interactively query them to find and aggregate error patterns. Which tool is BEST?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake.
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Amazon Athena with no setup.
Amazon QuickSight Q.

explanation: Logs Insights provides an interactive query language to search and aggregate the CloudWatch log data. Not "AWS CloudTrail Lake.": CloudTrail Lake queries CloudTrail API events, not arbitrary invocation logs already in CloudWatch Logs. Not "Amazon Athena with no setup.": Athena would require exporting and cataloging the data first; Logs Insights queries the logs directly. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers over prepared BI datasets, not ad hoc CloudWatch log querying. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A model on a SageMaker real-time endpoint must be continuously monitored for DATA DRIFT against a baseline, with automated alerts. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
CloudWatch alarms on CPU only.
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify run once at training time.

explanation: Model Monitor continuously checks a deployed endpoint for data quality and drift against a baseline and can alert. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails filter content; they do not monitor endpoint data drift. Not "CloudWatch alarms on CPU only.": Infrastructure metrics do not detect data drift. Not "Amazon SageMaker Clarify run once at training time.": A one-time Clarify analysis measures bias/explainability but is not continuous endpoint drift monitoring. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A finance team must ATTRIBUTE Bedrock usage and cost to specific applications and teams that SHARE the same models. Which approach is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Use AWS Cost Explorer without any tagging.
Use AWS CloudTrail.
Use Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles with cost allocation tags.
Use model invocation logging.

explanation: Application inference profiles tag and route invocations so usage and cost can be attributed per application or team. Not "Use AWS Cost Explorer without any tagging.": Cost Explorer alone cannot split a shared model's spend across applications without attribution tags. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records who called the API, not per-application cost attribution. Not "Use model invocation logging.": Invocation logging stores content, not cost attribution. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: After launch, a team wants ongoing assurance of a generative feature's quality, catching regressions as prompts and models change. Which practice is MOST effective?

options.text: Log responses and run periodic automated evaluations on sampled production traffic, alerting on regressions.
Run one pre-launch test and never re-check.
Monitor only CPU and memory.
Wait for user complaints.

explanation: Response logging plus scheduled automated evaluation on samples gives continuous, data-driven quality monitoring. Not "Run one pre-launch test and never re-check.": A one-time test misses regressions introduced by later changes. Not "Monitor only CPU and memory.": Infrastructure metrics do not reveal generation-quality regressions. Not "Wait for user complaints.": Relying on complaints is reactive and lets defects reach users. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A mobile app's end users sign in and must then receive scoped, TEMPORARY AWS credentials to call Bedrock, with no AWS keys embedded in the app. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Use an Amazon Cognito user pool by itself.
Embed a shared IAM access key in the app.
Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to exchange the sign-in for temporary, scoped AWS credentials.
Create one IAM user per end user.

explanation: Identity pools federate authenticated users to temporary AWS credentials tied to an IAM role, with no embedded keys. Not "Use an Amazon Cognito user pool by itself.": A user pool authenticates users but does not itself vend AWS credentials; the identity pool provides AWS credentials. Not "Embed a shared IAM access key in the app.": Embedding long-lived keys in a distributed app is a serious security risk. Not "Create one IAM user per end user.": IAM users issue long-lived keys and do not scale or provide temporary access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: INTERNAL employees must authenticate through the corporate SAML identity provider to access Bedrock with temporary credentials (workforce SSO). Which solution is BEST?

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center with SAML federation to the corporate IdP.
Access keys distributed to employees.
An Amazon Cognito identity pool.
IAM users for each employee.

explanation: IAM Identity Center is the workforce SSO service that federates corporate identities to temporary AWS access. Not "Access keys distributed to employees.": Distributing long-lived keys is insecure and unmanageable. Not "An Amazon Cognito identity pool.": Cognito targets application/customer identities; workforce SSO via the corporate IdP is IAM Identity Center. Not "IAM users for each employee.": IAM users rely on long-lived keys and do not integrate with the corporate IdP. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A regulated company must call Bedrock from its VPC WITHOUT traffic traversing the public internet. Which solution is correct?

options.text: Set up VPC peering.
Route Bedrock calls through a NAT gateway.
Create VPC interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock.
Use an internet gateway with TLS.

explanation: Interface endpoints via PrivateLink keep traffic to Bedrock on the AWS network. Not "Set up VPC peering.": VPC peering connects VPCs to each other, not your VPC privately to the Bedrock service. Not "Route Bedrock calls through a NAT gateway.": A NAT gateway still sends traffic over the public internet. Not "Use an internet gateway with TLS.": TLS encrypts traffic but it still traverses the public internet. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An application in Account A must call Bedrock resources governed by Account B using temporary credentials and no shared long-lived keys. Which mechanism is correct?

options.text: Make the Bedrock resources public.
Use the same root user across both accounts.
Create an IAM role in Account B and have Account A assume it via AWS STS AssumeRole.
Share Account B's IAM access keys with Account A.

explanation: Cross-account role assumption provides scoped, temporary credentials without sharing long-lived keys. Not "Make the Bedrock resources public.": Public access removes the required access control. Not "Use the same root user across both accounts.": Sharing root credentials is a severe security violation. Not "Share Account B's IAM access keys with Account A.": Sharing long-lived keys is insecure and unmanageable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An agent's Lambda must use a third-party API key that has to be stored securely WITH automatic rotation and fine-grained access. Which service is BEST?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString.
A hard-coded constant in the function.
A plaintext environment variable.
AWS Secrets Manager.

explanation: Secrets Manager stores credentials with IAM-controlled access and supports built-in automatic rotation. Not "AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString.": Parameter Store can hold encrypted values but does not provide built-in managed rotation for arbitrary third-party secrets the way Secrets Manager does. Not "A hard-coded constant in the function.": Hard-coded secrets cannot be rotated and risk exposure. Not "A plaintext environment variable.": Plaintext secrets are insecure and cannot be rotated safely. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: Security policy requires that a specific IAM role be able to invoke ONLY one approved foundation model in Bedrock. How is this BEST enforced?

options.text: Allow all models and tell developers to use only the approved one.
Choose the model only in application code.
Write a least-privilege IAM policy that allows invoke actions only on the approved model's resource ARN.
Apply the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.

explanation: Scoping the policy to the specific model ARN technically restricts the role to that model. Not "Allow all models and tell developers to use only the appr…": A verbal rule is not a technical control. Not "Choose the model only in application code.": Application-side selection is not an access control and can be bypassed. Not "Apply the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.": That condition enforces that a guardrail is applied; it does not restrict which model the role may invoke. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A company must encrypt Bedrock-related data at rest using keys it can CONTROL, ROTATE, and AUDIT. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Rely on the default AWS owned key.
Store the data unencrypted for simplicity.
Use a client-side passphrase hard-coded in the app.
Encrypt with an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).

explanation: A customer managed key gives control over key policy and rotation, and CloudTrail audits its use. Not "Rely on the default AWS owned key.": AWS owned keys encrypt data but give the customer no control, rotation policy, or usage auditing. Not "Store the data unencrypted for simplicity.": Unencrypted data fails the requirement. Not "Use a client-side passphrase hard-coded in the app.": A hard-coded passphrase is insecure and not an auditable managed key. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A compliance team must ensure customer prompts are processed only within an approved Region and are NOT used to train the base models. Which statement and action are correct?

options.text: Accept that data may be processed globally.
Self-host the model, since only that prevents base-model training on your data.
Use Bedrock in the approved Region; it processes the data in that Region and does not use your prompts/outputs to train the base models.
File a support ticket to opt out, or your data trains the models by default.

explanation: Bedrock keeps inference data in the Region you call and does not use customer inputs/outputs to train base models. Not "Accept that data may be processed globally.": Inference data is processed in the Region you invoke, not globally. Not "Self-host the model, since only that prevents base-model …": Using Bedrock already prevents your data from training base models; self-hosting is unnecessary for that guarantee. Not "File a support ticket to opt out, or your data trains the…": No opt-out is required; Bedrock does not use your data to train base models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A team must filter harmful content (hate, insults, violence, sexual, misconduct) in BOTH prompts and responses, with adjustable strictness PER category. Which Guardrails feature is correct?

options.text: Word filters.
Stop sequences.
Content filters with configurable strength per harmful category.
Denied topics.

explanation: Content filters detect and block harmful categories in input and output with per-category strength settings. Not "Word filters.": Word filters block specific words/phrases, not graded harmful-content categories. Not "Stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not classify harmful content. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block specific subjects you define, not the built-in harmful-content categories. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A banking assistant must refuse a specific prohibited SUBJECT (individualized investment advice) even when users rephrase it in new ways. Which Guardrails feature is BEST?

options.text: Denied topics, defined with a description and examples.
Word filters listing banned terms.
Content filters.
The PII filter.

explanation: Denied topics block a subject by semantic description and examples, catching varied phrasings. Not "Word filters listing banned terms.": A keyword list misses rephrasings and is brittle for a whole subject. Not "Content filters.": Content filters target harmful categories, not an arbitrary business subject. Not "The PII filter.": The PII filter handles personal data, not topic restriction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: An assistant must ensure PII in model RESPONSES is masked or blocked before reaching users, as a managed guardrail control. Which feature is correct?

options.text: Denied topics.
Content filters.
The Guardrails sensitive information (PII) filter.
Run Amazon Comprehend on each response in custom code.

explanation: The PII filter detects and masks or blocks personal information in inputs and outputs. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not PII entities. Not "Content filters.": Content filters handle harmful categories, not PII masking. Not "Run Amazon Comprehend on each response in custom code.": Comprehend can detect PII but is a separate custom step, not the managed in-guardrail control the scenario asks for. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A public chatbot faces users trying to override its instructions and jailbreak it. Which Guardrails capability specifically detects these attempts?

options.text: Content filters for hate/violence.
Lowering the temperature.
The prompt attack filter.
Denied topics.

explanation: The prompt attack filter flags prompt injection and jailbreak inputs so they can be blocked. Not "Content filters for hate/violence.": Those categories do not target instruction-override attacks. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not detect prompt attacks. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not injection attempts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A brand must block an EXACT list of competitor names and specific profane terms from outputs. Which Guardrails feature is the BEST fit?

options.text: Content filters.
The PII filter.
Denied topics.
Word filters (a custom word/phrase list plus managed profanity).

explanation: Word filters block specific, exact terms such as competitor names and profanity. Not "Content filters.": Content filters address harmful categories, not a specific custom term list. Not "The PII filter.": The PII filter handles personal data, not competitor names. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics target whole semantic subjects, which is heavier than blocking an exact word list. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the guardrail itself should block responses NOT supported by the retrieved source or off-topic from the query, using a tunable threshold. Which capability fits?

options.text: Content filters.
The contextual grounding and relevance checks.
Word filters.
Denied topics.

explanation: These checks score grounding in the source and relevance to the query and can block low-scoring responses at a configured threshold. Not "Content filters.": Content filters target harmful content, not grounding. Not "Word filters.": Word filters block specific terms, not ungrounded responses. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not ungrounded answers within an allowed subject. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A self-managed pipeline calls a model hosted OUTSIDE Bedrock but wants to apply the same Bedrock guardrail policy to arbitrary text at chosen points. Which capability enables this?

options.text: Defining denied topics in the guardrail.
Inline guardrails only on Bedrock InvokeModel.
The ApplyGuardrail API.
Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: ApplyGuardrail evaluates input/output text against a guardrail independently of a Bedrock model call, covering external models and arbitrary points. Not "Defining denied topics in the guardrail.": Denied topics is a policy type, not the independent evaluation API. Not "Inline guardrails only on Bedrock InvokeModel.": Inline-only guardrails cannot cover text from a non-Bedrock model or arbitrary pipeline steps. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput is a capacity feature, unrelated to guardrail evaluation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A regulated insurer needs strong assurance that policy answers conform to its written rules, with VERIFIABLE logical checks rather than only probabilistic filtering. Which newer Guardrails capability fits?

options.text: The contextual grounding check.
Content filters.
Lowering the temperature.
Automated Reasoning checks.

explanation: Automated Reasoning checks use formal, logic-based verification against an encoded policy to validate responses. Not "The contextual grounding check.": Grounding checks whether a response is supported by provided source text, not formal verification against encoded policy rules. Not "Content filters.": Content filters handle harmful content, not policy conformance verification. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not verify outputs against policy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: Governance requires that EVERY InvokeModel and Converse call from many IAM roles apply a specific guardrail, enforced as efficiently as possible. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Manually set the guardrail in each application's config.
Add an IAM policy with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key to all roles that access Bedrock.
Store the guardrail ID in Parameter Store and fetch it per call.
Route all calls through a Lambda proxy that injects the guardrail.

explanation: The condition key centrally and efficiently enforces that the guardrail is applied across all relevant API calls. Not "Manually set the guardrail in each application's config.": Per-app configuration is not centrally enforced and is easy to miss. Not "Store the guardrail ID in Parameter Store and fetch it pe…": Per-call retrieval adds latency and maintenance. Not "Route all calls through a Lambda proxy that injects the g…": A proxy is a bottleneck and custom code to maintain, less efficient than the IAM condition. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: Compliance records must be stored so they CANNOT be altered or deleted for a mandated period, even by administrators or the root user. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: S3 versioning alone.
A bucket policy that denies deletes.
Amazon S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the retention period.
Amazon S3 Object Lock in governance mode.

explanation: Compliance mode enforces WORM immutability that no one, including root, can override until retention expires. Not "S3 versioning alone.": Versioning preserves versions but does not prevent deletion or enforce retention. Not "A bucket policy that denies deletes.": A bucket policy can be changed by administrators, so it is not immutable retention. Not "Amazon S3 Object Lock in governance mode.": Governance mode can be overridden by users with special permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability against administrators. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: An auditor must determine which IAM principals called which Bedrock APIs and when. Which service provides this trail?

options.text: AWS Config.
Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: CloudTrail records API calls with principal, action, and time. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration, not API caller activity. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures prompt/response content, not the account-wide API caller audit trail. Not "Amazon CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics are numeric aggregates, not caller identity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: For regulatory reconstruction, a company must retain the ACTUAL prompt and response content of every Bedrock call in immutable storage. Which combination is correct?

options.text: Rely on CloudWatch metrics.
Print prompts to the application console.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 and apply S3 Object Lock for the retention period.
Enable AWS CloudTrail only.

explanation: Invocation logging captures full content, and Object Lock makes the stored logs immutable for retention. Not "Rely on CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics do not store prompt or response text. Not "Print prompts to the application console.": Console output is not durable, complete, or immutable. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail only.": CloudTrail captures API metadata, not the full prompt/response content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A company wants to keep chat transcripts for analytics but is prohibited from RETAINING PII. What is the BEST approach before storage?

options.text: Lower the model temperature.
Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII.
Redact PII with Amazon Comprehend, then store the sanitized transcripts.
Store the raw transcripts unchanged.

explanation: Detecting and redacting PII before storage keeps useful analytics data while complying with the no-PII rule. Not "Lower the model temperature.": Temperature does not remove PII from stored text. Not "Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII.": Encryption protects data at rest but does not satisfy a rule against retaining PII at all. Not "Store the raw transcripts unchanged.": Storing raw PII violates the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: Stored embeddings and invocation logs contain sensitive data, and the security team must CONTROL and AUDIT the encryption keys. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Encrypt with AWS KMS customer managed keys and audit usage via key policies and CloudTrail.
Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.
Use one shared password stored in code.
Leave the data unencrypted for easy access.

explanation: Customer managed keys give control and rotation, and CloudTrail records key usage for auditing. Not "Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.": Public storage exposes the data and is the opposite of the requirement. Not "Use one shared password stored in code.": A hard-coded shared secret is insecure and not auditable. Not "Leave the data unencrypted for easy access.": Unencrypted sensitive data fails the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A user invokes their right to erasure. Their documents were ingested into a knowledge base whose embeddings live in a vector store. What must you do to FULLY remove their data?

options.text: Delete only the source files from Amazon S3.
Delete only the CloudWatch logs.
Rely on S3 Object Lock to expire the data.
Delete the source documents AND remove/re-sync them from the knowledge base so the corresponding vector embeddings are deleted.

explanation: Embeddings persist in the vector store until the knowledge base is updated, so both the source and the ingested vectors must be removed. Not "Delete only the source files from Amazon S3.": Deleting the source leaves the already-ingested embeddings in the vector store, so the data is not fully removed. Not "Delete only the CloudWatch logs.": Logs are unrelated to the embeddings retained in the vector store. Not "Rely on S3 Object Lock to expire the data.": Object Lock prevents deletion during retention, which is the opposite of fulfilling an erasure request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
